questions.question: What happens to the bread and wine in the Eucharist, and how is Christ present?
shared_ground: 'This is my body' and 'this is my blood' quoted or affirmed (excludes memorial, decides nothing among the other four)
Christ's body and blood are truly given or received in the Supper (shared by spiritual presence, sacramental union, real change, transubstantiation)
Calling the Eucharist the body and blood of Christ, or the bread of life (all realist positions)
The Supper must be received worthily; unworthy eating brings judgment
The Supper is done in remembrance of Christ's death (all five positions)
Christ's body is in heaven at the Father's right hand (all positions affirm the ascension)

positions.name: Memorial

defined.source: Huldrych Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles, Article 18 (1523)
defined.quote: the mass is not a sacrifice, but is a remembrance of the sacrifice and assurance of the salvation which Christ has given us.

defined.source: Baptist Faith and Message, Article VII (2000)
defined.quote: The Lord's Supper is a symbolic act of obedience whereby members of the church, through partaking of the bread and the fruit of the vine, memorialize the death of the Redeemer and anticipate His second coming.

defined.source: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths
defined.quote: a memorial of his suffering and death

positions.statement: The bread and wine are symbols that call Christ's death to mind; Christ's body and blood are neither present in them nor received through them.
positions.mark: The passage says the bread and wine only represent or remind of Christ's body and blood, and that nothing more than this remembrance is given in the rite.
positions.first_defined: Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles (1523); Baptist Faith and Message (1925, revised 2000)

positions.name: Spiritual presence

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 29.7 (1646)
defined.quote: the body and blood of Christ being then, not corporally or carnally, in, with, or under the bread and wine; yet, as really, but spiritually, present to the faith of believers in that ordinance

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXVIII (1571)
defined.quote: The Body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten, in the Supper, only after an heavenly and spiritual manner. And the mean whereby the Body of Christ is received and eaten in the Supper is Faith.

defined.source: Second London Baptist Confession, 30.7 (1689)
defined.quote: spiritually receive, and feed upon Christ crucified, and all the benefits of his death

defined.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: The body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten in the Supper, only after a heavenly and spiritual manner. And the mean whereby the body of Christ is received and eaten in the Supper is faith.

defined.source: Confession of Faith of the Evangelical United Brethren Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: partake of the body and blood of Christ in a spiritual manner until he comes

positions.statement: Believers truly receive Christ's body and blood in the Supper, but spiritually and by faith; the body is not in or under the bread, and unbelievers receive only the outward signs.
positions.mark: The passage says Christ's body is received only spiritually or by faith (not by the mouth), or that unbelievers who eat receive the sign but not the body.
positions.first_defined: Consensus Tigurinus (1549); Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571); Westminster Confession (1646)

first_uncertain.author: Severianus of Gabala
first_uncertain.text: Since the Lamb was offered, we also eat his body. Food is accustomed to be distributed into the body of the one who eats—clearly we eat his body spiritually. It is distributed into our body, and so we are flesh from his flesh and bone from his bones.

memorial.audited: Severianus on Ephesians: 'Since the Lamb was offered, we also eat his body... It is distributed into our body, and so we are flesh from his flesh and bone from his bones.' Believers eat Christ's body - the elements are not mere reminders.

spiritual-presence.quote: clearly we eat his body spiritually
spiritual-presence.audited: 'Clearly we eat his body spiritually. It is distributed into our body, and so we are flesh from his flesh and bone from his bones.' Reception of the body is expressly spiritual - this position's defining mark.

sacramental-union.quote: clearly we eat his body spiritually
sacramental-union.audited: The eating is spiritual ('clearly we eat his body spiritually'), not the oral reception of a true body present in, with, and under the bread by all who eat, worthy or unworthy.

first_uncertain.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

positions.name: Sacramental union

defined.source: Augsburg Confession, Article X (1530)
defined.quote: Of the Supper of the Lord they teach that the Body and Blood of Christ are truly present, and are distributed to those who eat the Supper of the Lord

defined.source: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration VII.35 (1577)
defined.quote: under the bread, with the bread, in the bread [the body of Christ is present and offered], are employed, is that by means of them the papistical transubstantiation may be rejected and the sacramental union of the unchanged essence of the bread and of the body of Christ indicated

positions.statement: Christ's true body and blood are present in, with and under the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine in their essence, and are received by the mouth by all who eat, worthy or unworthy.
positions.mark: The passage says the bread remains bread (keeps its nature or substance) while Christ's true body is present with it or given with it.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession, Article X (1530); Formula of Concord, Article VII (1577)

positions.name: Real change, manner undefined

defined.source: Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, Epiclesis
defined.quote: And make this bread the precious Body of Your Christ. ... And that which is in this cup the precious Blood of Your Christ. ... Changing them by Your Holy Spirit.

defined.source: Longer Catechism of St Philaret of Moscow, q. 340 (1830s)
defined.quote: the word transubstantiation is not to be taken to define the manner in which the bread and wine are changed into the Body and Blood of the Lord; for this none can understand but God

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1375
defined.quote: It is by the conversion of the bread and wine into Christ's body and blood that Christ becomes present in this sacrament.

defined.source: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, The Faith of the Church (text by V. C. Samuel, 1970)
defined.quote: During the service of the Holy Liturgy, the bread turns into the true flesh of the Son of God and the wine into the true blood of the Son of God.

defined.source: Assyrian Church of the East, Diocese of California, FAQ
defined.quote: The elements of bread and wine are transformed in the eucharistic prayer, in a mystical way, by the unseen action of the Holy Spirit who operates through the priest celebrating this most sacred action.

positions.statement: By God's action at the consecration the bread and wine are changed into, and become, Christ's body and blood, so that they are no longer simply bread and wine; how the change happens is not defined.
positions.mark: The passage says the bread and wine are changed, transformed or made into Christ's body and blood (a change in what they are), without saying how.
positions.first_defined: Prayed in the eastern epiclesis; stated by the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) and, for Catholics, Lateran IV (1215) and Trent (1551)

first_uncertain.author: Epiphanius of Salamis
first_uncertain.text: May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ—a divine body, a body that brings salvation to souls and bodies. And may what has been mixed in this cup into one reality become the blood of Christ, the blood of the new covenant, blood that brings salvation to us. Grant this so that we may wholly share in your mysteries in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter.

memorial.quote: May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ—a divine body, a body that brings salvation to souls and bodies
memorial.audited: Epiphanius, Greek Anaphora: 'May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ - a divine body, a body that brings salvation to souls and bodies. And may what has been mixed in this cup into one reality become the blood of Christ.' The church prays for the elements to BECOME the body and blood - the opposite of symbols that only remind.

spiritual-presence.quote: May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ… and may … become the blood of Christ.
spiritual-presence.audited: The body is located in the changed element itself: the bread is prayed to 'be changed and become the body of Christ.' This position requires that the body be absent from the bread and received only by faith.

sacramental-union.quote: May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ
sacramental-union.audited: 'May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ' denies the union's mark outright: the bread does not remain bread in its essence alongside the body; it becomes the body.

eucharistic-change.quote: May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ
eucharistic-change.audited: 'May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ... and may what has been mixed in this cup into one reality become the blood of Christ, the blood of the new covenant' - a change in what the elements are, prayed for without any account of how. This position's exact mark.

first_uncertain.attribution_note: Authorship and date of this anaphora are uncertain.

positions.name: Transubstantiation

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 13, Canon 2 (1551)
defined.quote: that wonderful and singular conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the Body, and of the whole substance of the wine into the Blood-the species Only of the bread and wine remaining-which conversion indeed the Catholic Church most aptly calls Transubstantiation

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 13, ch. 1 (1551)
defined.quote: He be, in many other places, sacramentally present to us in his own substance, by a manner of existing, which, though we can scarcely express it in words

positions.statement: The whole substance of the bread and wine is converted into the substance of Christ's body and blood, while the appearances (everything the senses or any physical test can detect) remain; so the change is not physical or chemical.
positions.mark: The passage distinguishes what the bread is (now Christ's body) from what it still appears to be to the senses (bread), saying the appearance remains while the reality is changed.
positions.first_defined: Fourth Lateran Council (1215); Council of Trent, Session 13 (1551)

passages.author: Justin Martyr
passages.text: We call this food the Eucharist, and no one may share in it except the person who believes that what we teach is true, who has been washed in the bath for the forgiveness of sins and for rebirth, and who lives as Christ handed down. For we do not receive these as common bread or common drink. Rather, just as Jesus Christ our Savior was made flesh through the word of God and took on flesh and blood for our salvation, so we have been taught that the food sanctified by the word of prayer — the food from which our flesh and blood are nourished through transformation — is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh. The apostles, in the memoirs they composed — which are called Gospels — handed down that Jesus took bread, gave thanks, and said, "Do this in remembrance of me; this is my body" (Luke 22:19-20). In the same way he took the cup, gave thanks, and said, "This is my blood" (L

memorial.quote: the food sanctified by the word of prayer...is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh
memorial.audited: Justin, First Apology 66: 'we do not receive these as common bread or common drink... the food sanctified by the word of prayer - the food from which our flesh and blood are nourished through transformation - IS the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh.' The elements are identified as Christ's flesh and blood, not symbols that only call his death to mind.

spiritual-presence.quote: we do not receive these as common bread or common drink... the food ... is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh
spiritual-presence.audited: Justin locates the body in the food itself: the sanctified food IS Christ's flesh and blood, and by it 'our flesh and blood are nourished through transformation' - a bodily reception of the body in the food. This position requires reception only spiritually or by faith, with the body not in or under the bread.

passages.author: Justin Martyr
passages.text: The offering of fine flour, gentlemen, was said to be presented on behalf of those being cleansed from leprosy. It served as a type of the bread of the Eucharist, which Jesus Christ our Lord commanded us to perform in remembrance of the passion he endured on behalf of those being cleansed in their souls from all human wickedness, so that we might at once give thanks to God for having brought the world into being with all that it contains for the sake of humanity, for having freed us from the evil in which we were ensnared, and for having brought the rulers and authorities to nothing through the suffering that came to pass according to his will. Therefore, concerning the sacrifices you were offering at that time, God says — as I mentioned before — through Malachi, one of the twelve: "I have no pleasure in you," says the Lord, "and I will not accept your sacrifices from your hands. For fro

memorial.quote: the bread of the Eucharist and likewise the cup of the Eucharist

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: But how elegantly divine wisdom arranged the order of prayer! After heavenly things, that is, after God's name, God's will, and God's kingdom, it also made room for earthly necessities in our petition. For the Lord had commanded: "Seek first the kingdom, and then these things will also be added to you" (Matthew 6:33). Nevertheless, we should understand "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11) spiritually rather than carnally. For Christ is our bread, because Christ is life, and the bread of life. "I am," he says, "the bread of life" (John 6:35), and a little before that: "The bread is the word of the living God, who comes down from heaven" (John 6:33). Then too his body is reckoned in the bread: "This is my body" (Matthew 26:26). Therefore, by asking for daily bread, we ask for permanence in Christ and indivisibility from his body. But because this phrase is also admitted carnal

memorial.quote: his body is reckoned in the bread: 'This is my body'
memorial.audited: Tertullian, On Prayer 6 - its subject is the Lord's Prayer, but the eucharistic premise is stated as doctrine: 'his body is reckoned in the bread: This is my body (Matthew 26:26). Therefore, by asking for daily bread, we ask for permanence in Christ and indivisibility from his body.' A body reckoned IN the bread contradicts the claim that the body is neither present in the elements nor received through them.

passages.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea
passages.text: Since the Spirit is the bread of the coming age, which is a food of life for the one approaching the age, and 'the bread which I will give' to you is 'my flesh for the life of the world' (John 6:51), and the blood is living in the body; and for this reason Moses said 'the life of all flesh' (Leviticus 17:11) regarding 'the blood' as being unified by blood. He clearly distinguished the type by the name of the truth, saying: 'this is my body'; and for this reason he named the types with the names of the truth, so that they would not be trivialized by what is seen, but would marvel at the power. Thus, eating and drinking showed the participation which would not have occurred without a body; for if the divine power had not been joined to a body and unified by blood, we would not have had communion through it to God.

memorial.quote: eating and drinking showed the participation which would not have occurred without a body; for if the divine power had not been joined to a body and unified by blood, we would not have had communion through it to God
memorial.audited: ATTRIBUTION: a catena fragment; the Greek opens 'τύπον δὲ ποιεῖ Ἀπολινάριος' ('Apollinaris makes [it] a type'), so a compiler is reporting him. It affirms 'this is my body' and says the types bear the names of the truth 'so that they would not be belittled for what is seen, but marvelled at for the power', which excludes a mere reminder. The English section omits the opening clause on 'participation in the body and blood accomplished in spirit for believers'.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Evagrius Ponticus
passages.text: They wear away the flesh of Christ and squander the blood, regarding it as common; for he says, 'He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day' (John 6:54).

memorial.quote: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life
memorial.audited: Evagrius, Scholia on Proverbs, rebukes those who 'wear away the flesh of Christ and squander the blood, regarding it as common; for he says, He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life (John 6:54).' The rebuke presupposes that what is eaten is truly Christ's flesh and blood - not common - and that eating it gives eternal life: more than remembrance is given in the rite.

passages.author: Severianus of Gabala
passages.text: Since the Lamb was offered, we also eat his body. Food is accustomed to be distributed into the body of the one who eats—clearly we eat his body spiritually. It is distributed into our body, and so we are flesh from his flesh and bone from his bones.

memorial.audited: Severianus on Ephesians: 'Since the Lamb was offered, we also eat his body... It is distributed into our body, and so we are flesh from his flesh and bone from his bones.' Believers eat Christ's body - the elements are not mere reminders.

spiritual-presence.quote: clearly we eat his body spiritually
spiritual-presence.audited: 'Clearly we eat his body spiritually. It is distributed into our body, and so we are flesh from his flesh and bone from his bones.' Reception of the body is expressly spiritual - this position's defining mark.

sacramental-union.audited: The eating is spiritual ('clearly we eat his body spiritually'), not the oral reception of a true body present in, with, and under the bread by all who eat, worthy or unworthy.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Epiphanius of Salamis
passages.text: May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ—a divine body, a body that brings salvation to souls and bodies. And may what has been mixed in this cup into one reality become the blood of Christ, the blood of the new covenant, blood that brings salvation to us. Grant this so that we may wholly share in your mysteries in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter.

memorial.quote: May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ—a divine body, a body that brings salvation to souls and bodies
memorial.audited: Epiphanius, Greek Anaphora: 'May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ - a divine body, a body that brings salvation to souls and bodies. And may what has been mixed in this cup into one reality become the blood of Christ.' The church prays for the elements to BECOME the body and blood - the opposite of symbols that only remind.

spiritual-presence.audited: The body is located in the changed element itself: the bread is prayed to 'be changed and become the body of Christ.' This position requires that the body be absent from the bread and received only by faith.

eucharistic-change.audited: 'May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ... and may what has been mixed in this cup into one reality become the blood of Christ, the blood of the new covenant' - a change in what the elements are, prayed for without any account of how. This position's exact mark.

passages.author: Epiphanius of Salamis
passages.text: to the apostles, saying, “Take, eat; this is my body, which is being broken for you for the forgiveness of sins.” In the same way, after supper, he took the cup, having mixed it from two elements—from the fruit of the vine and water—sealed the cup of immortality, and gave it to his disciples, saying, “Drink from it, all of you; this is my blood of the new covenant, which is being poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins.”

memorial.quote: this is my body, which is being broken for you for the forgiveness of sins
memorial.audited: The anaphora speaks the institution words over the elements as the church's own prayer: 'Take, eat; this is my body, which is being broken for you for the forgiveness of sins... Drink from it, all of you; this is my blood of the new covenant, which is being poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins.' The gifts are given FOR the forgiveness of sins - more is given in the rite than a reminder of Christ's death.

passages.attribution_note: Authorship and date of this anaphora are uncertain.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: That Christ is life and life-giving. From the letter to the Corinthians: “I speak as to the wise; judge what I say. The cup of blessing that we bless — is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break — is it not a sharing in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we the many are one body; for we all partake of the one bread.” (1 Corinthians 10:15–17) Human flesh, as far as its own nature goes, would not be life-giving, nor would human blood if it were common and by itself; but Christ’s body and precious blood give life — and being able to give life belongs to God alone…

memorial.quote: The cup of blessing that we bless — is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break — is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?
memorial.audited: Cyril comments on 1 Cor 10 that 'Christ's body and precious blood give life', so the sharing is a real giving of the body, not a reminder only.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: The Lord gives thanks when he takes the cup — that is, in the form of prayer he converses with God the Father, declaring him as it were sharer and co-approver of the life-giving blessing that will be given to us, and at the same time giving us a pattern first to give thanks and thus to break the bread and distribute it. That is why we too, setting what was said before God’s face, beg intently that it be remolded for us into the spiritual blessing, so that by partaking of them we may be sanctified bodily and spiritually. He said demonstratively, “This is my body” (Matthew 26:26–28) and “This is my blood,” so that you may not think what appears is a mere type, but that through some ineffable energy of the God who can do all things what has been brought forward is truly changed into the body and blood of Christ — of which, when we partake, we take in Christ’s life-giving and sanctifying pow

memorial.quote: through some ineffable energy of the God who can do all things what has been brought forward is truly changed into the body and blood of Christ
memorial.audited: 'Truly changed into the body and blood of Christ' (μεταποιεῖσθαι εἰς σῶμα καὶ αἷμα Χριστοῦ κατὰ τὸ ἀληθές), and 'that you may not think what appears is a mere type', rule out a sign only.

spiritual-presence.quote: we take in Christ's life-giving and sanctifying power...mingled in us...through his holy flesh and precious blood
spiritual-presence.audited: What is set forth is 'truly changed into the body and blood of Christ' and is seen as 'flesh and blood lying before us on the holy tables', so the body is in what is received, not only by faith; the grader's quote was not the deciding line.

sacramental-union.quote: what has been brought forward is truly changed into the body and blood of Christ
sacramental-union.audited: 'What has been brought forward is truly changed (μεταποιεῖσθαι) into the body and blood' denies that the offerings stay what they were.

eucharistic-change.quote: what has been brought forward is truly changed into the body and blood of Christ
eucharistic-change.audited: 'Through some ineffable energy of God... what has been brought forward is truly changed into the body and blood of Christ'; the Greek μεταποιεῖσθαι... κατὰ τὸ ἀληθές is faithfully rendered, and 'ineffable' leaves the manner undefined.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: I myself receive by faith the flesh of the life-giving Word which gives life; therefore the Savior said, 'Those who eat from this bread will never taste death for eternity' (John 6:51); those who…

memorial.quote: I myself receive by faith the flesh of the life-giving Word which gives life
memorial.audited: ATTRIBUTION: the 'Dialogus cum Nestorio' is of doubtful authenticity as a work of Cyril. 'I myself receive by faith the flesh of the life-giving Word' (πίστει μεταλαμβάνω τὴν... ζωοποιοῦσαν σάρκα) says the flesh itself is received, which is more than a reminder.

passages.attribution_note: Widely doubted as Cyril's; some lines are given to Nestorius.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Since after the resurrection Christ was about to be taken up to the Father with a body, for this reason he has given us his own body and blood, so that his flesh and blood, dwelling in us, may make us holy and sharers of immortality (Matthew 26:26–28).

memorial.quote: he has given us his own body and blood, so that his flesh and blood, dwelling in us, may make us holy
memorial.audited: 'He has given us his own body and blood, so that his flesh and blood, dwelling in us, may make us holy' says the body is truly given, which excludes a sign only.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Cyril: That one who has become a sharer in Christ — by partaking of his holy flesh and blood — must also have his mind and love to go forward through inward achievements, understanding well what concerns him, he hinted at once by saying that head must be eaten with the feet and the inward parts. (Ex 12:9; Jn 6:53-56)

memorial.quote: by partaking of his holy flesh and blood
memorial.audited: 'One who has become a sharer in Christ by partaking of his holy flesh and blood' says the flesh and blood are truly partaken, more than a reminder.

passages.author: Ammonius of Alexandria
passages.text: As if the matter were contrary to nature they disbelieve; as soulish they do not understand the Lord's spiritual body. He does not speak of eating flesh, but of sharing in the mysteries.

memorial.audited: Ammonius on John: the critics 'do not understand the Lord's spiritual body. He does not speak of eating flesh, but of sharing in the mysteries.' A carnal eating is denied, but a real sharing in the mysteries is affirmed - a participation given in the rite, which this position denies ('nothing more than remembrance').

spiritual-presence.quote: He does not speak of eating flesh, but of sharing in the mysteries
spiritual-presence.audited: 'They do not understand the Lord's SPIRITUAL body. He does not speak of eating flesh, but of sharing in the mysteries.' The body is spiritual and the reception a sharing in mysteries, not an eating of flesh by the mouth - this position's mark.

sacramental-union.quote: He does not speak of eating flesh, but of sharing in the mysteries.
sacramental-union.audited: The denial is express: 'He does not speak of eating flesh.' Sacramental union requires the true body, present with the bread, to be received by the mouth by all who eat; Ammonius removes the mouth-eating of the body itself.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

questions.question: Is the Eucharist a sacrifice, and if so, of what kind?
shared_ground: Christ's sacrifice on the cross was once for all and complete (all positions affirm this)
The Supper remembers or proclaims Christ's death
Thanksgiving and praise are offered at the Eucharist (praise and propitiatory positions both affirm it)
Calling the Eucharist an 'offering' or 'sacrifice' with no statement of what is offered or for what purpose (decides between no-sacrifice and the others only)
Malachi 1:11 'pure offering' applied to Christian worship without further specification

positions.name: Not a sacrifice

defined.source: Huldrych Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles, Article 18 (1523)
defined.quote: the mass is not a sacrifice, but is a remembrance of the sacrifice and assurance of the salvation which Christ has given us.

positions.statement: The Supper is a remembrance of Christ's once-for-all sacrifice and is not itself a sacrifice in any sense.
positions.mark: The passage says the Supper is not a sacrifice at all, only a remembrance.
positions.first_defined: Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles (1523)

positions.name: Sacrifice of praise and commemoration only

defined.source: Apology of the Augsburg Confession, XXIV.19 (1531)
defined.quote: The other species is the eucharistic sacrifice, which does not merit the remission of sins or reconciliation, but is rendered by those who have been reconciled, in order that we may give thanks

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 29.2 (1646)
defined.quote: In this sacrament, Christ is not offered up to his Father; nor any real sacrifice made at all, for remission of sins of the quick or dead; but only a commemoration of that one offering up of himself

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXXI (1571)
defined.quote: Wherefore the sacrifices of Masses, in the which it was commonly said, that the Priest did offer Christ for the quick and the dead, to have remission of pain or guilt, were blasphemous fables

positions.statement: The Supper includes a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving and commemorates Christ's sacrifice, but Christ is not offered to God in it and it obtains no forgiveness for the living or the dead.
positions.mark: The passage limits the Eucharistic offering to praise, thanksgiving or remembrance, denying that Christ is offered or that it obtains forgiveness for anyone.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession XXIV and Apology XXIV (1530-31); Thirty-Nine Articles XXXI (1563/71); Westminster 29.2 (1646)

first_states.author: Tertullian
first_states.text: For this is the spiritual sacrifice that has abolished the old sacrifices. “What use to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?” God says. “I am full of burnt offerings of rams, and I do not want the fat of lambs and the blood of bulls and goats. For who has required these things from your hands?” (Isaiah 1:11–12). What God has sought instead, the gospel teaches. “The hour is coming,” Jesus says, “when the true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For God is spirit, and so He requires such worshippers” (John 4:23–24). We are the true worshippers and the true priests, who pray in the Spirit and in the Spirit sacrifice prayer as the victim proper to God and acceptable to Him—the very victim He has required and provided for Himself. passages.author: Irenaeus
passages.text: The Church's offering, which the Lord commanded to be offered throughout the world, is regarded as a pure sacrifice before God and is accepted by Him; God does not need a sacrifice from us, but the one who offers is glorified in the very act of offering, provided his gift is accepted. Gifts presented to a king demonstrate honor and affection, and the Lord, desiring us to offer in all simplicity and innocence, taught this when He said: when you bring your gift to the altar and remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, go first and be reconciled to your brother, and then return to offer your gift (Matthew 5:23-24). passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: In the same way, many people think that on fast days they should not take part in the prayers of the sacrifices, because the fast day must be ended when the body of the Lord has been received. Does the Eucharist, then, undo a service devoted to God, or does it bind us more closely to God? Will your fast day not be more solemn if you also stand at the altar of God? When the body of the Lord has been received and reserved, both things are preserved: participation in the sacrifice and performance of the duty. If the fast day takes its name from a military example, for we are also God's army, then surely no joy or sorrow that comes upon the camp breaks up the soldiers' watches. For joy will carry out the teaching more willingly, and sorrow more carefully.

no-sacrifice.audited: Tertullian, On Prayer 19, on the fast-day question: Christians stay away from 'the prayers of the sacrifices' because receiving the Lord's body ends the fast; 'When the body of the Lord has been received and reserved, both things are preserved: participation in the sacrifice and performance of the duty.' passages.author: Origen of Alexandria
passages.text: With God permitting, then, and secondly the bishops, and thirdly the presbyters and the people too, I will speak again of what is stirring me at this point. The offering is always made to God Almighty through Jesus Christ, as offering his divinity to the Father. Let the offering not be made twice, but to God through God.

no-sacrifice.audited: Kept. In a liturgical setting (bishops, presbyters, people) Origen says 'the offering is always made to God Almighty through Jesus Christ' (Greek Ἀεὶ προσφορὰ γίνεται Θεῷ παντοκράτορι διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ), calling the eucharistic prosphora an offering to God; the English is faithful. The year given is Origen's death; the Dialogue dates c. 245.

no-sacrifice.audited: Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church 17: the schismatic 'dares to set up another altar, to make another prayer with unlawful words, to profane the truth of the Lord's victim through false sacrifices.' 'False sacrifices' profane 'the truth of the Lord's victim' - the contrast presupposes the Church's altar has the true sacrifice of the Lord as victim.

passages.text: And yet he received him alive and brought him down unharmed. How then did he not spare him? The sword did not stain the boy's throat, it did not cut his neck—yet it is a sacrifice even without blood. The initiated know what this means. no-sacrifice.audited: Chrysostom, On Eustathius 4, on Isaac: 'yet it is a sacrifice even without blood. The initiated know what this means. And that sacrifice was made without blood precisely because it was going to be a type of THIS ONE.' The bloodless sacrifice of Isaac prefigured 'this one' - the bloodless sacrifice known to the initiated, the church's own rite. The Supper is a (bloodless) sacrifice.

passages.author: Augustine of Hippo
passages.text: Since this is so, we should not think that anything reaches the dead for whom we are caring except what we solemnly pray for them through the sacrifices of the altar, of prayers, and of alms. Yet these do not benefit all for whom they are offered, but only those for whom, while they lived, provision was made that they might benefit. But because we cannot discern who these are, we ought to offer them for all the baptized, so that none of those to whom these benefits can and should reach may be passed over. For it is better that these things be in excess for those whom they neither harm nor help than that they be lacking for those whom they help. Still, each person does these things more diligently for his own dear ones, so that the same may be done for him by his own. Whatever is spent on burying a body, however, is not a safeguard of salvation but a service of human kindness, according t

no-sacrifice.quote: what we solemnly pray for them through the sacrifices of the altar
no-sacrifice.audited: Augustine, Care for the Dead 22: 'we should not think that anything reaches the dead for whom we are caring except what we solemnly pray for them THROUGH THE SACRIFICES OF THE ALTAR, of prayers, and of alms.' Obtaining benefit for the dead is exactly what this position denies.

propitiatory-sacrifice.quote: what we solemnly pray for them through the sacrifices of the altar

passages.text: Cyril: So then the matter is fruit-bearing, O Palladius, and a mystical word has also been woven for it, I think, carrying the riddle up unto Emmanuel, and unto us ourselves; and I will speak again as I am able. For when the holy and true tent has been shown in this world—that is, the Church—Christ conspicuous in it many-formedly and all but from us and for us is brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father, a ransom and exchange of the life of all, one worth-all. For when the Only-begotten has become human as one from us, he has brought himself forward to God and Father, as some firstfruit and firstling of the human nature fragrant in sanctification, existing naturally and essentially, according as he is thought and is God, and again having been mixed in through the human. And being one also himself, he was being written according to many manners, as at least in the bringing-for

no-sacrifice.quote: Christ conspicuous in it many-formedly and all but from us and for us is brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father
no-sacrifice.audited: Kept. 'Christ will be brought forward toward us and for us, being sacrificed mystically in the holy tents' (Greek μυστικῶς ἱερουργούμενος ἐν ταῖς ἁγίαις σκηναῖς), with a daily offering in the Church.

sacrifice-of-praise.quote: brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father, a ransom and exchange of the life of all
sacrifice-of-praise.audited: Kept. In the Church 'Christ ... from us and for us is brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father' (Greek ὡς ἱερὸν προσάγεται θύμα τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρί), so Christ himself is offered.

propitiatory-sacrifice.quote: Christ ... is brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father, a ransom and exchange of the life of all
propitiatory-sacrifice.audited: Kept. Christ is named as the victim offered in the churches, 'from us and for us ... a sacred victim to God and Father, a ransom and exchange of the life of all', and 'being sacrificed mystically in the holy tents' daily; Greek checked and faithful (ὡς ἱερὸν προσάγεται θύμα; μυστικῶς ἱερουργούμενος). Note the first clause carries Cyril's hedge μονονουχί ('all but'); the later clause does not.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Cyril: …for we approach the holy things, for no other grace, than so as to share the holy Christ through the unspeakable and spiritual sacrifice. And the vessels serving the sacrifices are also thoroughly cleansed, so that they may not become for some other, nor may the things having liturgized for the sacred be carried under to humans’ needs. And the law has been kept, and is saved in churches. And that being blessed is fitting for those playing-the-man, the law will clarify again saying: ‘Every male among the priests will eat them.’ (Leviticus 6:30)

no-sacrifice.quote: share the holy Christ through the unspeakable and spiritual sacrifice
no-sacrifice.audited: Kept. 'We approach the holy things ... so as to share the holy Christ through the unspeakable and spiritual sacrifice' (Greek διά τε τῆς ἀπορρήτου καὶ πνευματικῆς θυσίας) calls the communion rite a sacrifice.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Cyril: …and, having offered up the praise together with the perfect, he departs from the still more mystical, and is barred from the sacrifice upon Christ. no-sacrifice.audited: Kept. The catechumen joins the praise but 'departs from the still more mystical, and is barred from the sacrifice upon Christ' (Greek θυσίας εἴργεται τῆς ἐπὶ Χριστῷ); the rite catechumens are barred from is the Eucharist, and it is called a sacrifice.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Cyril: But whether then in churches according to multitude the victim should be brought near by us, or whether then it should be done in other places, and somehow each one, or also somehow according to two, and three, and still more, undistinguished is the standing of those accustomed to hymn-speak, and having run together unto this; for, together with those already cleansed through the holy baptism, the one still a catechumen also joins in offering up the victim of praise (Psalm 116:13) (Acts 4:32);

A victim - even a victim of praise - is offered; a sacrifice in some sense exists, which this position denies in every sense.

questions.question: What authority does the bishop of Rome hold over the whole Church?
shared_ground: Peter was a leading apostle, named first in the lists
Peter and Paul taught and died in Rome; Rome is an apostolic church
Rome is an important church whose faith is praised
Communion between churches, including with Rome, matters

first_states.author: Irenaeus
first_states.text: The apostolic plan stands revealed throughout the whole world; it is present for all who wish to see the truth to behold in every church. We can enumerate those whom the apostles instituted as bishops in the churches, along with their successions down to us — men who taught nothing of the kind, nor knew it, the very thing these people rave about. If the apostles had known hidden mysteries, which they taught separately and secretly to the perfect, they would have handed them over especially to those to whom they also entrusted the churches themselves. They wanted those they left as successors to be very strong and irreproachable in all things, so that by handing over their own place of teaching great benefit would come to those who act rightly, but the greatest calamity to those who fall away. Since it would be far too long to enumerate the successions of all the churches in a volume of t

no-special-authority.quote: to this church, because of its more powerful principality, every church must convene
no-special-authority.audited: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3: Rome is 'the greatest, most ancient, and universally known church, founded and established at Rome by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul... For to this church, because of its more powerful principality, every church must convene.' One church holds a superior principality to which all others must resort - not an equality without rank.

primacy-of-honour.quote: to this church, because of its more powerful principality, every church must convene
primacy-of-honour.audited: Rome's first place is affirmed - 'because of its more powerful principality, every church must convene' to it - and its ground is given: Rome is 'the greatest, most ancient, and universally known church,' founded by Peter and Paul, in which the apostles' tradition 'has always been preserved by those who come from everywhere.' No governing power over other bishops (judging, deposing, binding) is claimed or exercised, and the rank is not grounded in a grant to Peter's successor. First rank without jurisdiction, grounded in the church's foundation and antiquity rather than in Christ's grant to Peter.

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 2 (1870)
defined.quote: Therefore whoever succeeds to the chair of Peter obtains by the institution of Christ himself, the primacy of Peter over the whole church.

defined.source: Council of Florence, Laetentur Caeli (1439)
defined.quote: to him was committed in blessed Peter the full power of tending, ruling and governing the whole church

positions.statement: By Christ's institution, the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor holds full and immediate power to govern the whole Church.
positions.mark: The passage says Rome's bishop, as Peter's successor, has authority (not only honour) over all churches, such as to judge, depose or bind other bishops, by Christ's grant.
positions.first_defined: Council of Florence (1439); First Vatican Council (1870)

positions.name: Infallibility of solemn papal definitions

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (1870)
defined.quote: when the Roman pontiff speaks EX CATHEDRA, that is, when, in the exercise of his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole church, he possesses ... that infallibility which the divine Redeemer willed his church to enjoy

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (1870)
defined.quote: such definitions of the Roman pontiff are of themselves, and not by the consent of the church, irreformable.

positions.statement: When the bishop of Rome solemnly defines a doctrine of faith or morals for the whole Church, he cannot err, and the definition binds without the Church's later consent.
positions.mark: The passage says a Roman bishop's doctrinal decision cannot be in error, or is final in itself without needing a council's or the churches' acceptance.

passages.text: They insisted that the men they were leaving behind as successors be thoroughly blameless and irreproachable in every respect, so that great benefit would come to those who would act in their place of teaching, while the greatest calamity would befall those who fell away. But because it would take far too long to list the successions of every church in a work of this scope, we will set forth the tradition that comes from the Apostles and the faith proclaimed to humanity, which has reached us through the succession of bishops from the most glorious two Apostles, Peter and Paul, who founded and established the church at Rome. By doing so we confound all those who, in any manner — whether through self-pleasing evil, empty glory, blindness, or bad judgment — gather in any way other than what is fitting. For every church must convene to this church on account of its more powerful principality

no-special-authority.quote: For every church must convene to this church on account of its more powerful principality
no-special-authority.audited: The fuller window of the same text: 'For every church must convene to this church on account of its more powerful principality; that is, the faithful from everywhere must come together here, because in this church the tradition that comes from the Apostles has always been preserved.' A superior principality over the churches is asserted - equality without rank is contradicted.

primacy-of-honour.quote: For every church must convene to this church on account of its more powerful principality

The 'must' is agreement in the preserved apostolic faith (the passage's purpose is to 'confound all those who... gather otherwise than is fitting'), grounded in Rome's foundation, antiquity, and custody of the tradition - a first place to which all resort, with no governing power over other bishops claimed. Primacy of honour's shape.

passages.author: Irenaeus
passages.text: The plan of the Apostles stands open to view in every church throughout the world, for all who truly desire to see it; we can trace the bishops appointed by the Apostles and their unbroken succession down to our own day, and none of them ever taught the fancies these people now proclaim. If the Apostles had possessed secret mysteries, reserved for a select few and taught in private, they would surely have entrusted them above all to those to whom they also committed the care of the churches. They wanted those successors to be steadfast and blameless in everything, so that their right stewardship of the apostolic office would bring great benefit, while their failure would bring utter disaster. But to list the succession of every church would swell this work beyond measure; therefore we set forth the tradition of that greatest and most ancient church, known to all, which the two most glori

no-special-authority.quote: For every church must agree with this church — that is, with the faithful everywhere — because in it the tradition from the Apostles has been preserved without interruption

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: If you want to put your curiosity to better use for your own salvation, then make the rounds of the apostolic churches. In those churches the very chairs of the apostles still preside in their original places, and their authentic letters are read aloud, echoing each apostle's voice and preserving his likeness. Is Achaia nearby? You have Corinth. Not far from Macedonia? You have Philippi and the Thessalonians. Able to reach Asia? You have Ephesus. If you border Italy, you have Rome, from which authority is also close at hand for us. What a blessed church! The apostles poured out their entire teaching there with their own blood; Peter matched the Lord's passion there; Paul was crowned with John's death there; and the apostle John, after being plunged into boiling oil and suffering no harm, was exiled to an island. Let us see what he learned and taught when he contended with the African chu

no-special-authority.quote: If you border Italy, you have Rome, from which authority is also close at hand for us.

passages.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
passages.text: And when the blessed Polycarp visited Rome in the time of Anicetus, though they had some small disagreements with one another about other matters, they immediately made peace, not being eager to quarrel with one another over this point. For neither could Anicetus persuade Polycarp not to observe the fast, since Polycarp had always observed it with John the disciple of our Lord and the rest of the apostles with whom he had associated; nor could Polycarp persuade Anicetus to observe it, since Anicetus said he was bound to hold to the custom of the bishops before him. And since matters stood thus, they shared communion with one another; and in the church Anicetus yielded the Eucharist to Polycarp, clearly out of respect, and they parted from one another in peace, with the whole church—both those who observed the fast and those who did not—holding peace.

primacy-of-jurisdiction.audited: Irenaeus's letter to Victor on Polycarp and Anicetus: 'neither could Anicetus persuade Polycarp not to observe the fast... nor could Polycarp persuade Anicetus to observe it, since Anicetus said he was bound to hold to the custom of the bishops before him. And since matters stood thus, they shared communion with one another; and in the church Anicetus yielded the Eucharist to Polycarp, clearly out of respect.' Rome's bishop neither commands nor binds another church's apostolic practice; the difference is settled by mutual tolerance, equality, and communion - the opposite of full immediate governing power in act.

passages.author: Cyprian
passages.text: A brief look at these matters makes long arguments unnecessary; the truth sums itself up in a way faith grasps at once. The Lord says to Peter, "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of the underworld will not conquer it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven: whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven" (Matt 16:18–19). After the resurrection he tells him again, "Feed my sheep" (John 21:17), and he builds his Church on this one man, entrusting his flock to his care. True, the risen Lord gives all the apostles equal authority — "As the Father sent me, so I send you. A primacy given by Christ's own decree exists - ministers are not all equal without God-given rank.

primacy-of-honour.quote: he builds his Church on this one man, entrusting his flock to his care... decreeing by his own authority that this unity must spring from one source
primacy-of-honour.audited: The primacy's ground is Christ himself: 'decreeing BY HIS OWN AUTHORITY that this unity must spring from one source... the primacy is given to Peter,' with the whole flock entrusted to his care ('Feed my sheep'). no-special-authority.quote: He builds the Church upon one man...the beginning proceeds from unity, so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one
no-special-authority.audited: Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church 4: 'He builds the Church upon one man... to make unity manifest, he arranged by his own authority that the origin of this same unity should begin from one. Nature’s order is overcome; for he willed, he was able, he came down, he saved — all things run together for God. Today the One who is is born, and the One who is becomes what he was not. Being God, he becomes human without leaving off being God. He did not become human by departing from deity, nor become God by climbing up from humanity. Being Word, he became flesh without suffering change; his nature remained unchanged.” (Malachi 4:2) He adds: “He who sits on a high and lifted throne is laid in a manger. The untouchable, simple, bodiless one is wrapped by human hands. He who breaks the bonds of sin is tangled in swaddling cloths.” (Isaiah 6:1)

christotokos.quote: Being God, he becomes human without leaving off being God. He did not become human by departing from deity
christotokos.audited: Borderline but met: said 'of the holy virgin', 'Today the One who is is born ... Being God, he becomes human' says God was born of her. ATTRIBUTION: Cyril quotes these as John Chrysostom 'on the divine birth'; they are not Cyril's words, and the Chrysostom ascription should be checked.

passages.attribution_note: Quoted by Cyril as Chrysostom; the ascription still needs checking.

passages.author: Antiochus of Ptolemais (quoted by Cyril)
passages.text: From bishop Antiochus: “For yesterday, in undefiled birth pangs, the life-bearer, the fair-bearer, the great-bearer, the light-bearer, the hope-bearer, the God-bearer, the strange-bearer, the virgin-mother Mary brought us a Savior.” (John 1:14)

theotokos.quote: the God-bearer, the virgin-mother Mary brought us a Savior
theotokos.audited: 'the God-bearer ... Mary'; Greek 'ἡ θεοτόκος' confirmed in the list of titles. ATTRIBUTION: these are Antiochus of Ptolemais's words (d. c. 408) quoted by Cyril, not Cyril's own.

christotokos.quote: the God-bearer, the virgin-mother Mary brought us a Savior
christotokos.audited: Calls Mary 'the God-bearer' (ἡ θεοτόκος), which excludes mother-of-Christ-only. Words are Antiochus of Ptolemais's, quoted by Cyril.

passages.author: Severian of Gabala (quoted by Cyril)
passages.text: From bishop Severianus: “For the Word begotten from above from the Father — beyond speech, beyond telling, beyond grasp, eternally — is himself begotten in time from below from the virgin Mary, so that those first born from below may be born from above from a second birth, that is, from God.” (John 3:3–7)

theotokos.quote: the Word ... is himself begotten in time ... from the virgin Mary
theotokos.audited: 'the Word begotten from above from the Father ... is himself begotten in time from below from the virgin Mary': the Word is born of her. Greek 'ὁ αὐτὸς ἐν χρόνῳ γεννᾶται κάτωθεν ἐκ παρθένου Μαρίας' confirmed. ATTRIBUTION: Severian of Gabala's words (d. after 408), quoted by Cyril.

christotokos.quote: the Word ... is himself begotten in time ... from the virgin Mary
christotokos.audited: 'the Word ... is himself (ὁ αὐτός) begotten in time ... from the virgin Mary' says God the Word was born of her. Words are Severian of Gabala's, quoted by Cyril.

passages.author: Ammonius of Adrianople (quoted by Cyril)
passages.text: From Ammonius, bishop of Adrianople: “For he too said somewhere about the Word of God: But if he himself is God by nature, as God’s Only-begotten Son, and in taking the slave’s form was also counted worthy to be called firstborn son of the holy virgin, he gave himself as a ransom for all.” He goes on: “I have already shown the impiety into which the Arians fall when they say the God-bearer Mary needed the sacrifices then offered under the law for women who give birth.”

theotokos.quote: the God-bearer Mary
theotokos.audited: 'the God-bearer Mary'; Greek 'τὴν θεοτόκον Μαρίαν' confirmed. ATTRIBUTION: Ammonius of Adrianople's words, quoted by Cyril, not Cyril's own.

christotokos.quote: the God-bearer Mary
christotokos.audited: Calls her 'the God-bearer Mary' (θεοτόκον Μαρίαν). Words are Ammonius of Adrianople's, quoted by Cyril.

passages.author: Nestorius (as quoted)
passages.text: Nestorius says: When the divine Scripture speaks of the birth of Christ from Mary the virgin, it nowhere appears as God, but as Christ or the Lord Jesus, because these three terms are significant of the two natures, now referring to one, now to the other; I mean: When the birth from the Virgin is announced to us of Christ, the Apostle says, 'God sent his Son, born of a woman'; he did not say, 'Sent God the Word'; but he takes the name indicating the two births, namely God and man, because Christ is double; for the Virgin bore a Son of God, as he breathed; but you are gods and sons of the Most High all, whence we learned to say Christotokos, Kyriotokos, anthropotokos from Scripture, but we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos, that is, God-bearer or Mother of God.

theotokos.quote: we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos, that is, God-bearer or Mother of God
theotokos.audited: Nestorius's words: 'we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos'. Greek confirmed: 'Θεοτόκον δὲ οὐδαμῶς ἐδιδάχθημεν λέγειν τὴν ἁγίαν Παρθένον'. ATTRIBUTION: these are Nestorius's words, not Cyril's, and the Dialogue with Nestorius is widely treated as not by Cyril; credit them to Nestorius (c. 428-431).

christotokos.quote: we learned to say Christotokos, Kyriotokos, anthropotokos from Scripture, but we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos, that is, God-bearer or Mother of God
christotokos.audited: 'we learned to say Christotokos, Kyriotokos, anthropotokos ... but never ... Theotokos' (Χριστοτόκον ... Θεοτόκον δὲ οὐδαμῶς) is the mark: it refuses Mother of God and prefers mother of Christ. ATTRIBUTION: the speaker is Nestorius; the dialogue's ascription to Cyril is doubtful.

passages.attribution_note: Nestorius' words, quoted in a dialogue whose ascription to Cyril is doubted.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: From Luke. “And it came to pass while they were there that the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her son, the firstborn, and wrapped him and laid him in the manger, because there was no place for them in the lodging.” (Luke 2:6–7) The holy virgin has borne one and only son, Emmanuel. How then does it say “her son, the firstborn” (Romans 8:29)? For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin. So it is marked from the God-breathed scripture: the Only-begotten Word of God has been named firstborn. For he has shared blood and flesh and similarly to us shared the same things. Thus he became firstborn among many brothers; yet as God he is worshiped by us ourselves and by the spirits above.

theotokos.quote: the holy virgin has borne ... the Only-begotten Word of God has been named firstborn
theotokos.audited: Borderline but met: 'The holy virgin has borne one and only son, Emmanuel ... the Only-begotten Word of God has been named firstborn' identifies her firstborn son with the Only-begotten Word, so the Word was born of her. Greek 'μόνον τέτοκεν υἱὸν τὸν Ἐμμανουὴλ ἡ ἁγία παρθένος' confirmed.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: If the church belongs to God and Christ has presented it to himself, then it is clear that God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary.

theotokos.quote: God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary
theotokos.audited: 'God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary': calls her God-bearing and says God came from her.

christotokos.quote: God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary
christotokos.audited: 'God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary' says God was born of her.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: We say that this same Only-begotten Word, begotten beyond speech from the substance of God the Father, maker of the ages, the one through whom and in whom all things are, the true light, the nature that gives life to all — for he has appeared as life from the Father’s life — in the last times of the age, when the Father was pleased to save the race on earth that had fallen under a curse and been brought down by sin into death and decay, took hold of Abraham’s seed, as the Scriptures say, shared blood and flesh — that is, became human — and taking flesh and making it his own, was born in the flesh through the holy God-bearer Mary (Hebrews 2:16).

theotokos.quote: was born in the flesh through the holy God-bearer Mary
theotokos.audited: 'was born in the flesh through the holy God-bearer Mary'; Greek 'διὰ τῆς ἁγίας καὶ θεοτόκου Μαρίας' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: was born in the flesh through the holy God-bearer Mary
christotokos.audited: 'the holy God-bearer Mary' (θεοτόκου Μαρίας) uses the title the position refuses.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: But the word God-bearer was already customary even with the holy fathers before us, who are admired for right faith, and still with all under heaven, so to speak. I thought I had to declare that as true.

theotokos.quote: the word God-bearer was already customary even with the holy fathers before us
theotokos.audited: 'the word God-bearer was already customary even with the holy fathers ... I thought I had to declare that as true': Cyril affirms the title.

christotokos.quote: I thought I had to declare that as true
christotokos.audited: Affirming 'the word God-bearer' as true and customary rules out refusing it.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: But we do say this: look — all the best and wisest fathers of our times also name the holy virgin God-bearer, and they affirm that the Word from God has been united by nature to the flesh, that he came to be in the virgin’s womb, and that he came forth from her according to the flesh.

theotokos.quote: all the best and wisest fathers of our times also name the holy virgin God-bearer
theotokos.audited: 'all the best and wisest fathers of our times also name the holy virgin God-bearer'; Greek 'θεοτόκον ὀνομάζουσι τὴν ἁγίαν παρθένον' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: all the best and wisest fathers of our times also name the holy virgin God-bearer
christotokos.audited: Endorses naming the virgin 'God-bearer' (θεοτόκον), the title the position refuses.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: For the Son from God the Father by nature, taking to himself an ensouled and intelligent body, has been begotten according to the flesh through the holy virgin and Theotokos Mary — not turned into flesh (far from it!), but rather taking it on, and not neglecting to be God.

theotokos.quote: through the holy virgin and Theotokos Mary
theotokos.audited: 'begotten according to the flesh through the holy virgin and Theotokos Mary'; Greek 'διὰ τῆς ἁγίας παρθένου καὶ θεοτόκου Μαρίας' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: through the holy virgin and Theotokos Mary
christotokos.audited: Uses 'Theotokos' (θεοτόκου Μαρίας) as her title.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: — not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself enfleshed, with a body from her as his own. That is why he is said to have been begotten in the flesh: he makes the begetting of his own flesh his.

theotokos.quote: not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself enfleshed, with a body from her as his own
theotokos.audited: 'not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself enfleshed ... he is said to have been begotten in the flesh': the Word was born of her.

christotokos.quote: not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself enfleshed
christotokos.audited: 'not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself' rejects 'she bore only a man' directly.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Those who senselessly deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer are forced to say there are two sons of God. For if she did not bear in the flesh the enfleshed God, they must admit — willing or not — that she bore only a common human, with nothing more than we have.

theotokos.quote: Those who senselessly deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer are forced to say there are two sons of God
theotokos.audited: 'Those who senselessly deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer'; Greek 'θεοτόκον οὐκ εἶναι τὴν ἁγίαν παρθένον' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: Those who senselessly deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer
christotokos.audited: Condemns those who 'deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer', which is the christotokos position itself.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: So if they say that the one born from the holy virgin is true God — that is, the Word from God the Father united by nature to flesh — why do they fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer?

theotokos.quote: why do they fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer?
theotokos.audited: 'why do they fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer?': urges the title outright.

christotokos.quote: why do they fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer?
christotokos.audited: Rebukes those who 'fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer'.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: In the same breath he sets down two things proper to God, and not fitting for human nature. Of the one born from Mary he said that those saved through him are his own people, and that he himself will also free them from sins. All things belong to God, and to him alone it would befit to be able to free sinners from sins. So the one begotten from the holy virgin is God, whose own people we are; and he has freed us from sins, as one who has authority for that too.

theotokos.quote: So the one begotten from the holy virgin is God, whose own people we are
theotokos.audited: 'So the one begotten from the holy virgin is God': God was born of her.

christotokos.quote: So the one begotten from the holy virgin is God, whose own people we are
christotokos.audited: 'the one begotten from the holy virgin is God' says God was born of her.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Since he emptied himself by becoming in the likeness of a man, and was found in the form of a man, he receives the common name, that is, Christ and Jesus, or rather, Emmanuel. The name Emmanuel signifies 'God with us.' For it is written, 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel' (Isaiah 7:14). For the blessed Gabriel revealed the mystery to the holy and God-bearing virgin, saying, 'Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with God, and behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he shall save his people from their sins' (Matthew 1:21-23). Are the prophet and the blessed angel inconsistent with one another? Not at all. For the blessed prophet speaks mysteries by the Spirit, having foretold a God who has become with us, naming him so both from his nature and from the economy of the flesh.

theotokos.quote: the holy and God-bearing virgin
theotokos.audited: 'the holy and God-bearing virgin': Cyril calls her God-bearer.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: This statement shows the manifest confession, namely the exaltation, and the phrase 'You are my Son' establishes His eternal nature, while the phrase 'I have today begotten you' reveals His birth according to the flesh, which He willingly underwent through the Holy Virgin; and for this reason she is named Theotokos.

theotokos.quote: for this reason she is named Theotokos
theotokos.audited: 'by which He is also named Theotokos'. TRANSLATION: the Greek is 'ταύτῃ τοι καὶ θεότοκος ὠνόμασται', meaning the holy Virgin, through whom he was born in the flesh, is for this reason named Theotokos. 'He' is wrong; it should be 'she'. ATTRIBUTION: catena fragment; same text as the Psalm fragment b0c5e1ecd5244d19.

christotokos.quote: for this reason she is named Theotokos
christotokos.audited: Greek 'ταύτῃ τοι καὶ θεότοκος ὠνόμασται' names the Virgin Theotokos, which excludes mother-of-Christ-only. The English 'He is named' is a mistranslation.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Cyril says: You see the confession at the very start, that is, the declaration. For the Father has set down the words "You are" in order to show the Son's eternal being. He did not become Son in time; he always was this—that is, Son. Then the Father brought in the words "Today I have begotten you" (Psalm 2:7) in order to show his newest birth according to the flesh, which he willingly underwent through the holy Virgin. This is why she has been named Mother of God. For she gave birth not to a mere human being simply joined to God by an external connection, but rather to the very Word from God the Father, who put on human poverty and became a human being like us.

theotokos.quote: This is why she has been named Mother of God. For she gave birth not to a mere human being simply joined to God by an external connection, but rather to the very Word from God the Father, who put on human poverty and became a human being like us.
theotokos.audited: 'This is why she has been named Mother of God. For she gave birth not to a mere human being ... but rather to the very Word'. A direct statement of the mark.

christotokos.quote: This is why she has been named Mother of God. For she gave birth not to a mere human being simply joined to God by an external connection
christotokos.audited: 'she gave birth not to a mere human being simply joined to God ... but rather to the very Word' rejects the excluding claim word for word.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: The Jews once came to Christ saying: “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” Jesus answered them: “I told you, and you do not believe; the works that I do in my Father’s name, these testify about me.” (John 10:24–25) What then do those who foolishly divide a duality of sons and split the one Lord Jesus Christ into two Christs say even about this? About whom were the Jews saying: “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly”? And who is the one saying: “The works that I do in my Father’s name, these testify about me”? Whose own Father do we say God is? Of the one from a woman, thought of separately and particularly — or of the Only-begotten? Yet being able to accomplish the works of the deity would not fit a human nature — how could it? Far from it. But since Christ was fulfilling the works of the Father, he would not be understood as a bare human, but rather as God who has remained what he

christotokos.quote: God who has remained what he was in blood and flesh
christotokos.audited: Cyril, On the Right Faith, against 'those who foolishly divide a duality of sons and split the one Lord Jesus Christ into two Christs': the one from a woman is 'not... a bare human, but rather as God who has remained what he was in blood and flesh,' doing the Father's works. The one Mary bore is God in the flesh, not a human son alongside the Word - the division this position rests on is condemned.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: “Jesus did many other signs before his disciples that are not written in this book; but these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:30–31) Emmanuel born from the holy virgin was named Jesus by the angel’s voice. When therefore he himself—and not another—is the Son of God, and the one who believes has eternal life in his name, how are they not mad who divide and say there is one son and another the Word from God, and the one from the holy virgin? For in these the evangelist appears, and very clearly, knowing and proclaiming one and only Jesus Christ from both—that is, the Word from God the Father who has shared blood and flesh similarly to us, as it is written (Hebrews 2:14).

theotokos.quote: Emmanuel born from the holy virgin
theotokos.audited: Cyril: 'Emmanuel born from the holy virgin was named Jesus... When therefore he himself - and not another - is the Son of God... how are they not mad who divide and say there is one son and another the Word from God, and the one from the holy virgin?... one and only Jesus Christ from both - that is, the Word from God the Father who has shared blood and flesh similarly to us.' God the Word himself is the one born of the virgin.

christotokos.quote: the one from the holy virgin...the Word from God the Father who has shared blood and flesh similarly to us
christotokos.audited: Dividing Christ into 'one son and another the Word from God, and the one from the holy virgin' is called madness; the one from the virgin IS the Word. The two-subject scheme behind 'mother of Christ only' is condemned.

passages.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
passages.text: Therefore, even that which is being born shall be called the holy Son of God. Do you see how immense the dignity of the Mother of God is, being a virgin.

theotokos.quote: Do you see how immense the dignity of the Mother of God is, being a virgin.
theotokos.audited: 'Do you see how immense the dignity of the Mother of God is'; Greek 'τὸ τῆς θεοτόκου παρθένου ... ἀξίωμα' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: Do you see how immense the dignity of the Mother of God is, being a virgin.
christotokos.audited: Calls her the Theotokos virgin (τῆς θεοτόκου παρθένου).

passages.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
passages.text: But just as you have heard the charges against woman, come now and learn the achievement that came from her. A woman brought virginity into the world. She contained in her womb the God whom creation cannot contain. She bore in the flesh the one who fashioned our race. She was the first to receive Jesus from the dead, the first to begin the proclamation of the rising, the first to announce the joy to the disciples.

theotokos.quote: She contained in her womb the God whom creation cannot contain.
theotokos.audited: Hesychius: 'She contained in her womb the God whom creation cannot contain. She bore in the flesh the one who fashioned our race.'

christotokos.quote: She contained in her womb the God whom creation cannot contain.
christotokos.audited: 'She contained in her womb the God whom creation cannot contain' - the one she bore is God himself.

passages.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
passages.text: But Joseph and his mother, hearing what Simeon had said, marveled that Christ should consent to become a son of man. Mary marveled that a woman’s womb had contained God, that the servant had given birth to the One who sets creation free.

theotokos.quote: a woman’s womb had contained God, that the servant had given birth to the One who sets creation free
theotokos.audited: Hesychius on the Presentation: 'Mary marveled that a woman's womb had contained God, that the servant had given birth to the One who sets creation free.' God was contained in her womb and born of her.

christotokos.quote: the servant had given birth to the One who sets creation free
christotokos.audited: She 'gave birth to the One who sets creation free,' whose womb 'had contained God' - she bore God, not humanity alone.

passages.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
passages.text: "A woman who," it says, "has conceived" (Leviticus 12:2). But the Mother of God was a woman, yet she did not undergo what women undergo. For her womb did not receive a man's seed. The field of Mary saw no plow; the virginal vineyard endured no mattock. So the offering was not for her sake, but for the sake of the whole race.

theotokos.quote: the Mother of God was a woman
theotokos.audited: Hesychius, in terms: 'But the Mother of God was a woman, yet she did not undergo what women undergo. For her womb did not receive a man's seed.' The title itself.

christotokos.quote: the Mother of God was a woman
christotokos.audited: Mary is called 'the Mother of God' outright - the refused title, used as her name.

passages.author: John of Damascus
passages.text: Juvenal took up the word and answered: 'In holy and God-inspired Scripture the facts of the end of the holy Mother of God Mary are not recorded; but we have received from an ancient and most truthful tradition that at the time of her glorious falling asleep all the holy apostles (there was no small grief in the midst over this, Pulcheria not knowing these things), as they were traveling through the world for the salvation of the nations, were gathered in an instant, lifted up on high, to Jerusalem; and as they stood by her, an angelic vision appeared to them, and a divine hymnody of the higher Powers was heard. And so, in divine and heavenly glory, she gave up her holy soul into the hands of God, in a manner beyond words. And her God-receiving body, carried out and buried with angelic and apostolic hymnody, was laid in the tomb in Gethsemane; and in that place, for three days, the choir
