ever-virgin.quote: For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin.
ever-virgin.audited: 'For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin' (Greek οὐ γὰρ γεγόνασιν ἕτεροι μετ' αὐτόν, μεμένηκε δὲ παρθένος; checked, faithful): no other children and virginity after the birth.

other-children.quote: For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin.
other-children.audited: 'Others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin' denies other children of Mary.

passages.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
passages.text: The Virgin Mary kept her breasts untouched and nursed a child without knowing the child's father. She became a mother without becoming a bride, a remarkable and unprecedented event. A son was being raised, and yet, a father was not found. The field was bearing fruit, but the fruit had no farmer to tend to it. It yielded a harvest, but it did not receive seed. A river was flowing, and its source was closed from everywhere, signifying that Mary had become a mother without suffering the things that mothers normally experience. She gave birth like a woman, but she was not corrupted like a woman. Her pregnancy was according to the law of nature, as she waited for the appointed time of childbirth. However, her conception was contrary to the law of nature. You introduced the king, with the doors closed, but again you led him out. For neither when he was being conceived nor when he was being bor

ever-virgin.quote: neither when he was being conceived nor when he was being born did the king of glory open the doors of your womb or loosen the bonds of your virginity
ever-virgin.audited: The sealed fountain is glossed as 'no marital branch' drawing from her spring (Greek κλάδος γαμικὸς τὴν σὴν ...), i.e. no married union. Borderline: most of the passage is virginity in birth, and English 'you have remained untouched' adds 'remained' to the aorist οὐχ ἥψατο.

other-children.quote: no sickle of corruption and no harvesting ever touched you
other-children.audited: The sealed fountain from which no marital use drew rules out Mary bearing children to Joseph. Borderline for the same reason as ever-virgin.

questions.question: Was Mary free from sin, and from when?
shared_ground: Mary is holy, blessed, highly favoured
Mary as the new Eve, obedient where Eve disobeyed
Mary needed and received God's grace

positions.name: Mary had personal faults
positions.statement: Mary, though holy, committed some personal faults, such as doubt or vanity, like other believers.
positions.mark: The passage attributes a sin, fault, doubt or weakness to Mary.
positions.first_defined: No confession defines it

first_states.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
first_states.text: The sign of contradiction is the cross. For when the Jews crucified him, the sun withdrew; the synagogue slandered him, and the earth shook. The crowd cried out, “Crucify him” (Luke 23:21), but the rocks, unable to bear the weight of the blasphemy, split apart. The elders and the scribes said, “We remember that this deceiver said while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise’” (Matthew 27:63). But the centurion cried out, “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matthew 27:54). And even to this day the word of the cross is “a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to us who are called, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23-24). “And a sword will pierce your own soul also, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke 2:35). The sword is called division of mind, because just as a sword cuts and divides bodies, so division of mi

faults.quote: The sword is called division of mind... For even if she was a virgin, she was also a woman; even if she was the Mother of God, she was from our own clay. So the sword passed through her soul... enduring great doubt about these things because of the turmoil of the passion.
faults.audited: Hesychius on the Presentation, expounding Luke 2:35: 'The sword is called division of mind, because just as a sword cuts and divides bodies, so division of mind leads souls to doubt. For even if she was a virgin, she was also a woman; even if she was the Mother of God, she was FROM OUR OWN CLAY. So the sword passed through her soul... enduring GREAT DOUBT about these things because of the turmoil of the passion.' Doubt - one of the faults this position's mark names - is expressly attributed to Mary.

personal-sinlessness.quote: the sword passed through her soul ... enduring great doubt
personal-sinlessness.audited: The same passage attributes 'great doubt' to Mary during the passion. On this question's own framing, doubt is one of the personal faults (the faults mark expressly includes doubt); a Mary who endured great doubt is not a Mary who never committed any personal fault. (The graders' split turns on whether doubt counts as sin; the dossier's definitions settle it.)

positions.name: Free from personal sin

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 6, Canon 23 (1547)
defined.quote: except by a special privilege from God, as the Church holds in regard of the Blessed Virgin

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 6 (1672)
defined.quote: and especially the Mother of God the Word, the ever-virgin Mary, did not experience these [sins], or such like faults.

positions.statement: Mary never committed any personal sin during her life, by a special grace of God.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary committed no sin, or was wholly pure in her life, without saying anything about her conception.
positions.first_defined: Council of Trent, Session 6, Canon 23 (1547); Synod of Jerusalem, Decree 6 (1672)

positions.name: Immaculate Conception

defined.source: Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus (1854)
defined.quote: the most Blessed Virgin Mary, in the first instance of her conception, by a singular grace and privilege granted by Almighty God, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Savior of the human race, was preserved free from all stain of original sin

positions.statement: From the first moment of her conception Mary was preserved from original sin, by a grace given in view of Christ's merits.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary was without original sin, or holy from her conception, not only free from personal sin.
positions.first_defined: Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus (1854)

passages.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea
passages.text: We hear of innocence especially in the case of Christ—the purity from all evil that the Creator sought among human beings, who were made for this purpose: to be worthy of their Maker and to remain in what is good, since all the works of God are exceedingly good (Ps 40:13). Yet when he sought it, he found it in none of Adam’s descendants, but only in the one who was from Adam according to the flesh and had not displayed the marks of Adam’s transgression, but possessed the divine form remaining even with the fleshly covering. This is what the heavenly voice testifies: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

immaculate-conception.quote: he found it in none of Adam's descendants, but only in the one who was from Adam according to the flesh and had not displayed the marks of Adam's transgression
immaculate-conception.audited: Apollinaris on the Psalms: the Creator sought innocence - 'the purity from all evil' - among human beings, 'yet when he sought it, he found it in NONE of Adam's descendants, but only in the one who was from Adam according to the flesh and had not displayed the marks of Adam's transgression' (Christ, Matthew 3:17). Mary is a descendant of Adam; the passage's universal ('none... but only') leaves her among those who displayed the marks of Adam's transgression - not preserved from original sin.

questions.question: How did Mary's earthly life end?
shared_ground: Mary's earthly life came to an end
Mary is honoured in heaven
Mary's 'falling asleep' named without saying what happened to her body (fits all three)

positions.name: Died and was buried; nothing further held
positions.statement: Mary died and was buried like other believers, and awaits the general resurrection.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary's body lies in the grave or awaits the general resurrection, or that her end is unknown.
positions.first_defined: No confession defines it

positions.name: Died, then taken bodily to heaven (Dormition)

defined.source: Troparion and Kontakion of the Dormition (Orthodox Church in America)
defined.quote: in falling asleep you did not forsake the world, O Theotokos.

defined.source: Kontakion of the Dormition (Orthodox Church in America)
defined.quote: Neither the tomb, nor death had power over the Theotokos

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), The Holy Virgin Saint Mary
defined.quote: The Church believes in the Ascent of the body of The Virgin to heaven, and celebrates that feast on the 16th of Misra.

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), The Holy Virgin Saint Mary
defined.quote: in commemoration of her death on the 21st of Tubah

positions.statement: Mary truly died (fell asleep), and was then raised and taken into heavenly life; neither tomb nor death held her.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary died and that afterwards her body did not remain in the tomb, or that she was raised.
positions.first_defined: Liturgical feast of the Dormition (from the 6th century); not defined as dogma

positions.name: Assumed body and soul (Catholic dogma)

defined.source: Pius XII, Munificentissimus Deus, 44 (1950)
defined.quote: that the Immaculate Mother of God, the ever Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory.

positions.statement: At the end of her earthly life Mary was taken body and soul into heavenly glory; the dogma leaves open whether she first died.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary was taken body and soul into heaven.
positions.first_defined: Pius XII, Munificentissimus Deus (1950)

passages.author: Gregory of Tours
passages.text: At last, when the blessed Mary had completed the course of this life and was now being called from the world, all the apostles gathered from their several regions to her house. And when they heard that she was to be taken up from the world, they kept watch with her together; and behold, the Lord Jesus came with his angels, and receiving her soul, he handed it to Michael the archangel, and departed. At daybreak the apostles lifted her body with the bier, laid it in a tomb, and guarded it, awaiting the coming of the Lord. And behold, the Lord stood by them again, and ordered the holy body he had taken up to be carried on a cloud into paradise: where now, her soul restored to her, she rejoices with his chosen ones and enjoys the good things of eternity, which will never come to an end.

death-and-burial.quote: ordered the holy body he had taken up to be carried on a cloud into paradise: where now, her soul restored to her

dormition.quote: when the blessed Mary had completed the course of this life and was now being called from the world... receiving her soul... ordered the holy body he had taken up to be carried on a cloud into paradise: where now, her soul restored to her

assumption.quote: receiving her soul... ordered the holy body he had taken up to be carried on a cloud into paradise

passages.author: John of Damascus
passages.text: 'After the third day, when the angelic hymnody had ceased, the apostles who were present (one of them, Thomas, had been left behind, and arrived after the third day, and wanted to venerate the God-receiving body) opened the tomb. And her all-hymned body they could not find at all; finding only her grave-cloths lying there, and filled with the ineffable fragrance that came from them, they secured the tomb. Struck with wonder at the mystery, they could only conclude that the One who was pleased to take flesh in his own person and become man from her, and to be born in the flesh, God the Word and Lord of glory, and who after the birth kept her virginity incorrupt, himself was pleased, after her departure from this life, to honour her undefiled and unstained body with incorruption, and with a translation before the common and universal resurrection.'

death-and-burial.quote: her all-hymned body they could not find at all; finding only her grave-cloths lying there

assumption.quote: honour her undefiled and unstained body with incorruption, and with a translation before the common and universal resurrection

passages.author: John of Damascus
passages.text: You see, dear fathers and brothers, in what terms this most glorious tomb addresses us. And that this is so is also written, word for word, in the Euthymius History, book three, chapter forty: 'It was said above how Saint Pulcheria built many churches to Christ in Constantinople. One of them is the church built in Blachernae at the beginning of the reign of Marcian, of divine memory. When they had built there a venerable house to the all-hymned and all-holy Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, and adorned it with every ornament, they began to search for her all-holy, God-receiving body; and summoning Juvenal, the archbishop of Jerusalem, and the bishops from Palestine who were then staying in the imperial city because of the council that had been held at Chalcedon, they say to them: "We hear that in Jerusalem there is the first and most distinguished church of the all-holy Mother of God a

death-and-burial.quote: where her life-bearing body was laid in a tomb

dormition.quote: where her life-bearing body was laid in a tomb. We wish, then, to bring this relic here

assumption.quote: where her life-bearing body was laid in a tomb. We wish, then, to bring this relic here

passages.author: John of Damascus
passages.text: Juvenal took up the word and answered: 'In holy and God-inspired Scripture the facts of the end of the holy Mother of God Mary are not recorded; but we have received from an ancient and most truthful tradition that at the time of her glorious falling asleep all the holy apostles (there was no small grief in the midst over this, Pulcheria not knowing these things), as they were traveling through the world for the salvation of the nations, were gathered in an instant, lifted up on high, to Jerusalem; and as they stood by her, an angelic vision appeared to them, and a divine hymnody of the higher Powers was heard. And so, in divine and heavenly glory, she gave up her holy soul into the hands of God, in a manner beyond words. And her God-receiving body, carried out and buried with angelic and apostolic hymnody, was laid in the tomb in Gethsemane; and in that place, for three days, the choir

death-and-burial.quote: her God‑receiving body ... was laid in the tomb in Gethsemane; and in that place, for three days, the choir and hymnody of the angels continued without ceasing.

questions.question: What is the relationship between Christians on earth and the saints in heaven?
shared_ground: The saints are honoured and remembered as examples of faith (Augsburg XXI: 'the memory of saints may be set before us')
Living Christians should pray for one another
Christ is the one mediator between God and humanity
Feasts or remembrance of martyrs on their days

positions.name: Remembered as examples only

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 21.2 (1646)
defined.quote: Religious worship is to be given to God, the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; and to him alone; not to angels, saints, or any other creature

positions.statement: The saints are remembered as examples of faith; no claim is made that they pray for us, and they are not to be addressed in prayer.
positions.mark: The passage says prayer is to be made to God alone and never to departed saints, without saying the saints pray for us.
positions.first_defined: Westminster Confession, 21.2 (1646)

positions.name: The saints pray for the Church, but are not to be invoked

defined.source: Apology of the Augsburg Confession, XXI.9 (1531)
defined.quote: concerning the saints we concede that, just as, when alive, they pray for the Church universal in general, so in heaven they pray for the Church in general

defined.source: Augsburg Confession, Article XXI (1530)
defined.quote: But the Scripture teaches not the invocation of saints or to ask help of saints, since it sets before us the one Christ as the Mediator

positions.statement: The saints in heaven pray for the Church in general, but Christians should not call on them or ask their help.
positions.mark: The passage says departed saints pray for the Church while denying that Christians should address them.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession XXI (1530); Apology XXI (1531)

first_states.author: Augustine of Hippo
first_states.text: memorial shrines of martyrs, this seems to me to benefit the deceased only in this way: that by commending him also to the intercession of the martyrs, the affection of prayer for him may be increased.

commemoration-only.quote: by commending him also to the intercession of the martyrs, the affection of prayer for him may be increased
commemoration-only.audited: Augustine's own conclusion (Care for the Dead 22): burial at a martyr's shrine 'seems to me to benefit the deceased only in this way: that by commending him also to the intercession of the martyrs, the affection of prayer for him may be increased.' The intercession of the martyrs is affirmed in the author's own voice as a real thing to which the dead are commended - a claim that the saints do intercede, which this position makes no room for.

pray-but-not-invoked.audited: Augustine affirms the martyrs' intercession ('commending him also to the intercession of the martyrs') while locating the benefit in the living's increased affection of prayer - the commendation described is not an address to the martyrs, and the same work denies the dead know our affairs. Saints intercede; Christians do not call on them: this position's shape.

positions.name: Asking the saints to pray for us

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 25, On the invocation of saints (1563)
defined.quote: the saints, who reign together with Christ, offer up their own prayers to God for men; that it is good and useful suppliantly to invoke them

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 8 (1672)
defined.quote: Notwithstanding, in [our] prayers and supplications unto Him, we say the Saints are intercessors, and, above all, the undefiled Mother of the very God the Word

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), Comparative Theology (1988)
defined.quote: We reply that we do not pray to the saints; we only ask their prayers and their support for us.

positions.statement: Departed saints pray for the living, and it is right to address them directly and ask for their prayers.
positions.mark: The passage addresses a departed saint directly (such as 'pray for us') or teaches that Christians should ask departed saints for their prayers.
positions.first_defined: Council of Trent, Session 25 (1563); Synod of Jerusalem (1672)

first_states.author: Pseudo-Cyprian
first_states.text: may obtain pardon, so that by the merits of your righteousness the offenses of our life may be cleansed. For I am confident that it is the likeness of martyrdom for a sinner to deserve salvation by the petition of a righteous martyr, and that when you can do little for yourself by your prayers, you are set free by the merits of a martyr. Thus righteous Job is shown about to pray to God for the sins of his three friends and to obtain it, and the proof of his fear and faith is marked by the Lord’s own voice as witness. Therefore, dearest one, when on the day of your liberation you begin to present yourself before the face of Christ, when you pass into eternity and the endlessness of living to reign with Christ by a happy lot, for the Lord’s mercy keep me in mind, and Celsus your boy, most holy one.

commemoration-only.quote: for the Lord's mercy keep me in mind, and Celsus your boy, most holy one
commemoration-only.audited: Pseudo-Cyprian, To Vigilius 10: the writer asks the confessor, for when he stands before Christ after his liberation, 'for the Lord's mercy keep me in mind, and Celsus your boy, most holy one,' confident that 'a sinner may deserve salvation by the petition of a righteous martyr' and be 'set free by the merits of a martyr.' Prayer is here directed to the saint for his post-mortem intercession - not to God alone.

pray-but-not-invoked.quote: when you can do little for yourself by your prayers, you are set free by the merits of a martyr... keep me in mind, ... most holy one.
pray-but-not-invoked.audited: The same letter directly asks the saint to keep the writer and his son in mind before Christ and rests the sinner's pardon on the martyr's petition and merits - Christians here do call on the saint and ask his help, which this position says they should not do.

invocation.quote: for the Lord's mercy keep me in mind, and Celsus your boy, most holy one
invocation.audited: The letter is the practice itself: the writer addresses the martyr ('most holy one') and asks him to remember him and his son when he stands 'before the face of Christ,' so that by the martyr's petition and merits their offenses 'may be cleansed.' Asking a saint for his prayers before God after death is taught and performed.

passages.author: Basil of Caesarea
passages.text: What a wonder! They do not fall short in number, nor do they admit any increase. If you divide them into a hundred, they do not leave their proper number; if you gather them into one, they remain forty, just as fire behaves. For fire passes to the one who lights from it, and yet remains whole with the one who has it; so the Forty are all together, and all are present with each one. This is ungrudging beneficence, grace that is not spent, ready help for Christians, a church of martyrs, an army of trophy-bearers, a company of those who glorify God. How much would you have toiled to find even one person to entreat the Lord on your behalf? Here are forty, sending up a harmonious prayer. Where two or three are gathered in the name of the Lord, there He is in the midst of them (Matthew 18:20). Where there are forty, who can doubt the presence of God? The one who is afflicted flees for refuge t

commemoration-only.quote: The one who is afflicted flees for refuge to the Forty; the one who rejoices runs to them

passages.author: Asterius of Amasea
passages.text: Thus a father or mother, taking up a sick child and embracing it, passes by the clinics and doctors and flees to help that needs no skill; and coming to one of the martyrs, she presents her petition to the Lord through him, using such cries toward the go-between: 'You who suffered for Christ, intercede for suffering and sickness. You have boldness; use your voice for your fellow-servants. Even if you left our life behind, you still know the sufferings of humanity; you too once called on the martyrs before you became a martyr. Then you sought and received; now that you have, give. As your prize, ask this gain for us. May we be healed by your wounds, as the world is by Christ's.'

commemoration-only.quote: coming to one of the martyrs, she presents her petition to the Lord through him
commemoration-only.audited: Asterius, Homily 14: the mother at the martyr's shrine cries to the departed martyr, 'You who suffered for Christ, intercede for suffering and sickness. You have boldness; use your voice for your fellow-servants... Then you sought and received; now that you have, give.' A departed saint is directly addressed in prayer for his intercession.

pray-but-not-invoked.quote: You who suffered for Christ, intercede for suffering and sickness. You have boldness; use your voice for your fellow-servants.
pray-but-not-invoked.audited: The passage depicts and commends direct address to a departed martyr - 'intercede for suffering and sickness... May we be healed by your wounds' - exactly the calling-on this position forbids.

invocation.quote: coming to one of the martyrs, she presents her petition to the Lord through him
invocation.audited: The homily gives the words of invocation itself: 'You who suffered for Christ, intercede for suffering and sickness. You have boldness; use your voice for your fellow-servants... As your prize, ask this gain for us. May we be healed by your wounds, as the world is by Christ's.' A departed saint is addressed and asked for his prayers.

passages.author: Asterius of Amasea
passages.text: For our prayer is not sufficient to move God in the time of necessity or misfortune, for our plea is not a persuasion, but a remembrance of sins; therefore we fly to the fellow-servants who are loved by the Lord, so that they might heal our defects through their own achievements. What then is the charge, that while honoring martyrs we ourselves strive to please God? What accusation is there in flying to protectors? Let us examine also these things, if the accuser cleanses the charge. And how can it be said, that you do not honor myriads of dead men, but worship them as gods?

commemoration-only.quote: we fly to the fellow-servants who are loved by the Lord, so that they might heal our defects through their own achievements
commemoration-only.audited: 'We flee to the fellow-servants loved by the Lord, so that they might heal our faults by their own achievements' and 'we enjoy their patronage before God' (Greek προσφεύγομεν, προστασίας... πρὸς Θεόν) is seeking help from departed martyrs.

pray-but-not-invoked.quote: we fly to the fellow-servants who are loved by the Lord, so that they might heal our defects through their own achievements
pray-but-not-invoked.audited: Asterius, Homily 14: 'our prayer is not sufficient to move God in the time of necessity... therefore we fly to the fellow-servants who are loved by the Lord, so that they might heal our defects through their own achievements... What accusation is there in flying to protectors?' Christians are taught to fly to the departed saints for help - calling on them, which this position forbids.

invocation.quote: we fly to the fellow-servants who are loved by the Lord, so that they might heal our defects through their own achievements
invocation.audited: 'We fly to the fellow-servants who are loved by the Lord, so that they might heal our defects through their own achievements' - the homily defends recourse to the departed martyrs as protectors whose help is sought; asking the saints for their aid is the commended practice.

passages.author: Asterius of Amasea
passages.text: Another, hastening to a marriage, makes the prayer in the martyr-shrines a prelude to the bridal chambers; and someone rushing to a voyage does not first loosen the moorings of the ship, before he invokes the Lord of the sea through the martyrs; and for the poor and the needy, they have gained a common table and food, the rest of the martyrs; and the martyrs are sung of throughout the earth and the sea. Appropriately and according to their worth. For not as many do the righteousness correctly...

commemoration-only.quote: invokes the Lord of the sea through the martyrs
commemoration-only.audited: Asterius, Homily 14: the voyager 'does not first loosen the moorings of the ship, before he invokes the Lord of the sea through the martyrs,' and the wedding guest 'makes the prayer in the martyr-shrines a prelude to the bridal chambers.' Prayer is routed through the martyrs as its channel - saintly mediation in prayer, not prayer to God alone with the saints as mere examples.

pray-but-not-invoked.quote: invokes the Lord of the sea through the martyrs
pray-but-not-invoked.audited: Invoking the Lord 'through the martyrs' calls on the martyrs as the prayer's mediators; this position holds Christians should not call on the saints at all.

invocation.quote: invokes the Lord of the sea through the martyrs
invocation.audited: Within this homily's teaching (the same homily that bids us 'fly to the fellow-servants'), the commended ordinary practice is to invoke the Lord through the martyrs and to pray in their shrines - the martyrs' intercession is sought as the channel of prayer, which is asking departed saints for their prayers.

passages.author: Asterius of Amasea
passages.text: The martyrs are not respected even for the greatness of the miracles. Instead, people call them many-maned, and their tombs and their resting places are named as such, and they cleanse themselves as if rubbing against a contagion, not even mentioning that God-breathed saying praised by every mouth: 'Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints' (Psalm 116:15). Therefore, let us pray to God, and let us call on the martyrs to implore our common Master, so that a spirit of compunction may be given to those acting under the error of heresy, and the division may be loosed like a dividing wall or a barrier, so that all may come together in brotherly unity in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belongs the glory forever. Amen.

commemoration-only.quote: let us call on the martyrs to implore our common Master
commemoration-only.audited: 'Let us entreat the martyrs (παρακαλέσωμεν δὲ μάρτυρας) to implore our common Master' asks departed martyrs to pray.

pray-but-not-invoked.quote: let us call on the martyrs to implore our common Master
pray-but-not-invoked.audited: Christians are told to 'entreat the martyrs' (παρακαλέσωμεν δὲ μάρτυρας), the request this position forbids.

invocation.quote: let us call on the martyrs to implore our common Master
invocation.audited: 'Let us pray to God, and let us entreat the martyrs to implore our common Master' (παρακαλέσωμεν δὲ μάρτυρας τὸν κοινὸν δυσωπῆσαι Δεσπότην) teaches asking the martyrs for prayer. The English 'revile the Lord in common' is a serious mistranslation of δυσωπῆσαι ('implore').

passages.author: Augustine of Hippo
passages.text: 63:16). If such great patriarchs did not know what was happening to the people begotten from them—the very people promised from their stock to those believing in God—how do the dead mix themselves into the affairs and actions of the living, to know and help them? How do we say that those who died before the evils came which followed their death were spared, if even after death they feel whatever happens in the calamity of human life? Or perhaps we say these things in error, and think those are at rest whom the restless life of the living disturbs? What then is this, that God promised the most pious king Josiah as a great benefit that he would die before seeing the evils that threatened to come upon that place and people? These are the words of God: "Thus says the Lord God of Israel: My words which you have heard, and you feared before my face when you heard what I spoke about this place

pray-but-not-invoked.quote: There, then, are the spirits of the dead, where they do not see whatever is done or happens in this life of human beings.
pray-but-not-invoked.audited: Augustine, Care for the Dead 16, argues the dead are not present to the living: the spirits of the dead are 'where they do not see whatever is done or happens in this life of human beings'; 'If such great patriarchs did not know what was happening to the people begotten from them... how do the dead mix themselves into the affairs and actions of the living, to know and help them?' A saint who neither knows the Church's affairs nor mixes into them cannot be praying for the Church in the sense this position claims. Judged on this passage; Augustine qualifies the point elsewhere.

invocation.quote: How do the dead mix themselves into the affairs and actions of the living, to know and help them?
invocation.audited: If the dead 'do not see whatever is done or happens in this life' and cannot 'mix themselves into the affairs and actions of the living, to know and help them,' addressing them for their prayers or help is ruled out at its premise.

passages.author: Augustine of Hippo
passages.text: memorial shrines of martyrs, this seems to me to benefit the deceased only in this way: that by commending him also to the intercession of the martyrs, the affection of prayer for him may be increased.

commemoration-only.quote: by commending him also to the intercession of the martyrs, the affection of prayer for him may be increased
commemoration-only.audited: Augustine's own conclusion (Care for the Dead 22): burial at a martyr's shrine 'seems to me to benefit the deceased only in this way: that by commending him also to the intercession of the martyrs, the affection of prayer for him may be increased.' The intercession of the martyrs is affirmed in the author's own voice as a real thing to which the dead are commended - a claim that the saints do intercede, which this position makes no room for.

pray-but-not-invoked.audited: Augustine affirms the martyrs' intercession ('commending him also to the intercession of the martyrs') while locating the benefit in the living's increased affection of prayer - the commendation described is not an address to the martyrs, and the same work denies the dead know our affairs. Saints intercede; Christians do not call on them: this position's shape.

passages.author: Augustine of Hippo
passages.text: Why should we not believe that these angelic operations happen through the dispensation of God's providence, who uses both good and evil well, according to the unsearchable depth of his judgments? Whether the minds of mortals are instructed by them, or deceived, or comforted, or terrified—as mercy is to be offered to each one, or punishment inflicted, by him to whom the church not in vain sings of mercy and judgment. Let each person take what I say as he will. If the souls of the dead were present in the affairs of the living, and they themselves spoke to us when we see them in dreams—to say nothing of others—my pious mother would not desert me on any night, she who followed me by land and sea so that she might live with me. Far be it that she became cruel in a happier life, to such a degree that when something troubles my heart she would not console her grieving son, whom she loved uniq

pray-but-not-invoked.quote: If therefore our parents have forsaken us, how are they present in our cares and affairs? But if parents are not present, who are the other dead who know what we are doing or suffering?
pray-but-not-invoked.audited: Augustine presses the point with his own mother: 'If the souls of the dead were present in the affairs of the living... my pious mother would not desert me on any night... If therefore our parents have forsaken us, how are they present in our cares and affairs? But if parents are not present, who are the other dead who know what we are doing or suffering?' The dead neither know nor attend to the living - no informed prayer for the Church is possible on this showing.

invocation.quote: If therefore our parents have forsaken us, how are they present in our cares and affairs? But if parents are not present, who are the other dead who know what we are doing or suffering?
invocation.audited: 'Who are the other dead who know what we are doing or suffering?' - on this passage the departed cannot hear or know our petitions at all, which excludes addressing them.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Beloved, a timely occasion has arisen to bring remembrance of good martyrs. This remembrance imitates the celebration of the heavenly orders, for the intercession and salvation of our souls. So all of you who know God, stretch out your ears here today, so that you may be deemed worthy of the prize of the martyrs now being spoken of. For these are the ones we must praise and marvel at: they had not yet seen the incarnation of Christ, nor the death of the Immortal One, nor the resurrection from the dead, and yet even before the bodily coming they were his confessors and martyrs.

commemoration-only.quote: the intercession and salvation of our souls
commemoration-only.audited: Cyril of Alexandria, Sermon on the Three Boys, opening: 'a timely occasion has arisen to bring remembrance of good martyrs. This remembrance imitates the celebration of the heavenly orders, for the intercession and salvation of our souls.' The martyrs' remembrance is kept FOR their intercession - the saints intercede for our souls, a claim this position does not make.

passages.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
passages.text: It should be believed that he is truly the holy Longinus, the centurion who confessed Christ on the cross, by whose intercession and entreaty may we all be preserved, both those who read and those who hear, in Christ.

commemoration-only.quote: by whose intercession and entreaty may we all be preserved
commemoration-only.audited: 'Holy Longinus... by whose intercession (πρεσβείᾳ) we are all preserved' says a departed saint intercedes for the living. The Greek is a wish ('may we be preserved', διαφυλαχθείημεν).

pray-but-not-invoked.quote: by whose intercession and entreaty may we all be preserved
pray-but-not-invoked.audited: Hesychius on Longinus: 'by whose intercession and entreaty may we all be preserved, both those who read and those who hear, in Christ.' The homily itself calls down the departed saint's intercession and entreaty upon the congregation - calling on the saint, which this position forbids.

invocation.quote: by whose intercession and entreaty may we all be preserved
invocation.audited: 'By whose intercession and entreaty may we all be preserved' - the preacher seeks the departed Longinus's intercession for the living in the prayer's own optative form; asking the saint for his prayers is performed and taught.

questions.question: Is Scripture the only infallible rule of faith, or is Church tradition also binding?
shared_ground: Scripture is inspired by God and true
Scripture is sufficient to refute heretics or to teach the faith (praise of Scripture alone decides nothing)
Heretics misinterpret Scripture
The 'rule of faith' or creed summarizes apostolic teaching
Church teachers and councils are to be respected

positions.name: Scripture the only infallible rule

defined.source: Formula of Concord, Epitome, Rule and Norm, 1 (1577)
defined.quote: the sole rule and standard according to which all dogmas together with [all] teachers should be estimated and judged are the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures of the Old and of the New Testament alone

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 1.10 (1646)
defined.quote: The supreme judge by which all controversies of religion are to be determined, and all decrees of councils, opinions of ancient writers, doctrines of men, and private spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture.

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article VI (1571)
defined.quote: Holy Scripture containeth all things necessary to salvation: so that whatsoever is not read therein, nor may be proved thereby, is not to be required of any man, that it should be believed as an article of the Faith

defined.source: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths
defined.quote: The Bible is our all-sufficient rule for faith and practice.

defined.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: The Holy Scripture containeth all things necessary to salvation; so that whatsoever is not read therein, nor may be proved thereby, is not to be required of any man that it should be believed as an article of faith

defined.source: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995)
defined.quote: Other claims on our understanding of Christian faith and life, such as tradition, culture, experience, reason, and political powers, need to be tested and corrected by the light of Holy Scripture.

positions.statement: Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith; councils, fathers and traditions are judged by it, and nothing not provable from it may be required as necessary belief.
positions.mark: The passage says nothing may be believed as necessary unless proved from Scripture, or that councils and church teachers are to be judged by Scripture as the final norm.
positions.first_defined: Formula of Concord (1577); Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571); Westminster Confession (1646)

positions.name: Scripture with binding Church tradition

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 4 (1546)
defined.quote: receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety, and reverence, all the books both of the Old and of the New Testament ... as also the said traditions, as well those appertaining to faith as to morals

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 2 (1672)
defined.quote: the witness also of the Catholic Church is, we believe, not of inferior authority to that of the Divine Scriptures.

defined.source: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, Canonical books
defined.quote: The word of God is not contained in the Bible alone, it is to be found in tradition as well.

positions.statement: Unwritten apostolic tradition, kept in the Church, binds with the same authority as Scripture, and the Church's interpretation of Scripture is authoritative.
positions.mark: The passage says some practice or doctrine is held from unwritten apostolic tradition with binding force, or that the Church's tradition holds equal authority with Scripture.

first_states.author: Irenaeus
first_states.text: When they are refuted from the Scriptures, they turn around and accuse the Scriptures themselves, as if the Scriptures were not rightly constituted, lacked authority, and contradicted themselves because they were expressed in various ways. They claim that truth cannot be discovered from the Scriptures by those who do not know the tradition. After all, the tradition was handed down not in writing, but by living voice. That is why Paul said, "We speak wisdom among the mature, yet a wisdom not of this world" (1 Corinthians 2:6-7). Each of these heretics then claims that this wisdom is exactly what he has discovered on his own — an obvious fiction — so that truth may appear worthy on his own terms: at one time in Valentinus, at another in Marcion, then in Cerinthus, later in Basilides, and even in the one who argues against the rest, though he could speak nothing that saves. Every single one

scripture-alone.quote: they claim that truth cannot be discovered from the Scriptures by those who do not know the tradition. After all, the tradition was handed down not in writing, but by living voice.
scripture-alone.audited: Irenaeus's own move, against the heretics' reported claim, is decisive: 'when we appeal to the tradition that comes from the Apostles - the tradition preserved in the Churches through the succession of Presbyters - they reject it.' Rejection of the Church's preserved apostolic tradition is treated as culpable error; a norm beyond Scripture is required, which the alone-position denies.

scripture-and-tradition.quote: When we appeal to the tradition that comes from the Apostles — the tradition preserved in the Churches through the succession of Presbyters
scripture-and-tradition.audited: Irenaeus appeals in his own voice to 'the tradition that comes from the Apostles - the tradition preserved in the Churches through the succession of Presbyters' as the authority the heretics wrongly reject - unwritten apostolic tradition kept in the Church, appealed to as binding.

passages.author: Irenaeus
passages.text: When they are confronted with Scripture, they turn their attack against Scripture itself, claiming it is not rightly preserved, lacks authority, contradicts itself in its varied expressions, and cannot yield truth to those who lack the tradition. For that tradition was not handed down in writing but by living voice — which is why Paul declared, "We speak wisdom among the perfect, but not the wisdom of this world" (1 Corinthians 2:6). Each of these teachers claims that this wisdom is his own private discovery, a mere invention, so that truth might be whatever suits him: one moment it appears in Valentinus, another in Marcion, then in Cerinthus, later in Basilides, even in the one who argues against the rest yet could speak nothing that saves. Every single one of them is thoroughly perverted; without shame each makes himself the rule of truth, distorting it as he preaches. But when we appe

scripture-alone.quote: cannot yield truth to those who lack the tradition. For that tradition was not handed down in writing but by living voice
scripture-alone.audited: Second translation of the same passage: apostolic truth is guarded in the tradition 'handed down not in writing but by living voice' and preserved through the succession of presbyters; necessary truth is not confined to Scripture.

scripture-and-tradition.quote: the tradition that comes from the Apostles — the tradition guarded through the succession of presbyters in the churches
scripture-and-tradition.audited: The tradition from the Apostles, 'guarded through the succession of presbyters in the churches,' is appealed to as the standing authority against the heretics - unwritten tradition with binding force alongside Scripture.

passages.author: Irenaeus
passages.text: They insisted that the men they were leaving behind as successors be thoroughly blameless and irreproachable in every respect, so that great benefit would come to those who would act in their place of teaching, while the greatest calamity would befall those who fell away. But because it would take far too long to list the successions of every church in a work of this scope, we will set forth the tradition that comes from the Apostles and the faith proclaimed to humanity, which has reached us through the succession of bishops from the most glorious two Apostles, Peter and Paul, who founded and established the church at Rome. By doing so we confound all those who, in any manner — whether through self-pleasing evil, empty glory, blindness, or bad judgment — gather in any way other than what is fitting. For every church must convene to this church on account of its more powerful principality

scripture-alone.quote: the faithful from everywhere must come together here, because in this church the tradition that comes from the Apostles has always been preserved
scripture-alone.audited: Against Heresies 3.3.2: the apostolic tradition preserved at Rome is set forth to confound all who gather otherwise, and 'every church must convene to this church' because there 'the tradition that comes from the Apostles has always been preserved' - tradition as the rule to which churches must submit.

scripture-and-tradition.quote: we will set forth the tradition that comes from the Apostles... this church the tradition that comes from the Apostles has always been preserved
scripture-and-tradition.audited: The tradition from the Apostles, reached 'through the succession of bishops from the most glorious two Apostles, Peter and Paul,' and preserved in the Roman church, binds every church to convene there - unwritten apostolic tradition with authoritative force.

passages.author: Irenaeus
passages.text: The apostolic plan stands revealed throughout the whole world; it is present for all who wish to see the truth to behold in every church. We can enumerate those whom the apostles instituted as bishops in the churches, along with their successions down to us — men who taught nothing of the kind, nor knew it, the very thing these people rave about. If the apostles had known hidden mysteries, which they taught separately and secretly to the perfect, they would have handed them over especially to those to whom they also entrusted the churches themselves. They wanted those they left as successors to be very strong and irreproachable in all things, so that by handing over their own place of teaching great benefit would come to those who act rightly, but the greatest calamity to those who fall away. Since it would be far too long to enumerate the successions of all the churches in a volume of t

scripture-alone.quote: We set forth the tradition it has from the apostles ... By this we confound all those who ... gather otherwise than is fitting.
scripture-alone.audited: Against Heresies 3.3.1: 'We set forth the tradition it has from the apostles and the faith proclaimed to humanity, coming down through the successions of bishops to us. By this we confound all those who... gather otherwise than is fitting.' The preserved tradition is the confounding standard - a required norm beyond Scripture.

scripture-and-tradition.quote: We set forth the tradition it has from the apostles and the faith proclaimed to humanity, coming down through the successions of bishops to us.
scripture-and-tradition.audited: The tradition from the apostles, coming down through the successions of bishops and set forth by the Roman church, is presented as the standard that confounds dissenters and to which every church must convene - apostolic tradition kept in the Church, binding.

passages.author: Irenaeus
passages.text: It is necessary to obey the presbyters who are in the Church, those who possess succession from the Apostles, just as we have shown; for they, together with the succession of the episcopate, have received a certain charisma of truth according to the will of the Father (Leviticus 10:1-2). But those others who stand apart from the principal succession, and who gather in whatever place, must be regarded with suspicion, whether as heretics and men of bad judgment, or as those who divide, are puffed up, and please themselves, or again as hypocrites who act for the sake of gain and vain glory (Numbers 16:31-33). All these, however, are far from the truth (1 Kings 12:26-33). The heretics, bringing foreign fire to the altar of God — that is, foreign doctrines — will be consumed by heavenly fire, just as Nadab and Abihu were. Those who rise up against the truth and urge others against the Church

scripture-alone.quote: It is necessary to obey the presbyters … who possess succession from the Apostles … they … have received a certain charisma of truth.
scripture-alone.audited: Against Heresies 4.26.2: 'It is necessary to obey the presbyters... who possess succession from the Apostles... together with the succession of the episcopate, have received a certain charisma of truth.' A divinely given charism of truth in the succession, with obedience necessary and those outside it 'far from the truth,' is a binding teaching authority not derived from Scripture.

passages.author: Irenaeus
passages.text: Since these demonstrations exist, it is no longer necessary to seek the truth from others, for it is easy to take it from the Church. The Apostles, as though pouring into a rich repository, have fully deposited all things of truth within it, so that anyone who wishes may draw from it the drink of life. For this is the entrance to life; all the rest, however, are thieves and robbers (John 10:1, 8-9). Therefore it is necessary to avoid them, but with the greatest diligence to love and to seize the tradition of truth that belongs to the Church. For what if there were a dispute about some small question? Would it not be necessary to have recourse to the most ancient churches, in which the Apostles conversed, and from them to take concerning the present question what is certain and clear? They wanted those successors to be steadfast and blameless in everything, so that their right stewardship of the apostolic office would bring great benefit, while their failure would bring utter disaster. passages.author: Irenaeus
passages.text: All these heretics came long after the bishops to whom the Apostles entrusted the churches, a point we proved in the third book with every care. Because they are blind to the truth, they are forced to wander off onto one divergent path after another, so the footprints of their teaching lie scattered in discordant, incoherent disarray. But those who belong to the Church walk the whole world over, bearing a firm tradition from the Apostles that lets us see one and the same faith everywhere: one and the same God the Father worshipped by all, the same mystery of the Son's incarnation believed, the same gift of the Spirit received, the same precepts pondered, the same pattern of ordination that serves the Church preserved, the same hope of the Lord's return cherished, and the same salvation of the whole person—soul and body—upheld. The Church's preaching is true and steadfast, and in it the s

scripture-and-tradition.quote: firm tradition from the Apostles that lets us see one and the same faith everywhere... The Church's preaching is true and steadfast, and in it the single way of salvation is displayed throughout the world.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: If this is how things stand—that truth is awarded to us who walk the rule the Church received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, and Christ from God—then the rationale behind our position is settled: heretics must not be admitted to a contest over Scripture. We have already proved, without using Scripture, that they have no connection to it. If they are heretics, they cannot be Christians; they possess nothing from Christ, yet they embrace the very name that marks their chosen faction. Not being Christians, they hold no right to Christian writings. So we are fully justified in demanding: Who are you? When and from where did you come? What are you doing in what is mine, not yours? By what right, Marcion, do you cut down my forest? By what license, Valentinus, do you divert my springs? By what power, Apelles, do you move my boundary markers? What are the rest of you doing, sowing

scripture-alone.quote: we have already proved, without using Scripture, that they have no connection to it.
scripture-alone.audited: Prescription 37: 'truth is awarded to us who walk the rule the Church received from the Apostles,' and heretics are barred from contesting Scripture at all because they have no connection to it - access to Scripture is governed by the Church's received rule, so Scripture alone is not the final norm.

scripture-and-tradition.quote: walk the rule the Church received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, and Christ from God
scripture-and-tradition.audited: The rule 'the Church received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, and Christ from God' awards truth and excludes heretics from Scripture itself; Tertullian holds the apostolic deposit as the Church's testament and inheritance - the kept tradition functioning with binding authority, beyond a mere creed summary.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: So we lay down our rule: if the Lord Jesus Christ sent the Apostles to preach, then no other preachers are to be accepted except the ones Christ himself appointed. For no one knows the Father except the Son, and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. And the Son does not appear to have revealed the Father to anyone except the Apostles he sent to preach — precisely what he revealed to them. Now, what they preached — that is, what Christ revealed to them — I insist must be proved in no other way than through the very churches the Apostles themselves founded, preaching to them in person, as they say, with living voice, and later by their letters. If that is how it stands, then it follows that any doctrine which agrees with those apostolic churches — the matrices and originals of the faith — is to be counted as true, beyond doubt holding what the Churches received from the Apostles, th

scripture-alone.quote: must be proved in no other way than through the very churches the Apostles themselves founded, preaching to them in person, ... and later by their letters.
scripture-alone.audited: Prescription 21: what the apostles preached 'must be proved in no other way than through the very churches the Apostles themselves founded, preaching to them in person... with living voice, and later by their letters,' and 'any doctrine which agrees with those apostolic churches... is to be counted as true' while every other 'is to be prejudged as a lie.' Proof runs through the churches' received faith, expressly not through Scripture alone.

scripture-and-tradition.quote: any doctrine which agrees with those apostolic churches ... is to be counted as true, beyond doubt holding what the Churches received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, Christ from God.
scripture-and-tradition.audited: The apostles preached 'with living voice' as well as by letters, and what 'the Churches received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, Christ from God' is the criterion of truth 'beyond doubt' - the received, partly unwritten apostolic delivery binds as the standard of doctrine.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: Still, if anyone dares to slot themselves into the apostolic age so they can claim the apostles handed them down—since they were 'under the apostles'—we can say: Let them produce the origins of their churches. Let them lay out the succession of their bishops, running unbroken from the start, so that their first bishop can show an apostle, or an apostolic man who stuck with the apostles, as his author and predecessor. That is how apostolic churches present their credentials: the church of Smyrna reports Polycarp was appointed by John; Rome produces Clement, ordained by Peter; likewise every other church exhibits bishops the apostles installed, as bearers of apostolic seed. Let the heretics fabricate a pedigree like that. What is forbidden them after blasphemy? But even if they forge one, they gain nothing. Their own doctrine, set beside the apostolic, will expose by its variety and contra

scripture-and-tradition.quote: Let them produce the origins of their churches… bishops … running unbroken from the start… as bearers of apostolic seed… because just as the apostles never taught conflicting things among themselves, so apostolic men never proclaimed anything contrary to the apostles.
scripture-and-tradition.audited: Prescription 32 (second translation): churches are tested by the succession of their bishops and by conspiring 'in the same faith' - the apostolic tradition maintained in the churches is the standard against which doctrine and churches are judged.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: If anyone dares to wedge themselves into the apostolic era just so they can claim the Apostles handed them down—on the grounds that they ‘lived under the Apostles’—we can answer bluntly: let them cough up the origins of their churches. Let them lay out the full line of their bishops, an unbroken succession from the very start, so that their first bishop can name an Apostle—or at least an apostolic man who stuck with the Apostles—as his author and predecessor. That is exactly how the apostolic churches present their credentials: the church of Smyrna records that John installed Polycarp; the Romans produce Clement, ordained by Peter. In the same way, every other church displays the men the Apostles themselves appointed to the episcopate, the living carriers of apostolic seed. Let the heretics try to fabricate a list like that. After blasphemy, what is left that they would not dare? Yet eve

scripture-and-tradition.quote: Therefore, churches that cannot name an Apostle ... are nevertheless judged apostolic because they conspire in the same faith; the kinship of doctrine makes them family.
scripture-and-tradition.audited: Prescription 32: churches are judged apostolic by the faith handed down in them - later churches 'are nevertheless judged apostolic because they conspire in the same faith; the kinship of doctrine makes them family,' and the bishops are 'living carriers of apostolic seed.' Conformity to the tradition kept in the churches is the binding test.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: Go ahead: suppose everyone got it wrong. Suppose the Apostle was duped when he bore witness to certain people. Suppose the Holy Spirit never glanced back to guide anyone into truth, even though Christ sent Him for that very purpose and the Father dispatched Him to be the teacher of truth. Suppose the steward of God, the vicar of Christ, neglected his job and let the churches understand and believe something different in the meantime from what He Himself had preached through the Apostles. Is it really plausible that so many and such great churches all erred their way into a single faith? Among many events there is not a single outcome; the error of the churches' doctrine should have varied. Yet what is found to be one and the same among many is not an error—it is a tradition. So let anyone dare to claim that the ones who handed it down were wrong.

scripture-alone.quote: what is found to be one and the same among many is not an error—it is a tradition.
scripture-alone.audited: Prescription 28: 'what is found to be one and the same among many is not an error - it is a tradition. So let anyone dare to claim that the ones who handed it down were wrong.' The churches' unanimous tradition is self-authenticating; necessary doctrine is secured by tradition itself, not by Scripture alone.

scripture-and-tradition.quote: So let anyone dare to claim that the ones who handed it down were wrong.
scripture-and-tradition.audited: The handed-down tradition of the churches, one and the same among so many, cannot be gainsaid: 'let anyone dare to claim that the ones who handed it down were wrong.' In this treatise that tradition is the operative standard of doctrine - unwritten apostolic tradition carrying binding force.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: If things stand this way—if the truth is awarded to us, who follow the rule that the Church received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, Christ from God—then the logic of our position is settled: heretics must not be admitted to a contest over Scripture, because we prove, even without Scripture, that they have no claim on it. If they are heretics, they cannot be Christians; they possess nothing from Christ, having chosen to follow their own preference and taken the name 'heretic.' Not being Christians, they hold no right to Christian writings. We are therefore justified in demanding: Who are you? When and where did you come from? What are you doing on my property—property that is not yours? By what right, Marcion, do you cut down my forest? By what license, Valentine, do you divert my springs? By what authority, Apelles, do you move my boundary markers? What are the rest of you

scripture-alone.quote: we prove, even without Scripture, that they have no claim on it.

scripture-and-tradition.quote: the rule that the Church received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, Christ from God

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: Come now — suppose they all erred. Suppose the Apostle was deceived in his testimony to certain people. Suppose the Holy Spirit never glanced back to guide the Church into truth, despite being sent by Christ for that very purpose, requested from the Father for that very purpose, to be the teacher of truth. Suppose the steward of God, the vicar of Christ, neglected his duty, letting the churches meanwhile understand and believe something other than what he himself preached through the apostles. Is it plausible that so many and such great churches would have erred their way into a single faith? Among many events there is not a single outcome: the error of the churches' doctrine should have varied. Yet what is found to be one across many is not error — it is tradition. So let someone dare to claim that those who handed it down were mistaken.

scripture-alone.quote: what is found to be one across many is not error — it is tradition

scripture-and-tradition.quote: what is found to be one across many is not error — it is tradition

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: Therefore we must not appeal to the Scriptures, nor set the contest in them, where the outcome is either no victory, an uncertain one, or a tie that is equally uncertain. Even if a comparison of the Scriptures did not end up leveling both sides, the logical order demanded that the primary question be raised first—the only question now at issue: To whom does the faith itself belong? Whose are the Scriptures? From whom, through whom, when, and to whom was the discipline that makes Christians handed down? For wherever the truth of Christian discipline and faith appears, there will be the truth of the Scriptures, of their interpretations, and of all Christian traditions.

scripture-alone.quote: we must not appeal to the Scriptures, nor set the contest in them

scripture-and-tradition.quote: To whom does the faith itself belong? Whose are the Scriptures? From whom, through whom, when, and to whom was the discipline that makes Christians handed down?

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: If this is how things stand, so that truth is adjudged to us who walk in that rule of faith which the church handed down from the apostles, the apostles from Christ, and Christ from God, then the reasoning of our position is established: we define that heretics must not be admitted to bring a challenge from the Scriptures, since we prove without the Scriptures that they have no claim to the Scriptures. For if they are heretics, they cannot be Christians, since they do not hold from Christ what they have followed by their own choice, and so they take on the name of heretics. Being therefore not Christians, they acquire no right to Christian writings, and to them it is rightly said: Who are you? When did you come, and from where? What are you doing on my property, you who are not mine? By what right, Marcion, do you cut down my forest? By what license, Valentinus, do you divert my springs?

scripture-alone.quote: heretics must not be admitted to bring a challenge from the Scriptures, since we prove without the Scriptures that they have no claim to the Scriptures
scripture-alone.audited: Prescription 37 (site translation): 'truth is adjudged to us who walk in that rule of faith which the church handed down from the apostles,' and heretics 'must not be admitted to bring a challenge from the Scriptures, since we prove without the Scriptures that they have no claim to the Scriptures' - the claim is established without Scripture, by the handed-down rule.

scripture-and-tradition.quote: the rule of faith which the church handed down from the apostles, the apostles from Christ, and Christ from God
scripture-and-tradition.audited: The 'rule of faith which the church handed down from the apostles, the apostles from Christ, and Christ from God' adjudges truth; the Church is 'the heir of the apostles,' holding what they 'provided in their testament... entrusted to faith... bound by oath' - the handed-down tradition as binding authority.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: So there must be no appeal to the Scriptures, and no contest established in them where victory is either nonexistent, or uncertain, or not certain enough. For even if a comparison of the Scriptures did not turn out in such a way as to make both sides stand equal, the order of things was requiring that this be proposed first, which alone is now to be disputed: to whom the faith itself belongs, whose the Scriptures are, from whom, and through whom, and when, and to whom was handed down the discipline by which people become Christians. For where it has appeared that the truth of the Christian discipline and faith is, there will be the truth of the Scriptures and of their interpretations and of all Christian traditions.

scripture-alone.quote: where it has appeared that the truth of the Christian discipline and faith is, there will be the truth of the Scriptures and of their interpretations
scripture-alone.audited: Prescription 19: 'there must be no appeal to the Scriptures... For where it has appeared that the truth of the Christian discipline and faith is, there will be the truth of the Scriptures and of their interpretations and of all Christian traditions.' Scripture's truth is found only after locating the Church that holds the faith - Scripture is expressly denied the role of first and final norm.

scripture-and-tradition.quote: the truth of the Scriptures and of their interpretations and of all Christian traditions.
scripture-and-tradition.audited: Where the truth of the Christian discipline and faith is found, 'there will be the truth of the Scriptures and of their interpretations and of all Christian traditions' - the Church's traditions stand in the truth-series with Scripture and its interpretation, certified by the Church's prior possession of the faith.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: If this is so, it is settled that every doctrine which agrees with those apostolic churches, the mothers and originals of the faith, is to be assigned to the truth. Such a doctrine undoubtedly holds what the churches received from the apostles, the apostles from Christ, and Christ from God. But every doctrine that savors against the truth of the churches and of the apostles of Christ and of God is to be judged beforehand as coming from falsehood.

scripture-alone.quote: every doctrine which agrees with those apostolic churches... is to be assigned to the truth.
scripture-alone.audited: Prescription 21 (site translation): 'every doctrine which agrees with those apostolic churches, the mothers and originals of the faith, is to be assigned to the truth... every doctrine that savors against the truth of the churches... is to be judged beforehand as coming from falsehood.' Agreement with the churches' received faith, not proof from Scripture, is the criterion.

scripture-and-tradition.quote: every doctrine which agrees with those apostolic churches... is to be assigned to the truth.
scripture-and-tradition.audited: What the churches 'received from the apostles, the apostles from Christ, and Christ from God,' held by the apostolic churches, is the standard that assigns doctrine to truth or falsehood - the received apostolic tradition binding as the test of doctrine.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: You prescribe that the solemn observances of this faith were established by the Scriptures or by the tradition of the elders, and that nothing further in the way of observance may be added, because innovation is unlawful. Stand on that ground if you can. For look, I meet you as people who fast beyond Passover, apart from those days on which the bridegroom was taken away, who insert the half-fasts of station days, and who sometimes live on bread and water, as each of you sees fit. In the end you answer that these things are to be done by choice, not by command. So you have moved from your ground by going beyond tradition, since you practice things that were not established. But what kind of reasoning is it, that you allow to your own choice what you do not grant to God's command? Will more be permitted to human will than to divine power? I remember that I am free with respect to the world

scripture-alone.quote: established by the Scriptures or by the tradition of the elders, and that nothing further ... may be added, because innovation is unlawful
scripture-alone.audited: On Fasting 13: the no-innovation principle - observances 'established by the Scriptures or by the tradition of the elders, and nothing further may be added' - is the opponents' ground, quoted to be attacked ('Stand on that ground if you can'); Tertullian defends observances commanded beyond it. The author's own stance rejects Scripture (even Scripture-or-tradition) as the sole binding limit.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: But as long as the form of the rule remains in its proper order, you may seek and discuss as much as you like and pour out all the desire of your curiosity, if anything seems to you to hang in ambiguity or be shadowed by obscurity. There is certainly some brother endowed with the gift of knowledge, some one among the trained, some curious person who has spent time with you—yet one who seeks with you. In the end he will know better that you should be ignorant, so that you may not know what you ought not to know, because you know what you ought to know. "Your faith," he says, "has saved you," not your exercise in the Scriptures. Faith is placed in the rule; it has law and salvation from observing the law. Exercise, however, consists in curiosity, having glory only from the pursuit of skill. Let curiosity yield to faith; let glory yield to salvation. Certainly let them either not clamor aga

scripture-alone.quote: Your faith has saved you, not your exercise in the Scriptures.
scripture-alone.audited: Prescription 14: ''Your faith has saved you,' not your exercise in the Scriptures. Faith is placed in the rule; it has law and salvation from observing the law... To know nothing against the rule is to know everything.' The received rule - not Scripture exercise - is the norm of saving faith, set over the reader's use of Scripture.

scripture-and-tradition.quote: Your faith has saved you, not your exercise in the Scriptures. Faith is placed in the rule; it has law and salvation from observing the law.
scripture-and-tradition.audited: Faith 'is placed in the rule; it has law and salvation from observing the law.' The rule handed down in the Church binds with law and salvation attached - the kept apostolic tradition exercising authority alongside, and over, private exercise in the Scriptures.

passages.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
passages.text: Such, then, as we said before, is their madness and boldness. But our faith is right, and it springs from apostolic teaching and the tradition of the Fathers, and is confirmed by both the New and the Old Testament. The prophets say: Send out your Word and your truth (Psalm 42:3 LXX); and: Behold, the Virgin shall conceive and bear a Son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which is translated, God with us (Isaiah 7:14).

scripture-alone.quote: our faith ... springs from apostolic teaching and the tradition of the Fathers, and is confirmed by both the New and the Old Testament
scripture-alone.audited: Athanasius, Letter to Adelphius 3: 'our faith is right, and it springs from apostolic teaching and the tradition of the Fathers, and is confirmed by both the New and the Old Testament.' Faith springs from the Fathers' tradition as a co-source and is confirmed by Scripture - tradition is not presented as judged by Scripture.

scripture-and-tradition.quote: our faith ... springs from apostolic teaching and the tradition of the Fathers, and is confirmed by both the New and the Old Testament
scripture-and-tradition.audited: Faith 'springs from apostolic teaching and the tradition of the Fathers' - the tradition of the Fathers is named as a source of the faith alongside the apostolic teaching, with Scripture confirming what springs from both.

passages.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
passages.text: But let only the faith confessed at Nicaea by the Fathers hold sway among you. In that council, as we said before, all the Fathers were present—even those now fighting against it—and they signed. So the Apostle may say about us: “I praise you because you remember me in everything and hold firmly to the traditions just as I handed them on to you” (1 Corinthians 11:2). For this council at Nicaea is truly an inscription set up against every heresy. It also overthrows those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit and call the Spirit a creature. For after the Fathers spoke about faith in the Son, they immediately added: “We believe also in the Holy Spirit,” so that by confessing a complete and full faith in the Holy Trinity they might make known in this the imprint of faith in Christ and the teaching of the Catholic Church. For it is clear both among you and among all people, and no Christian w

scripture-alone.audited: Athanasius, Letter to the Africans 8: 'let only the faith confessed at Nicaea by the Fathers hold sway among you... this council at Nicaea is truly an inscription set up against every heresy.' A council's confession is imposed as the sway-holding standard in itself - more than the respect the shared ground grants councils, and not a standard the passage submits to Scripture's judgment.

scripture-and-tradition.audited: The Nicene faith is to 'hold sway,' the council is 'an inscription set up against every heresy,' and Paul's word is applied to it: 'hold firmly to the traditions just as I handed them on to you' (1 Corinthians 11:2) - the Church's conciliar tradition functioning as the binding rule of faith.

first_states.author: Origen (anthology by Basil & Gregory)
first_states.text: In the passage on numbers, each number has a certain power among the things that exist, which the Maker of all used in composing sometimes the whole and sometimes some particular kind; so we must pay attention and trace out from the Scriptures what concerns them and each one of them. We should not overlook that the covenant books, as the Hebrews hand them down, are twenty-two, the same number as the letters of their alphabet, and this is not without reason. For as the twenty-two letters seem to be an introduction to wisdom and to the divine teachings stamped on people in these characters, so the twenty-two God-breathed books are an alphabet of the wisdom of God and an introduction to the knowledge of things that are.

hebrew-canon.quote: the covenant books, as the Hebrews hand them down, are twenty-two, the same number as the letters of their alphabet

passages.author: Origen of Alexandria
passages.text: You objected that I used Susanna as if unaware some call it uncanonical. I answer from the wider fact: in many holy books we find more or less than the Hebrews transmit — in Job and elsewhere verses stand with us that are absent there, and the church’s edification has long received these books. hebrew-canon.quote: the church's edification has long received these books

Γραφῇ), a section 'carried in every Church of Christ' though absent from the Hebrew, and refuses to move the churches' landmarks, so he counts Susanna as Scripture.
