positions.statement: God declares the sinner righteous by crediting Christ's righteousness to him, received by faith alone; inner renewal follows but is not the ground.
positions.mark: The passage says justification is God's verdict counting the sinner righteous on account of Christ's righteousness reckoned to him, received by faith without works.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession IV (1530); Formula of Concord III (1577); Westminster Confession 11 (1646)

first_states.author: Anonymous (Epistle to Diognetus)
first_states.text: For what else could cover our sins except his righteousness? In whom could we, lawless and impious as we are, be made righteous except in the Son of God alone? Oh, the sweet exchange! Oh, the unsearchable workmanship! Oh, the unexpected benefits! For the lawlessness of many was hidden in one righteous man, and the righteousness of one made many lawless people righteous.

forensic-imputation.quote: the righteousness of one made many lawless people righteous
forensic-imputation.audited: Diognetus 9, the 'sweet exchange': 'For what else could cover our sins except his righteousness? In whom could we, lawless and impious as we are, be made righteous except in the Son of God alone?... the lawlessness of many was hidden in one righteous man, and the righteousness of one made many lawless people righteous.' Sinners are made righteous wholly by the Righteous One's righteousness covering them and hiding their lawlessness in him - justification grounded in Christ's righteousness reckoned to the sinner, not in righteousness produced in the sinner.

infused-righteousness.quote: the righteousness of one made many lawless people righteous
infused-righteousness.audited: The mechanism is covering from outside: his righteousness COVERS our sins; our lawlessness is HIDDEN in the one righteous man. Nothing is said of grace or love poured into the heart making the sinner inwardly righteous as the ground - the righteousness that makes the lawless righteous remains Christ's.

positions.name: By faith working through love, with righteousness infused

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 6, ch. 7 (1547)
defined.quote: the charity of God is poured forth, by the Holy Spirit, in the hearts of those that are justified, and is inherent therein

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 13 (1672)
defined.quote: We believe a man to be not simply justified through faith alone, but through faith which works through love, that is to say, through faith and works.

positions.statement: In justification God makes the sinner inwardly righteous by grace and love poured into the heart; faith justifies as faith working through love, together with works.
positions.mark: The passage says the justified are made righteous by grace or love dwelling in them, or that faith justifies together with love or works.
positions.first_defined: Council of Trent, Session 6 (1547); Synod of Jerusalem, Decree 13 (1672)

first_states.author: Clement of Alexandria
first_states.text: But you, learn the way according to excess that Paul points to for salvation. "Love does not seek its own things," but is poured out upon the brother. It is frantic for him, and soberly raves for him. "Love covers a multitude of sins" (1 Peter 4:8). "Perfect love casts out fear" (1 John 4:18). "It does not boast; it is not puffed up. It does not rejoice in wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails. Prophecies are abolished; tongues cease; healings are left behind upon the earth. But these three remain: faith, hope, love; and the greatest of these is love" (1 Corinthians 13:4-8, 13). And rightly so. For faith departs when we are persuaded by seeing God with our own eyes, and hope vanishes when the things hoped for are handed over. But love comes together into fullness and grows all the more whe

infused-righteousness.quote: If someone casts this love into his soul, he can—even if he was born in sins, even if he has done many of the things that are forbidden—grow the love, receive pure repentance, and fight back against the things he has done wrong.
infused-righteousness.audited: Clement, Who Is the Rich Man Saved? 38, gives Paul's 'way according to excess' FOR SALVATION: 'If someone casts this love into his soul, he can - even if he was born in sins, even if he has done many of the things that are forbidden - grow the love, receive pure repentance, and fight back against the things he has done wrong,' under 'Love covers a multitude of sins' (1 Peter 4:8). Love indwelling the soul, growing there, covering sins and producing pure repentance, is the saving righteousness at work in the person.

positions.name: Salvation as union with God (theosis)
positions.statement: Salvation is the healing and deification of the person through participation in God's life, by grace and human cooperation; 'justification' is one aspect of that union.
positions.mark: The passage describes salvation as becoming god by grace or sharing in the divine nature, and treats this, not a legal verdict, as what saving righteousness is.
positions.first_defined: No conciliar definition; a frame of Orthodox theology

first_uncertain.author: Didymus the Blind
first_uncertain.text: But the diligent, through much boldness and the freedom of the gaze before God, have stood as genuine servants of justice, saying, 'Look upon me and have mercy on me' (Ps 51:1), and 'The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous and His gaze upon their prayer' (Ps 34:15). Do not be troubled, since we, the ones confessing and possessing beauty before the Lord, participate in this; and often, according to the Scripture, regarding those having certain states, it is said through the analogies of those states; for the Apostle, writing to men, says concerning him and them, 'That we might become the righteousness of God' (2 Cor 5:21) (meaning clearly, in Him, Christ).

theosis.quote: "that we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Cor 5:21) (meaning clearly, in Him, Christ)
theosis.audited: Didymus on the Psalms takes up 2 Corinthians 5:21 with his own gloss: ''That we might become the righteousness of God' (meaning clearly, in Him, Christ)... we, the ones confessing and possessing beauty before the Lord, PARTICIPATE in this.' Saving righteousness is a becoming - we become God's righteousness in Christ by participation - not a verdict counting an alien righteousness. Participation in what God is, in Christ, is the content of the righteousness.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: So those utterly wicked characters are stirring up these questions. They claim baptism isn't necessary for people who have faith, since Abraham pleased God through the sacrament of faith alone, without any water at all. But they're arguing backward: in every case, what comes later decides the matter, and the subsequent overrides the prior. Before the Lord's passion and resurrection, salvation was possible through bare faith. But once faith expanded to include belief in his birth, passion, and resurrection, the sacrament was amplified — baptism was added as a seal, a kind of garment for faith that had previously stood naked and lacked power without its own governing law. That law of baptizing was imposed, and the form was prescribed: "Go, make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matt 28:19). To that law this definition

passages.author: Severianus of Gabala
passages.text: The Savior, having received this voice, says: 'Today salvation has come to this house' (Luke 19:9). He justified himself, not because he simply saw Christ, but because he obeyed the laws of Christ. Today salvation has come to this house, because this man also is a son of Abraham. Before doing the works of Abraham, he does not call him a son of Abraham, but calls him Zacchaeus by the bare appellation; but when he fulfilled the works of the patriarch, promising charity and the restitution of the injustice, then he says: 'And this man also is a son of Abraham.'

forensic-imputation.quote: He justified himself, not because he simply saw Christ, but because he obeyed the laws of Christ
forensic-imputation.audited: 'He justified himself, not because he simply saw Christ, but because he obeyed the laws of Christ' (Αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν ἐδικαίωσεν... ἐπειδὴ τοῖς Χριστοῦ ὑπήκουσε νόμοις); salvation comes when he 'fulfilled the works of the patriarch'. Greek checked: faithful. Justification by obedience rules out faith-alone imputation. Borderline: homiletic, playing on his self-condemnation just before.

infused-righteousness.quote: He justified himself, not because he simply saw Christ, but because he obeyed the laws of Christ
infused-righteousness.audited: Zacchaeus is justified 'because he obeyed the laws of Christ', and the sermon continues 'let us adorn faith with works' (σεμνύνωμεν τοῖς ἔργοις τὴν πίστιν). That is justification by faith together with works. Borderline: a preacher's point, not a definition. ATTRIBUTION: De caeco et Zacchaeo is transmitted among Chrysostom's spuria and given to Severian only by modern scholars.

passages.attribution_note: Transmitted among Chrysostom's spurious works; given to Severian only by modern attribution.

passages.author: John Chrysostom
passages.text: We promised to show you that those who approach the washing become clean from all fornication, but the word has demonstrated something more: that they become not only clean, but also holy and righteous. For he did not say only, You were washed, but also, You were sanctified and justified. What could be more astonishing than this, when righteousness is born without labors and sweat and achievements? Such is the loving-kindness of the divine gift: it makes people righteous without sweat.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: And if, speaking briefly, we must also leap to certain ancient narratives, I will say again that God was promising to Abraham the grace through faith, and, as in a firstfruits of those shown mercy, he was making in him the forgiveness from gentleness older than the Law. For it is written that 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.' (Genesis 15:6) And Paul adds his witness, saying, 'How then was it counted? In circumcision or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, he says, but in uncircumcision; and he received a sign, circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which was in uncircumcision.' (Romans 4:10–11) And he heard God saying plainly that 'in you all the nations shall be blessed.' (Genesis 12:3) And the 'in you' would mean, according to your likeness. So Paul, understanding it this way, says, 'The Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the

forensic-imputation.quote: Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness
forensic-imputation.audited: Cyril, On Adoration 1, argues in his own voice: 'God was promising to Abraham the grace through faith... Abraham believed God, and it was COUNTED to him for righteousness (Genesis 15:6)... Circumcision, then, is a sign of the faith in uncircumcision, and he has been JUSTIFIED NOT FROM WORKS OF LAW, and the boasts through faith appear older than the circumcision in the flesh,' expounding Galatians 3:8-9 - 'God justifies the nations from faith.' Righteousness counted to believing faith, before and apart from works of the Law, as the author's own doctrinal conclusion.

infused-righteousness.quote: it was counted to him for righteousness… he has been justified not from works of Law.
infused-righteousness.audited: Cyril's own rule: 'The Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the nations FROM FAITH, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham... he has been justified not from works of Law.' The ground of justification is faith, to which righteousness is counted - not faith together with works as the ground.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: rs, and that God is able even to raise from the dead. Yet Paul makes the blessed David, a man famous for piety, a witness and helper of his own words, and wisely sets forth, as in the Spirit, the forgiveness that comes through faith and announces it to all people; for he knew that it would be present in Christ in due time. 'You see that faith was working together with his works, and by the works faith was made complete' (James 2:22). Cyril: He was bringing the rational sacrifice, bidding the laws of nature farewell, trampling the goad of a father's unyielding love, and setting nothing earthly against his love for God. 'And Abraham believed God' (James 2:23). Cyril: So the one who honors the God and Master of all with faith has righteousness as his prize. 'If anyone does not stumble in word, he is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body as well' (James 3:2).

forensic-imputation.quote: faith was working together with his works, and by the works faith was made complete
forensic-imputation.audited: Cyril's James commentary expounds James 2:22 with his own glosses ('Cyril: He was bringing the rational sacrifice, bidding the laws of nature farewell... So the one who honors the God and Master of all with faith has righteousness as his prize'): 'You see that faith was WORKING TOGETHER with his works, and by the works faith was MADE COMPLETE.' Abraham's faith justifying in synergy with, and completed by, his works contradicts justification by faith without works.

infused-righteousness.quote: faith was working together with his works, and by the works faith was made complete
infused-righteousness.audited: The same James exposition: Cyril presents 'faith was working together with his works, and by the works faith was made complete' (James 2:22) as the account of Abraham's righteousness, framed by his own commentary on the offering. Faith justifying together with works - this position's mark.

passages.author: Ammonius of Alexandria
passages.text: Through both fear and honor, then, he urges the human being toward salvation. So faith alone is not enough to save unless one also has good works.

forensic-imputation.quote: faith alone is not enough to save unless one also has good works
forensic-imputation.audited: Ammonius on John: 'faith alone is not enough to save unless one also has good works.' An express denial that faith alone saves - the forensic position's 'by faith alone, without works' is contradicted in terms.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Ammonius of Alexandria
passages.text: Not only for the disciples but also for all the faithful Christ asks that the grace given through the Holy Spirit be given—the grace that reshapes the human being into the divine image. And this union does not happen according to essence or according to hypostasis, but according to the agreement of faith, by which the faithful knew that the Son was incarnate by the Father’s good pleasure; for this is being sent.

theosis.quote: the grace that reshapes the human being into the divine image
theosis.audited: Ammonius on John: Christ asks 'that the grace given through the Holy Spirit be given - the grace that RESHAPES THE HUMAN BEING INTO THE DIVINE IMAGE. And this UNION does not happen according to essence or according to hypostasis, but according to the agreement of faith.' Salvation is union with God that reshapes the person into the divine image by grace - deification as the content of salvation, carefully distinguished from union by essence.

questions.question: From whom does the Holy Spirit eternally proceed?
shared_ground: The Spirit proceeds from the Father (John 15:26)
The Spirit proceeds 'from the Father through the Son' (claimed by both positions; never a position by itself, since no tradition here defines it as one)
The Spirit is called the Spirit of the Son or of Christ
The Son sends the Spirit into the world (temporal mission)
The Spirit is consubstantial with Father and Son
The Father is the source of the Godhead

positions.name: From the Father as sole source

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 1 (1672)
defined.quote: the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father, and consubstantial with the Father and the Son.

defined.source: Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs, 5.i (1848)
defined.quote: This novel opinion destroys the oneness from the One cause, and the diverse origin of the Persons of the Blessed Trinity

defined.source: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, The Faith of the Church (text by V. C. Samuel, 1970)
defined.quote: The Son is born of, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from, the Father.

positions.statement: The Father alone is the source and cause of the Spirit's eternal being; the Son is not a co-cause of the Spirit.
positions.mark: The passage says the Father alone is the cause or source of the Spirit's existence, or denies that the Spirit has his being from the Son.
positions.first_defined: Photius (9th c.); Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs (1848)

first_states.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
first_states.text: There is one God, the Father of the living Word, of subsisting wisdom and power, and of the eternal exact imprint: perfect, the perfect begetter, Father of the only-begotten Son. There is one Lord, alone from the Father alone, God from God, the exact imprint and image of the Godhead, the active Word, the wisdom that contains the constitution of all things, and the power that creates the whole creation: true Son of the true Father, invisible of the invisible, incorruptible of the incorruptible, immortal of the immortal, eternal of the eternal. And there is one Holy Spirit, who has existence from God and is manifested through the Son, that is, to human beings: the perfect image of the perfect Son, the cause of life for the living, the holy spring, holiness, the giver of holiness. In him God the Father is revealed, who is over all and in all, and God the Son, who is through all. The Trinity

from-the-father.quote: the Holy Spirit, who has existence from God and is manifested through the Son
from-the-father.audited: Gregory Thaumaturgus, Exposition of Faith: 'there is one Holy Spirit, who has existence from God and is manifested through the Son, that is, to human beings.' The sentence itself divides the relations: the Spirit's EXISTENCE is from God (the Father); the Son's part is expressly glossed as MANIFESTATION 'to human beings.' The source of the Spirit's being is the Father; the Son manifests him. The Father-alone claim is carried by that contrast.

defined.source: Council of Florence, Laetentur Caeli (1439)
defined.quote: the holy Spirit is eternally from the Father and the Son, and has his essence and his subsistent being from the Father together with the Son, and proceeds from both eternally as from one principle and a single spiration.

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 2.3 (1646)
defined.quote: the Holy Ghost eternally proceeding from the Father and the Son.

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article V (1571)
defined.quote: The Holy Ghost, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is of one substance, majesty, and glory, with the Father and the Son, very and eternal God.

defined.source: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths

passages.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
passages.text: In the Gospel the Son promises to give water to those who walk in thirst, saying to the Samaritan woman about the Holy Spirit: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4:10). And after a little while he says to her: “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst forever. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up to eternal life” (John 4:13-14). And for this reason David, singing to God, says: “For with you is the spring of life; in your light we will see light” (Psalm 36:9). For he knows that the Son, who is with God the Father, is the spring of the Holy Spirit. And through Jeremiah the Son says: “My people have done two evil things: they have forsaken me, the spr

from-the-father.quote: the Son, who is with God the Father, is the spring of the Holy Spirit
from-the-father.audited: Marcellus of Ancyra: David 'knows that the Son, who is with God the Father, is the spring of the Holy Spirit,' and the Son himself says through Jeremiah, 'they have forsaken me, the spring of living water' (Jeremiah 2:13). The Son is named the Spirit's SPRING - a source of the Holy Spirit - contradicting the claim that the Son is not a source of the Spirit.

passages.author: Augustine of Hippo
passages.text: But the Holy Spirit has not yet been discussed as fully and carefully by the learned and great interpreters of the divine Scriptures so that what is proper to him can be easily understood—the property by which it comes about that we cannot call him either Son or Father, but only Holy Spirit—except that they proclaim him to be the gift of God, so that we believe God does not give a gift inferior to himself. The learned interpreters maintain, however, that the Holy Spirit is not begotten, as a Son from the Father—for Christ alone is the only Son—nor from the Son, as a grandson of the supreme Father, and yet that he owes what he is to no one except the Father, from whom all things come, so that we do not set up two principles without beginning, which is utterly false and absurd and belongs not to the catholic faith but to the error of certain heretics.

from-the-father.quote: he owes what he is to no one except the Father, from whom all things come
from-the-father.audited: Augustine, On Faith and the Creed 19: the Spirit is 'not begotten, as a Son from the Father - for Christ alone is the only Son - NOR FROM THE SON, as a grandson of the supreme Father, and yet... he owes what he is TO NO ONE EXCEPT THE FATHER, from whom all things come, so that we do not set up two principles without beginning, which is utterly false and absurd.' The Father alone is the source of the Spirit's being, and being-from-the-Son is expressly denied.

filioque.quote: he owes what he is to no one except the Father, from whom all things come, so that we do not set up two principles without beginning
filioque.audited: 'He owes what he is to no one except the Father' - the Spirit does not have his being from the Father and the Son together; and the passage guards the point precisely so that there are not 'two principles without beginning.'

passages.author: Procopius of Gaza
passages.text: The only divine procession that could be called unoriginate and endless is the generation of the one and only Son from the one and only Father, and from the same Father the projection of the one and only Holy Spirit. In this procession the Father's single source, which is paternal and ruling, or rather pre-unoriginate, moved into the pair seen in the Son and the Spirit, and came to rest at the Trinity, as our Theologian Gregory says.

from-the-father.quote: the Father's single source, which is paternal and ruling, or rather pre-unoriginate
from-the-father.audited: Procopius of Gaza: 'the generation of the one and only Son from the one and only Father, and from the same Father the projection of the one and only Holy Spirit. In this procession THE FATHER'S SINGLE SOURCE, which is paternal and ruling, or rather pre-unoriginate, moved into the pair seen in the Son and the Spirit, and came to rest at the Trinity.' One single paternal source for both the Son's generation and the Spirit's projection - the Father alone is the cause of the Spirit's being.

filioque.quote: the generation of the one and only Son from the one and only Father, and from the same Father the projection of the one and only Holy Spirit
filioque.audited: Both the Son and the Spirit proceed from 'the same Father' and his 'single source'; the Son stands in the pair that proceeds FROM the source, not beside the Father as a co-source of the Spirit.

questions.question: What happens between death and the final judgment to those who die in faith but not fully purified, and can the living help them?
shared_ground: The souls of the dead live on and await the resurrection
The faithful departed are at rest or with Christ
Remembering the departed by name at worship, without asking that they be helped
Final judgment and resurrection of the body

positions.name: Purgatory

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 25, Decree concerning Purgatory (1563)
defined.quote: there is a Purgatory, and that the souls there detained are helped by the suffrages of the faithful, but principally by the acceptable sacrifice of the altar

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1030
defined.quote: All who die in God's grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, are indeed assured of their eternal salvation; but after death they undergo purification, so as to achieve the holiness necessary to enter the joy of heaven.

positions.statement: Some who die in grace undergo a temporary purification after death, involving punishment still owed for forgiven sins, and the prayers and Eucharist of the living help them.
positions.mark: The passage says saved souls are purified or punished for a time after death for sins already forgiven, before entering heaven.

positions.name: Prayer for the dead, purification not defined

defined.source: Pope Shenouda III (Coptic Orthodox), Comparative Theology (1988)

positions.statement: The Church prays and offers the Eucharist for the departed, who are helped by it before the final judgment, without defining a place or process of purifying punishment.

first_states.author: Augustine of Hippo
first_states.text: But since this is so, you indicate that you do not quite see how the apostle's saying is not contrary to this opinion: "For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what he did through the body, whether good or evil" (2 Corinthians 5:10). This apostolic sentence warns that what can help after death should be done before death, not at the time when each person must already receive what he did before death. But the question is solved this way: by a certain kind of life something is acquired while one lives in this body, so that these things may help the dead somewhat. And so, according to what they did through the body, they are helped by the things that are religiously done for them after the body. For there are some whom these things do not help at all—whether they are done for those whose merits are so evil that they are not worthy to be helped

prayer-no-defined-place.quote: whatever is piously done for him after he has left the body helps or does not help
prayer-no-defined-place.audited: Augustine's own solution (Care for the Dead 2): 'by a certain kind of life something is acquired while one lives in this body, so that these things may help the dead somewhat... according to what they did through the body, they are helped by the things that are religiously done for them after the body... whatever is piously done for him after he has left the body helps or does not help.' The dead are helped by the living's pious acts; no purifying punishment is described.

no-intermediate-purification.quote: whatever is piously done for him after he has left the body helps or does not help
no-intermediate-purification.audited: The dead 'are helped by the things that are religiously done for them after the body' - the living CAN help the dead, which this position denies.

positions.name: No purification or help after death

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 32.1 (1646)
defined.quote: Besides these two places, for souls separated from their bodies, the Scripture acknowledgeth none.

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXII (1571)
defined.quote: The Romish Doctrine concerning Purgatory, Pardons, Worshipping, and Adoration, as well of Images as of Reliques, and also invocation of Saints, is a fond thing vainly invented

positions.statement: At death believers' souls go at once into God's presence; there is no purifying state after death, and prayers or offerings do not change the state of the dead.
positions.mark: The passage says there is no place or state after death besides heaven and hell, or that the living cannot help the dead.
positions.first_defined: Thirty-Nine Articles XXII (1563/1571); Westminster Confession 32 (1646)

first_states.text: The angels rejoice with radiant ones, singing hymns, opening the heavens. And before all things the Savior himself comes to meet them, welcoming them, offering light without shadow, without ceasing, leading them into the bosom of the Father, into eternal life, into the kingdom of heaven. Let a person believe these things, both the disciples of God and God as guarantor, the prophecies, the gospels, the apostolic words. Living with these and giving ear to them and practicing their works, at the very moment of departure he will see the end and the demonstration of the teachings. For the one who receives the angel of repentance here will not repent then, when he leaves the body, nor will he be put to shame when he sees the Savior coming with his own glory and his army. He does not fear the fire. But if someone chooses to continue sinning continually in pleasures and prefers the luxury here t

no-intermediate-purification.audited: Clement, Who Is the Rich Man Saved? 42: at the faithful man's departure 'the Savior himself comes to meet them, welcoming them... leading them into the bosom of the Father, into eternal life, into the kingdom of heaven,' and this 'at the very moment of departure.' Repentance and purification belong to this life only: 'the one who receives the angel of repentance HERE will not repent THEN, when he leaves the body... He does not fear the fire.' The one who perishes does so because his soul 'perishes willingly' - his state is fixed by his life, and nothing after death purifies or alters it. For those who die in faith: immediate presence, no purifying interval.

passages.author: Origen of Alexandria
passages.text: And blessed is the one who has a part in the first resurrection, who has kept the baptism of the Holy Spirit. Who is the one saved in another resurrection? The one who needs the baptism from fire, when he comes to that fire, and the fire tests him, and that fire finds wood, hay, and stubble, so as to burn them. Therefore, these things being said, gathering as far as we can the words of the Scriptures, let us store them in the heart and try to live according to them, if perhaps we may be able to become clean before the departure, and, having prepared our works for the departure, going out may be taken up in those good things and be saved in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power to the ages of the ages. Amen (1 Corinthians 3:12–13) (Luke 3:16) (Deuteronomy 4:24).

no-intermediate-purification.quote: The one who needs the baptism from fire, when he comes to that fire, and the fire tests him
no-intermediate-purification.audited: 'The one saved in another resurrection... the fire tests him, and finds wood, hay, and stubble, so as to burn them' (ὁ ἐν ἑτέρᾳ σῳζόμενος ἀναστάσει... τὸ πῦρ αὐτὸν δοκιμάζῃ) describes a cleansing of the saved after death.

passages.text: e the body of a dearest one is buried, and the place occurs to it as venerable by the name of a martyr, the affection of the one remembering and praying commends that beloved soul to the same martyr. When this affection is shown to the dead by their dearest faithful ones, there is no doubt that it benefits those who, while they were living in the body, merited that such things would benefit them after this life. But even if some necessity, when no opportunity is given, prevents bodies from being buried at all, or from being buried in such places, prayers for the spirits of the dead must not be omitted. prayer-no-defined-place.quote: prayers for the spirits of the dead must not be omitted... those who lack parents or children or any relatives or friends to do these things may have them offered by the one pious common mother
prayer-no-defined-place.audited: Augustine (Care for the Dead 6): commendation to the martyr, 'when this affection is shown to the dead by their dearest faithful ones, there is NO DOUBT THAT IT BENEFITS those who, while they were living in the body, merited that such things would benefit them after this life... prayers for the spirits of the dead must not be omitted. The church has undertaken to make these prayers for all who have died in Christian and catholic fellowship... if those prayers were lacking... it would profit their spirits nothing.' The dead are helped by the church's prayers; no purifying punishment is defined.

no-intermediate-purification.quote: it benefits those who, while they were living in the body, merited that such things would benefit them after this life... if those prayers were lacking... it would profit their spirits nothing
no-intermediate-purification.audited: Prayers for the dead 'benefit' them, and without them 'it would profit their spirits nothing' - the living's prayers change the dead's state for the better, contradicting this position in terms.

passages.author: Augustine of Hippo
passages.text: That brief answer of mine could have been enough for your question, but pay attention for a moment to the other things that trouble people, which I think need a response. In the books of Maccabees we read that sacrifice was offered for the dead. But even if it were nowhere read in the old Scriptures at all, the authority of the whole church, which shines clearly in this custom, is not small: in the prayers of the priest that are poured out to the Lord God at his altar, the prayerful commending of the dead also has its own place.

no-intermediate-purification.quote: the prayerful commending of the dead also has its own place
no-intermediate-purification.audited: The same excerpt defended: sacrifice 'offered for the dead' on Scripture's example, and the commending of the dead at the altar upheld by 'the authority of the whole church' as a real ministry of the church to the departed. An authoritative, Scripture-cited defense of offerings FOR the dead stands against the claim that the living cannot help the dead and such offerings change nothing. (The help itself is stated in chapters 2 and 6.)

questions.question: Can the Church remit the temporal punishment still owed for forgiven sins?
shared_ground: Bishops may shorten or relax church penances they imposed (a church discipline, not punishment before God)
Martyrs' and confessors' intercession for the lapsed
Penance and satisfaction after baptism as church discipline

positions.name: Indulgences

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 25, Decree concerning Indulgences (1563)
defined.quote: the power of conferring Indulgences was granted by Christ to the Church; and she has, even in the most ancient times, used the said power

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1471
defined.quote: An indulgence is a remission before God of the temporal punishment due to sins whose guilt has already been forgiven

positions.statement: The Church has authority to remit before God temporal punishment owed for forgiven sins, drawing on the merits of Christ and the saints.
positions.mark: The passage says the Church (a bishop, or martyrs' intercession accepted by the Church) remits punishment owed before God, not only a church penalty.

positions.statement: The Church has no power to remit punishment before God; forgiveness through Christ leaves no punishment for the Church to lessen.
positions.mark: The passage says God's forgiveness leaves no remaining punishment, or that no church authority can lessen it.

first_states.author: Cyprian
first_states.text: Do not deceive yourselves; do not cheat yourselves. Only the Lord can show mercy. Forgiveness for sins committed against him can come only from the one who bore our sins, who suffered for us, and whom God handed over for our sins (Jeremiah 17:5). A human being cannot be greater than God, nor can a servant cancel or grant indulgence for a graver offense committed against the Lord. If the lapsed person does not know that it is written, 'Cursed is the man who puts his hope in man,' he will add this to his crime. The Lord must be prayed to; the Lord must be appeased by our satisfaction, because he said that whoever denies him will be denied, and because he alone received all judgment from the Father. We certainly believe that the merits and works of martyrs can carry great weight with the judge, but when the day of judgment arrives, when his people stand before the tribunal of Christ after t

indulgences.quote: A human being cannot be greater than God, nor can a servant cancel or grant indulgence for a graver offense committed against the Lord.
indulgences.audited: Cyprian, On the Lapsed 17: 'Only the Lord can show mercy. Forgiveness for sins committed against him can come only from the one who bore our sins, who suffered for us... A human being cannot be greater than God, nor can a servant cancel or grant indulgence for a graver offense committed against the Lord... We certainly believe that the merits and works of martyrs can carry great weight with the judge, but WHEN THE DAY OF JUDGMENT ARRIVES.' A servant cannot grant indulgence for an offense against God, and the martyrs' merits weigh at the judgment - they remit nothing now.

no-indulgences.quote: Only the Lord can show mercy. Forgiveness for sins committed against him can come only from the one who bore our sins, who suffered for us.
no-indulgences.audited: 'Nor can a servant cancel or grant indulgence for a graver offense committed against the Lord' - and 'the Lord must be prayed to; the Lord must be appeased by our satisfaction, because... he alone received all judgment from the Father.' No church power remits punishment before God; mercy for offenses against him is the Lord's alone. This position's mark, nearly verbatim.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: —and is seen distinguished with the dignities of the Godhead. For God has highly exalted him, and has gifted him the name above every name. And he shuts the mouth of the sin, according to what is hymned in the Psalms: ‘And every lawlessness will stop up its mouth’ (Philippians 2:9); having been told to cry down against those who have sinned from weakness, and have been justified in faith. For ‘God is the one justifying; who is the one condemning?’ (Psalm 107:42) And Christ having suffered for us, how was it consistent that the penalties for our own trespasses should still be demanded of us ourselves?

indulgences.quote: Christ having suffered for us, how was it consistent that the penalties for our own trespasses should still be demanded of us ourselves?
indulgences.audited: Cyril, On Adoration 1: 'God is the one justifying; who is the one condemning? (Romans 8:33-34) And Christ having suffered for us, how was it consistent that the penalties for our own trespasses should still be demanded of us ourselves?' For those justified in faith, no penalties remain still to be demanded - so there is no remaining temporal punishment for a church indulgence to remit.

no-indulgences.quote: Christ having suffered for us, how was it consistent that the penalties for our own trespasses should still be demanded of us ourselves?
no-indulgences.audited: The rhetorical question asserts it: Christ having suffered for us, penalties for our trespasses are NOT still demanded of us ourselves. God's justification leaves no remaining punishment - the first disjunct of this position's mark.

questions.question: Who should be baptized?
shared_ground: Adults who come to faith are baptized after instruction (catechumenate)
Baptism in the name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit
Repentance and faith are expected of adult candidates
Advice to delay baptism for prudential reasons (e.g. Tertullian) without saying infant baptism is invalid (compatible with both)

positions.name: Believers and their infants

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1250
defined.quote: Born with a fallen human nature and tainted by original sin, children also have need of the new birth in Baptism

defined.source: Augsburg Confession, Article IX (1530)
defined.quote: children are to be baptized who, being offered to God through Baptism are received into God's grace.

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 28.4 (1646)
defined.quote: Not only those that do actually profess faith in and obedience unto Christ, but also the infants of one, or both, believing parents, are to be baptized.

defined.source: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church (UMC Book of Discipline, para. 104)
defined.quote: The Baptism of young children is to be retained in the Church.

defined.source: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, The Faith of the Church (text by V. C. Samuel, 1970)
defined.quote: the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahido Church baptizes male infants at the age of 40 days and female infants at the age of 80 days

defined.source: Common Statement on Sacramental Life, Catholic Church and Assyrian Church of the East (2017)
defined.quote: both the Catholic and the Assyrian tradition practice the baptism of adults and the baptism of infants.

positions.statement: Infants of Christian parents should be baptized, before they can profess faith themselves.
positions.mark: The passage says infants or little children are, or should be, baptized.
positions.first_defined: Council of Carthage (418); Augsburg Confession (1530); Westminster Confession (1646)

first_states.author: Julian of Eclanum
first_states.text: Baptism is necessary at every age, so that the creature may be adopted among the children of God, not because it inherits anything from its parents that must be cleansed by the washing of rebirth (Titus 3:5; John 1:12–13; Romans 8:15).

infants-too.quote: Baptism is necessary at every age, so that the creature may be adopted among the children of God
infants-too.audited: 'Baptism is necessary at every age' (Baptismum omnibus aetatibus necessarium) is said in a dispute about infants, and Augustine contrasts it with 'little ones'. Latin checked (C. duas ep. Pel. 4.2.2): faithful. ATTRIBUTION: this is the Pelagian bishops' joint letter (c. 418) quoted by Augustine; 455 is Julian's death date, not the date of the text.

believers-only.quote: Baptism is necessary at every age
believers-only.audited: 'Baptism is necessary at every age' includes infants, which rules out baptism for professing believers only.

positions.name: Professing believers only

defined.source: Second London Baptist Confession, 29.2 (1689)
defined.quote: Those who do actually profess repentance towards God, faith in, and obedience to, our Lord Jesus Christ, are the only proper subjects of this ordinance.

defined.source: Baptist Faith and Message, Article VII (2000)
defined.quote: Christian baptism is the immersion of a believer in water in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

defined.source: Schleitheim Confession (1527)
defined.quote: This excludes all infant baptism

defined.source: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995)
defined.quote: water baptism is to be reserved for those old enough to make such a pledge.

positions.statement: Only those who personally profess repentance and faith should be baptized; infants should not be.
positions.mark: The passage says only those who can profess faith should be baptized, or that infants should not be.
positions.first_defined: Schleitheim Confession (1527); First London Confession (1644); Second London Confession (1689)

passages.author: Justin Martyr
passages.text: I will explain how we devoted ourselves to God after being renewed through Christ, so that by covering this point we may not appear to be doing something wrong in our account. Those who are persuaded and believe that what we teach and say is true, and who promise they can live accordingly, are taught to pray and ask God for forgiveness of their past sins while fasting, with us praying and fasting alongside them. Then we lead them to where there is water, and they are reborn in the same manner of rebirth that we ourselves experienced. For in the name of God, the Father of all and our Master, and of our Savior Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, they undergo the washing in the water. Christ said, "Unless you are born again, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven" (John 3:5). It is obvious to everyone that those who have been born once cannot re-enter the wombs of those who gave birth t

infants-too.quote: Those who are persuaded and believe that what we teach and say is true, and who promise they can live accordingly, are taught to pray and ask God for forgiveness of their past sins

believers-only.quote: Those who are persuaded and believe that what we teach and say is true, and who promise they can live accordingly, are taught to pray and ask God for forgiveness of their past sins

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: People whose job it is know that Baptism must not be accepted rashly. You hand your own to every petitioner, and that gift carries a title that counts just the same as almsgiving. Rather, you must grasp this: do not give holy things to dogs, and do not cast your pearls before swine, and do not impose hands easily, lest you become partners in strangers' sins (Matthew 7:6). If Philip baptized the eunuch so easily, consider that the Lord's manifest and evident dignity intervened. The Spirit had ordered Philip to take that road; the eunuch was found neither idle nor suddenly craving baptism, but he had gone to the temple to pray, impressed by divine Scripture. infants-too.quote: delaying Baptism is more useful, especially with young children.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: Candidates for baptism must pray with frequent prayers, fasts, kneeling, all-night vigils, and a confession of all past sins, so that they may also reenact John's baptism—Scripture says, "They were baptized, confessing their sins" (Mark 1:5). We should count it a gain if we do not have to confess our injustices or shameful deeds in public; in doing so we simultaneously settle the old conflicts between flesh and spirit and lay up defenses against the temptations that will follow. "Watch and pray, lest you fall into temptation" (Matthew 26:41). That, I think, is exactly why the disciples were tempted: they fell asleep, so that they abandoned the arrested Lord, and the one who stayed by him and even used a sword went on to deny him three times. After all, it had already been said: "No one untested will attain the heavenly kingdom." The Lord himself, immediately after his baptism, was hemmed

passages.author: Basil of Caesarea
passages.text: Are you young? Secure your youth with the bridle of baptism. Has your prime passed? Do not be deprived of the provisions for the journey; do not lose the amulet; do not think about the eleventh hour as if it were the first. For it is fitting even for the one beginning life to keep the end before his eyes.

believers-only.quote: Secure your youth with the bridle of baptism.

passages.text: We confess that Christ's grace is necessary for everyone, adults and infants alike. We condemn those who say that a child born to two baptized parents does not need to be baptized.

infants-too.audited: 'We condemn [anathematizamus] those who say that a child born to two baptized parents does not need to be baptized.' Latin checked (C. duas ep. Pel. 1.22.40): faithful. ATTRIBUTION: Augustine gives it as the Pelagians' words ('inquiunt') from a letter to Rome, c. 418; giving it to Julian personally rests on Augustine's framing, and 455 is his death date.

believers-only.quote: We condemn those who say that a child born to two baptized parents does not need to be baptized.
believers-only.audited: It anathematizes those who say a child of baptized parents need not be baptized.

passages.author: Julian of Eclanum
passages.text: Augustine says that the authors deny that infants inherit original sin needing remission in baptism. They nevertheless affirm, and indeed proclaim, that the washing of rebirth adopts them from being children of human beings into being children of God (Titus 3:5; John 1:12–13; Romans 8:15).

shared_ground: Baptism is commanded by Christ
Baptism is linked with repentance, forgiveness and new life (Acts 2:38) in quoting Scripture
Baptism joins a person to the visible church
Faith is required of adult candidates

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: Since the rule states that no one attains salvation without Baptism, grounded on the Lord's own pronouncement — "Unless someone is born of water, he will not have life" (John 3:5) — certain people raise scrupulous, or rather reckless, objections: how can this rule apply to the Apostles, whom we do not find baptized in the Lord except for Paul? Because Paul alone among them has put on Christ's Baptism, either the verdict on the danger facing the others who lack Christ's water must be prejudged so the rule stands, or the rule must be rescinded if salvation is also granted to the unbaptized. I have heard such things, with the Lord as my witness, so that no one thinks me so lost as to voluntarily stir up with my pen's lust what causes scruples for others. Now I will answer, as best I can, those who deny the Apostles were baptized. If they had undergone John's human baptism and desired the Lo

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: So those utterly wicked characters are stirring up these questions. They claim baptism isn't necessary for people who have faith, since Abraham pleased God through the sacrament of faith alone, without any water at all. But they're arguing backward: in every case, what comes later decides the matter, and the subsequent overrides the prior. Before the Lord's passion and resurrection, salvation was possible through bare faith. But once faith expanded to include belief in his birth, passion, and resurrection, the sacrament was amplified — baptism was added as a seal, a kind of garment for faith that had previously stood naked and lacked power without its own governing law. That law of baptizing was imposed, and the form was prescribed: "Go, make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matt 28:19). To that law this definition

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: When the rule is laid down that no one attains salvation without Baptism, based on the Lord's own pronouncement—"Unless someone is born of water, he will not have life" (John 3:5)—some people raise scrupulous, or rather reckless, objections: how can the Apostles qualify for salvation under that rule, since we do not find them baptized in the Lord, except for Paul? Indeed, since Paul alone among them put on the Baptism of Christ, either the verdict on the danger facing the rest, who lack Christ's water, must be prejudged so the rule stands, or the rule itself must be scrapped if salvation is also established for the unbaptized. I have heard such arguments, with the Lord as my witness, so no one may think me so lost as to stir them up voluntarily out of a lust for writing that only sows scruples in others. passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: How many natural safeguards, how many gracious privileges, how many disciplinary rites, figures, prefigurings, and prayers have established water's sacred role? (Exodus 14:28) First, when the people marched out of Egypt and crossed the sea, they escaped Pharaoh's power, while the water swallowed the king and his entire army. What figure could more clearly mirror the sacrament of Baptism? Nations are freed from the world through water, leaving behind the devil, their former master, crushed beneath the flood. (Exodus 15:25) Again, Moses' wood healed water poisoned by bitterness, turning it sweet for the people's benefit. That wood was Christ, who cures the deadliest veins of a poisonous, bitter nature through the waters of Baptism. This is the water that flowed from the rock that traveled with the people. If the rock is Christ, then beyond doubt we see the water in Christ blessed for Bapti

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: I've said enough on the points where the logic of Baptism first surfaces—points that already foreshadowed, by the mere fact of the Spirit's presence, how the Spirit of God, who hovered over the waters at creation, would one day reform those who are dipped. The Holy Spirit was certainly borne over what is holy, and it borrowed holiness from the holy element it hovered above. Because any underlying matter inevitably takes on the quality of what hangs over it—especially when the spiritual overshadows the physical—and because the spiritual easily penetrates and dwells in the physical through the subtlety of its substance, the nature of the waters was sanctified by the Holy One and thereby gained the power to sanctify in turn. No one should ask: Are we actually baptized in the very same waters that existed at the beginning? Of course not in those identical waters, except insofar as the genus

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: That is enough on the points where the rationale for Baptism first comes into focus—beginning with the very pattern that, even then, foreshadowed the rite. The Spirit of God, who from the beginning hovered over the waters, was destined to remake those who would be dipped. The Holy One was borne over the holy element; or, if you prefer, the waters drew their sanctity from the One who hovered above them. Since any subject matter inevitably absorbs the quality of what hangs over it—especially the physical drawing from the spiritual, because spirit penetrates and indwells so easily by its subtlety—the nature of the waters was sanctified by the Holy One, and the waters themselves acquired the power to sanctify. No one should ask: Are we baptized in those very same waters that existed at the start? Of course not—except insofar as the genus is one, even if the species are many. What belongs to

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: We do not receive the Holy Spirit in the waters; rather, once we have been cleansed in the water under the Angel, we are prepared for the Holy Spirit. This pattern also appeared earlier. Just as John went before the Lord as a forerunner to prepare his ways, so the Angel, the arbiter of Baptism, clears the way for the coming Holy Spirit through the washing away of sins—a washing that faith obtains, sealed in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. If every word stands on the testimony of three witnesses, how much more does the very number of the divine names guarantee our confident hope, now that we possess those same three as guarantors of our faith and sponsors of our salvation through the blessing? And when both the profession of faith and the pledge of salvation are made under those three, the mention of the Church becomes unavoidable; for where the three are—that is, the Father, th

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: The sacrament of our water is a blessed thing: through it we are washed clean of the sins that sprang from our original blindness and set free for eternal life. This treatise will not sit idle; it instructs both those undergoing the most rigorous formation and those who rest content with simple belief, never having probed the rationale behind the traditions, and who therefore carry a probable faith that remains untested through their own ignorance. And so, just recently, a certain viper of the Caian heresy, armed with its most poisonous doctrine, has seized many people, above all by destroying Baptism. This follows nature perfectly: for vipers, asps, and even king snakes habitually haunt dry, waterless places. But we are little fish, born in our ΙΧΘΥΣ Jesus Christ, and we survive only by staying in the water. Thus the monstrous Quintilla—who did not even possess a legitimate right to tea

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: Afterward, we step from the bath and are anointed with blessed oil, following the ancient rite by which priests were anointed with oil from a horn. This goes back to Aaron, whom Moses anointed. From that practice comes the very name ‘Christ,’ from ‘chrism’ meaning anointing—a title that fitted the Lord because He was made spiritual, anointed with the Spirit by God the Father, just as Acts says: ‘They were gathered together in this city against Your holy Son, whom You anointed’ (Acts 4:27). In the same way, the anointing runs on our bodies but works in our spirits, just as Baptism itself is a bodily act—we are plunged in water—whose spiritual effect is that we are freed from sins.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: I'm not sure there's anything left to air in the baptism debate, but I'll backtrack and cover what I skipped earlier so I don't look like I'm ducking the implications. There is exactly one baptism for us — grounded in the Lord's Gospel and the apostles' letters — because there is one Lord, one baptism, and one Church in heaven. But what rules apply to heretics? That's a fair question, since the call was handed to us. Heretics have zero share in our discipline; the very fact that we've cut communion with them brands them as outsiders. I'm not about to recognize in them what was commanded to me, because they don't worship the same God we do, nor the same Christ — that is, the identical one. So their baptism isn't the same either, because the source isn't the same. Since they don't have it rightly, they flat-out don't have it; you can't count what isn't there, and they can't receive what th

passages.author: Cyprian
passages.text: The very interrogation used in Baptism also bears witness to the truth. When we ask, "Do you believe in eternal life and the remission of sins through the holy Church?" we acknowledge that remission of sins is given only within the Church; among heretics, where the Church is not, sins cannot be forgiven. Consequently, those who claim heretics can baptize must either alter the interrogation or uphold the truth—unless they are willing to grant the Church to those they say possess Baptism. It is likewise necessary that the baptized person be anointed, so that by receiving the Chrism—that is, the Unction—he may become God's anointed and possess the grace of Christ within himself. Moreover, the Eucharist is the source from which the baptized are anointed with oil upon the sanctified altar. But one who had neither altar nor Church could not sanctify the creature of oil. It follows that spiritu

passages.author: Firmilian of Caesarea
passages.text: Since Stephanus and his allies claim that forgiveness of sins and a second birth can take place in the baptism of heretics—even though they themselves admit that the Holy Spirit is not present among them—they ought to consider and understand that a spiritual birth cannot happen without the Holy Spirit. The blessed apostle Paul demonstrates this: before the Lord had sent the Holy Spirit, he baptized again with a spiritual baptism those who had received John’s baptism, and then laid hands on them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit (Acts 19:1-6). So when we see Paul rebaptizing his disciples after John’s baptism, why should we hesitate to baptize those who come to the Church from heresy after their illicit and profane dipping? Unless, of course, these bishops—to whom Paul was inferior—are able to give the Holy Spirit to incoming heretics through the laying on of hands alone, while P

regeneration.quote: spiritual birth cannot happen without the Holy Spirit... Paul rebaptizing his disciples after John’s baptism, and then laid hands on them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit
regeneration.audited: Firmilian (Letter 74.8): 'forgiveness of sins and a second birth' are what baptism gives, and 'a spiritual birth cannot happen without the Holy Spirit' - which is why Paul 'baptized again with a spiritual baptism those who had received John's baptism.' The passage denies birth to heretical dipping because the Spirit is absent there; it affirms the Church's baptism as the means of forgiveness and second birth.

passages.author: Firmilian of Caesarea
passages.text: Someone may ask, "What will become of those who were admitted without the Church's baptism after coming from heretics?" If they have already died, we count them among those who were catechized here but passed away before receiving baptism. They not only gained the benefit of the truth and faith they reached after abandoning their error, even though death prevented them from receiving the full completion of grace. As for those who are still alive, they must be baptized with the Church's baptism so that they may obtain the forgiveness of sins. Otherwise, relying on someone else's presumption, they would remain in their former error and die without the completion of grace. Besides, what fault lies either with those who admit them or with those who are admitted, that without having their stains washed away in the Church's bath and without having their sins laid bare, they dare to touch the b

regeneration.quote: they must be baptized with the Church's baptism so that they may obtain the forgiveness of sins
regeneration.audited: Firmilian (Letter 74.21): converts still living 'must be baptized with the Church's baptism so that they may obtain the forgiveness of sins,' lest they die 'without having their stains washed away in the Church's bath' - baptism obtains forgiveness and washes stains.

sign-and-seal.quote: they must be baptized with the Church's baptism so that they may obtain the forgiveness of sins
sign-and-seal.audited: Forgiveness and 'the full completion of grace' are tied to receiving baptism itself: catechumens who died with the truth and faith still lacked the completion, and the living 'must be baptized... so that they may obtain the forgiveness of sins.' The grace waits on the water - the opposite of grace conveyed in God's time apart from the moment.

ordinance-symbol.quote: they must be baptized with the Church's baptism so that they may obtain the forgiveness of sins
ordinance-symbol.audited: Baptism obtains forgiveness and completes grace; it is not a testimony to a forgiveness already complete without it.

passages.author: Firmilian of Caesarea
passages.text: What does Stephanus really want — that the presence and sanctity of Christ be with those baptized among heretics? For if the Apostle is not lying when he says, "As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ" (Gal 3:27), then the one baptized there in Christ has put on Christ. But if he has put on Christ, he was able to receive the Holy Spirit, who is sent by Christ, and it is in vain that hands are laid on him when he comes to receive the Spirit — unless he puts on the Spirit from Christ in such a way that Christ is indeed present among heretics, but the Holy Spirit is not there.

ordinance-symbol.quote: the one baptized there in Christ has put on Christ... he was able to receive the Holy Spirit
ordinance-symbol.audited: Firmilian (in Cyprian, Letter 74.12) argues from the shared premise: 'As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ' (Galatians 3:27) - the one baptized in Christ 'has put on Christ... he was able to receive the Holy Spirit.' Baptism puts on Christ and enables the Spirit's reception - it conveys, not pictures.

passages.author: Lactantius
passages.text: Having spoken of the second birth, by which He revealed Himself to humanity in the flesh, we now turn to those marvelous works which, though they were heavenly signs of power, the Jews dismissed as sorcery. When He first began to mature, He was baptized by the prophet John in the Jordan River, that by a spiritual washing He might cleanse not His own sins — for He had none — but the sins of the flesh He had assumed. He did this so that, just as the Jews were saved through the circumcision they received, so also the Gentiles might be saved through baptism, that is, through the sprinkling of purifying dew. Then a voice was heard from heaven: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you" (Psalm 2:7). This same voice had been foretold by David. And the Spirit of God descended upon Him in the form of a white dove. From that moment He began to perform mighty deeds, not by magical tricks that disp

Let no one busy himself beyond the sacred names that have been spoken; let no one force the title of Son or generation onto the Spirit, but let him be content with the title and likeness that belong to the Spirit. Since by the grace of the good God, through the remembrance of the words of the only-begotten Son of the living God, and of his holy evangelists and apostles and prophets, who have made sufficiently clear to us the teaching concerning the baptism of the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have been instructed that the baptism in fire convicts all wickedness and receives t

From all these things there is one result: the building of the temple of the Lord, where everyone who is constituted there can truly bring glory to the Lord. passages.author: Basil of Caesarea
passages.text: John the Baptist preached a baptism of repentance, and all Judea went out to him. The Lord preaches a baptism of adoption—and who among those who have hoped in Him will not obey? That baptism was introductory; this one brings to completion. That one was a withdrawal from sin; this one is a kinship with God. John the Baptist's preaching was that of one man, and it drew everyone to repentance. But you—taught through the prophets, "Wash yourselves; become clean" (Isaiah 1:16); admonished through the psalms, "Come to Him, and be enlightened" (Psalm 34:6); evangelized through the apostles, "Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the promise of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:38); welcomed by the Lord Himself, who says, "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28)—f

passages.author: Basil of Caesarea
passages.text: Every moment, then, offers the opportunity for salvation through baptism—whether you name night or day, an hour or an instant, or the very briefest point of time. But surely the moment most closely related to baptism is the most fitting. What could be more akin to baptism than the day of Easter? That day is the memorial of the resurrection, and baptism is the power that leads to resurrection. On the day of resurrection, then, let us receive the grace of the resurrection. This is why the Church calls her nurslings together from afar with a loud proclamation, so that those for whom she long labored in birth she may bring forth on that day—and having weaned them from the words of instruction, she may give them a taste of the solid food of the teachings.

passages.author: Basil of Caesarea
passages.text: Elijah was not terrified when a chariot of fire and horses of fire came to him; he longed for the journey upward, and so he dared those fearful things. With great joy he mounted the flaming vehicle while still living in the flesh. But you are not about to mount a chariot of fire; you are about to ascend to heaven through water and the Spirit—and you do not run to the call? Elijah showed the power of baptism at the altar of whole burnt offerings, when he consumed the sacrifice not with fire but with water. By nature fire and water are at war with each other, but when the water was mystically poured over the altar a third time, it became the starting point for the fire and kindled the flame as if it were oil. “Take jars,” he says, “and pour water on the whole burnt offering and on the pieces of wood.” And he said, “Do it a second time,” and they did it a second time. “Do it a third time,”

passages.author: Basil of Caesarea
passages.text: Different times suit different things: there is a time for sleep and a time for waking, a time for war and a time for peace. But for baptism, the entire life of human beings is the time. A body cannot live without breathing, and a soul cannot hold together without knowing its Creator. Ignorance of God is the death of the soul. And the unbaptized person has not been enlightened. Without light, an eye cannot see what belongs to it, nor can a soul receive the contemplation of God.

passages.text: We stand and aim to become part of them; and the mother is certainly the church and the one who has nurtured you. So, if the heretic recognizes these, he knows the benefit from them, that through these he escaped the tyranny of the devil, and through these he was named a Christian? What do I say, 'Christian'? He clothed himself with Christ himself; for the scripture says: 'As many as were baptized into Christ, have clothed yourselves with Christ' (Gal 3:27), only if you have not again stripped yourself off by the serpent. What then is against these things? Do you recognize these, or have you denied even these? And what will you do? For if you have dishonored those who begat you according to the flesh, and have denied those who regenerated you through the bath of rebirth, from where will your life come?

passages.text: Let us sing the new song, for behold, Adam has been renewed and Eve has been carried up to the heavens, for the devil has been hurled into the fire. Let us borrow that song from Miriam, the sister of Moses, for it suits us now just as it suited them then. Let the chorus of those holy ones stand with us and sing what it sang then at the Red Sea: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously glorified” (Exodus 15:1). For what has he done? “Horse and rider he has thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:1). Horse and rider: the horse is the sin that is mad for women, and the rider is the demon seated upon sin, and in the baptismal washing he drowned them both. Let us sing then to the Lord, for he is gloriously glorified, for he has thrown Pharaoh and his power into the sea (Exodus 15:4)—that is, in the baptismal washing he has drowned in the sea the devil and the dark and accursed camp of his demon

For in baptism I put off the earth and put on heaven' - the washing itself drowns sin and the devil and clothes with heaven.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: And what greater proof could be found for this than that it renews and sanctifies in each one through baptism the Spirit of God, and calls back to the better and first form of life? This is also shown by the fact that it itself recalls, as the apostle says concerning those becoming fit through the new birth and enjoying the greatest of all things expected in every respect: 'that you might become according to the image of the one who created you' (2 Cor 3:18); and it also prophesies David in the Psalm: 'the people being created shall praise the Lord' (Ps 22:27). If it did not have a communion of essence, lordship, and energy with the Father and with the Son, 'through whom all things came to be' (John 1:3), it would not renew and sanctify.

regeneration.quote: it renews and sanctifies in each one through baptism the Spirit of God
regeneration.audited: The author's own words: the Spirit 'renews and sanctifies in each one through baptism', baptism being the means of renewal. ATTRIBUTION: De Trinitate's ascription to Didymus is disputed.

passages.attribution_note: Attribution of De Trinitate to Didymus is disputed.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: The Marcionites baptize living people on behalf of unillumined dead people, not knowing that baptism saves only the one who receives it. But the apostle calls our bodies dead, on whose behalf we are baptized; for by their own nature, without a soul, these do not live, but they have life from the souls that are present with them. Likewise Abraham also called the soulless body dead.

regeneration.quote: baptism saves only the one who receives it
regeneration.audited: Didymus, fragment on 1 Corinthians: the Marcionites baptize the living for the dead, 'not knowing that baptism saves only the one who receives it' - baptism itself saves its recipient.

ordinance-symbol.quote: baptism saves only the one who receives it
ordinance-symbol.audited: 'Baptism saves only the one who receives it' - a saving instrument, not a picture of salvation received without it.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: “You were baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the spirit of our God.” Therefore, look, look, how the name of the Son is entirely a divine name, and likewise that of the Holy Spirit; for one name has revealed both of them. And that the Holy Spirit, as if having gathered them ineffably from the beginning, now recreates. For to have loosed the old signified to be recreated. By this title: “having regenerated us through the bath of regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5). The Psalmist is no less worthy of being known regarding those already existing in generation who are now being created in the divine swimming pool spiritually. For he says: “A people being created praises the Lord” (Psalm 50:2).

regeneration.quote: having regenerated us through the bath of regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit

And the female and the male were not merely mixed—insofar as one sought through the word toward what was set before him—but if baptism brings the male and the female differing into one grace, how much more the Greek and the Jew.

passages.author: Asterius of Amasea
passages.text: Such things are achieved through a fall. For then we see well when we are cleansed by the mystical water; then the light of grace surrounds us, when the power of baptism washes away the stain of sins and the spots. And all who obey the command of Siloam see the spiritual light, which enlightens every man coming into the world. Oh, the wonder and the great energy!

passages.text: That these things happened before through the apostles is witnessed by the churches everywhere in the world, and by peoples, cities, and nations who ran to laymen and fishermen. For unlettered and poor and needy and lowly men would never have prevailed over the world if they had not had the help of signs. But neither have you been left without the grace of the Spirit. Even now many symbols of that gift remain, far greater and more wonderful than the ones just listed. For it is not the same thing to raise a body that has died and to deliver a soul that has been killed by sins from that destruction—which happens through baptism. It is not the same thing to drive out diseases of the flesh and to put off the burden of sins. It is not the same thing to restore a blinded eye and to illuminate a darkened soul with light. For if there were not a guarantee of the Spirit even now, baptism would no

passages.author: John Chrysostom
passages.text: And why, someone asks, if the washing forgives us all our sins, is it not called a washing of forgiveness of sins, nor a washing of cleansing, but a washing of regeneration? Because it does not simply forgive us our sins, nor simply cleanse us of our offenses, but does so as if we had been born again from above. For it creates us anew and fashions us again, not by molding us from earth, but by creating us from another element, the nature of the waters.

And what does this have to do with what was said, someone asks? For the question was to show whether the power of the washing cleanses away all these things. Then listen to what follows: And such were some of you, but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God (1 Corinthians 6:11).

passages.author: John Chrysostom
passages.text: You heard how those who were initiated long ago groaned and struck their chests when their conscience rose up against them here. Take care, beloved, that you never suffer the same thing. And how will you not suffer it, if you do not cast out the wicked habit of evil deeds? This is why I said before and say now, and will not stop saying: if anyone has not corrected the defects of his character and made virtue easy for himself, let him not be baptized. The washing can forgive former sins, but there is no small fear and no ordinary danger that we may return to them again, and the medicine may become a wound for us. For the greater the grace has been, the greater the punishment for those who sin afterward.

passages.author: John Chrysostom
passages.text: We promised to show you that those who approach the washing become clean from all fornication, but the word has demonstrated something more: that they become not only clean, but also holy and righteous. For he did not say only, You were washed, but also, You were sanctified and justified. What could be more astonishing than this, when righteousness is born without labors and sweat and achievements? Such is the loving-kindness of the divine gift: it makes people righteous without sweat.

passages.author: John Chrysostom
passages.text: The Jewish washing cleansed away that kind of stain. But the washing of grace does not cleanse that kind; it cleanses the uncleanness that is truly real, the stain that has been deeply impressed upon the soul along with the body. For it does not make clean those who have touched dead bodies, but those who have touched dead deeds. If a man is soft, if he is a fornicator, if he is an idolater, if he has done anything dreadful at all, if he possesses every wickedness found among human beings—when he falls into the pool of the waters, he comes up from the divine streams purer than the rays of the sun.

passages.author: Julian of Eclanum
passages.text: Augustine says that the authors deny that infants inherit original sin needing remission in baptism. passages.author: Julian of Eclanum
passages.text: Baptism makes people completely new. The apostle is a witness to this, for he testifies that through the washing of water the church gathered from the nations is made holy and spotless (Ephesians 5:26–27).

passages.author: Julian of Eclanum
passages.text: We acknowledge that the grace of baptism is beneficial to every age, so completely that we pronounce an eternal anathema on all who think it unnecessary even for infants. But we believe this grace to be rich in spiritual gifts. Abundant in its many favors and worthy of reverence for its powers, it heals the different kinds of weakness and the different conditions of human beings by one power that bestows both remedies and gifts. When it is administered, it does not need to be changed to suit particular cases: it distributes its own gifts according to the capacity of those who approach. No craft itself suffers loss or gain because of the different materials it takes up to work on; remaining always the same and in the same condition, it is adorned by a variety of effects. In the same way, according to the apostle, there is ‘one faith, one baptism’ (Ephesians 4:5). These multiply and expand

Baptism's grace bestows remedies and gifts by its own power - it conveys grace.
