passages.text: If it is established from the beginning that this practice is forbidden by so many and such great precepts, never committed with impunity, and attested by so many and such great examples, and that no crime counts as more arrogant before God than this kind of transgression, we ought to grasp of our own accord the intention behind divine warnings and punishments. Those intentions were already backed by martyrdoms then — not only not to be doubted, but to be endured. Prohibiting idolatry made room for those martyrdoms; otherwise they would not have happened. And God certainly established his own authority, wishing to bring about the very things for which he had made room. Now we are pricked by the will of God, and the scorpion doubles the blow, denying this will and accusing it — so as either to insinuate another God whose will this is not, or nonetheless to destroy our God whose will is of

passages.text: Therefore, in prohibiting the making of any likeness of things in heaven, on earth, or in the waters, He also reveals the reasons — those very substances that restrain idolatry — for He immediately adds: 'You shall not worship them nor serve them.' (Numbers 21:8-9) The bronze serpent, which the Lord later commanded Moses to make, did not fall under the heading of idolatry; it was a remedy for those being plagued by serpents. I pass over the figure of that remedy. Likewise, the golden Cherubim and Seraphim fashioned on the Ark were simply ornamentation, adapted to the Mercy Seat; they had causes far removed from the condition of idolatry on account of which a likeness is forbidden. They do not appear to violate the law against prohibited likenesses, because they were not caught in that state of likeness for which the likeness is prohibited. passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: You argue that the ornaments of secular gods turn up even in God's house, so that the crown on the head must be defended as common property. By that logic, you yourself have already ruled that anything not found in God's things has no place in the communion of use. What could be more unworthy of God than what counts as worthy of an idol? And what suits an idol better than what suits the dead? The dead, after all, are crowned the same way: they instantly become idols by their dress and the cult of their consecration, which is a second idolatry for us (Psalm 115:4-8). So the senseless will use that thing exactly as the senseless would, and as if they wanted to abuse it, if they weren't senseless. There is no difference between use and abuse when the truth of use ceases, because the very capacity to perceive has ceased; how can anyone abuse what they lack the faculty to use? For us, however

passages.text: But, someone says, "Let your works shine" (Matthew 5:16). At present, it is our shops and doors that shine. You can now find more pagan doors without lamps and laurels than Christian ones. What should we think of this practice too? If it is honor of an idol, then without doubt honor of an idol is idolatry. If it is done for a person's sake, let us remember that all idolatry is done for a person's sake. Let us remember that all idolatry is worship offered to human beings, since even their own records show that the gods of the pagans were once human. So it makes no difference whether this superstition is offered to men of an earlier age or of this one. Idolatry is condemned not because of the persons who are put forward, but because of the services themselves, which belong to demons. "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's" (Matthew 22:21). Idolatry is condemned not because of the persons who are put forward, but because of the services themselves.' Honour-services directed to an image for the person's sake are idolatry - the pass-through defense is expressly rejected.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: Suppose no law of God had forbidden us to make idols, and no voice of the Holy Spirit had threatened idol-makers no less than idol-worshippers. Even then, we could draw the conclusion from our very sacred commitment that arts of this kind are opposed to our faith. How have we renounced the devil and his angels if we make them? What divorce have we declared from them? I do not mean from those with whom we live, but from those by whom we live. What discord have we taken up against them, when for the sake of our display you acknowledge them? Do you destroy by word what you build by deed? Do you preach one God while you make so many? Do you preach the true God while you make false ones?

venerated.quote: arts of this kind are opposed to our faith
venerated.audited: Tertullian, On Idolatry 6: 'arts of this kind are opposed to our faith... Do you preach one God while you make so many? Do you preach the true God while you make false ones?' The image-making arts themselves are contrary to the faith - no room for honouring their products with outward acts.

permitted-not-venerated.quote: arts of this kind are opposed to our faith
permitted-not-venerated.audited: The passage condemns the arts themselves as opposed to the faith, not merely the honouring of images - Christians may not practice them at all, so images may not be kept even for decoration or teaching.

rejected.quote: arts of this kind are opposed to our faith
rejected.audited: Image-making is a breach of the renunciation itself: 'How have we renounced the devil and his angels if we make them? What divorce have we declared from them?' Images and their crafts have no place in the Christian life or worship.

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: But when the devil introduced into the world the craftsmen of statues and images and every kind of likeness, that rough business of human calamity took its name from idols and grew. From then on, every art that produces an idol in any way has become the head of idolatry.

rejected.audited: The craftsmen of 'statues and images and every kind of likeness' are the devil's introduction into the world, and every such art 'has become the head of idolatry' - images as such are placed outside the faith and its worship.

passages.author: Lactantius
passages.text: What madness is it either to fashion those things which they themselves afterward fear, or to fear what they have fashioned? "We do not fear them," they say, "but Him whose image they are, and who is in heaven." Therefore you do not fear what you see, but what you do not see; and while images are before your eyes, fear is turned elsewhere. But what need is there of images if God is to be worshiped? Are the gods so far from you that they are not known except through images? But if they are present, why do you not worship them present? If absent, why through images as if present? For if they can do everything, they need no help of images; if they can do nothing without them, they are not gods. But they say images are made so that through them divinity may be approached. What then? Can divinity be shut in wood or stone? Or rather is it not a crime that the human, who ought to look to heaven

venerated.quote: What need is there of images if God is to be worshiped? ... Why then do you not rather look to heaven
venerated.audited: Lactantius, Institutes 2.2 dismantles image-mediation as such: 'But what need is there of images if God is to be worshiped?... Can divinity be shut in wood or stone?... it is said the image is not worshiped, but the god who is worshiped through the image... Therefore you worship gods through that which is perishable.' The argument is framed for the worship of God himself and rejects the claim that worship reaches the depicted one through the image - the very mechanism this position asserts.

permitted-not-venerated.quote: What need is there of images if God is to be worshiped? ... Why to walls, wood, stone
permitted-not-venerated.audited: Lactantius asks why the worshipper looks 'to walls, wood, stone' at all and calls seeking God in fashioned matter a crime - images are rejected in the worship of God altogether, not kept under a no-honour condition.

rejected.quote: What need is there of images if God is to be worshiped? ... Why then do you not rather look to heaven, where you believe the gods are? Why to walls, wood, stone
rejected.audited: 'What need is there of images if God is to be worshiped?... the human, who ought to look to heaven, bends himself to earth and seeks God in dirt' - God is to be sought heavenward, not through pictures; images have no place in worship.

passages.author: Epiphanius of Salamis
passages.text: John says, "We know that when he appears, we shall be like him" (1 John 3:2), and Paul proclaimed that the saints are "conformed to the Son of God" (Romans 8:29). So how can you wish to see the saints, who are destined to shine in glory, in inglorious, dead, and voiceless matter, when the Lord says of them, "They will be like the angels of God" (Matthew 22:30)? And how can you paint angels, who are spirits and always alive, painting them in dead things and worship them, when the prophet says, "He who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flaming fire" (Psalm 103:4 LXX, 104:4 Hebrew)? I say that they themselves do not wish to be worshipped. "See that you do not do it; I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who hold the testimony of Jesus. Worship God," he says (Revelation 19:10). But the apostles did not wish to be worshipped either.

venerated.quote: how can you...worship them...'Worship God,' he says
venerated.audited: Epiphanius, Tract Against Those Who Make Images: 'how can you wish to see the saints, who are destined to shine in glory, in inglorious, dead, and voiceless matter...? And how can you paint angels... and worship them...? I say that they themselves do not wish to be worshipped. See that you do not do it; I am a fellow servant with you... Worship God (Revelation 19:10). But the apostles did not wish to be worshipped either.' Honouring saints and angels through images is rejected in terms.

permitted-not-venerated.quote: how can you wish to see the saints...in inglorious, dead, and voiceless matter
permitted-not-venerated.audited: The offense is the depicting itself - 'how can you paint angels, who are spirits and always alive, painting them in dead things' - not only the worship that follows; images of the saints in matter are condemned as a making, which leaves no adornment or teaching use standing.

passages.author: Epiphanius of Salamis
passages.text: Which of the ancient bishops dishonored Christ by painting him? Which of them made a public example of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, of Moses and the prophets, of Peter or Andrew or James or John or the rest of the apostles, and paraded them in triumph in this way? At the same time they are lying, fashioning forms of the saints from their own thought in different ways—sometimes making the same ones old men, sometimes younger—entering into things they have never seen. They paint the Savior with long hair based on conjecture, because he is called a Nazarene, since Nazirites have long hair. But those who try to connect the types to him go astray, for the Savior drank wine, which Nazirites did not drink. It is not fitting for us to have God painted in colors and limbs.

venerated.quote: It is not fitting for us to have God painted in colors and limbs.

Which of them made a public example of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, of Moses and the prophets, of Peter or Andrew or James or John...? It is not fitting for us to have God painted in colors and limbs.' Painting Christ and the saints is condemned outright - such images are not to exist, let alone be honoured.

rejected.quote: Which of the ancient bishops dishonored Christ by painting him? ... It is not fitting for us to have God painted in colors and limbs.
rejected.audited: 'It is not fitting for us to have God painted in colors and limbs,' argued from the ancient bishops' never having painted Christ or paraded the saints - painted images of God and the saints have no place with us.

passages.author: Epiphanius of Salamis
passages.text: The devil contrived idolatry in the world by his own evil art, sowed it in the world and established it, and turned human beings away from God. Now again, after the heresies and the idols, he has dragged the faithful down into the ancient idolatry and deceived them. Epiphanius brings himself forward in the letter as having followed the faith of the fathers at Nicaea from his youth, and as having parents who were born in that faith and held the same confession. For your piety will understand whether it is fitting for us to have a painted God made with colors. I have heard that some even promise to paint the incomprehensible Son of God; I do not recall ever seeing such a thing.

venerated.quote: whether it is fitting for us to have a painted God made with colors
venerated.audited: The letter's opening frames the painted-God fashion as the devil's work: 'he has dragged the faithful down into the ancient idolatry and deceived them... whether it is fitting for us to have a painted God made with colors... some even promise to paint the incomprehensible Son of God; I do not recall ever seeing such a thing.' The practice is characterized as a relapse into idolatry, not an open question.

passages.author: Epiphanius of Salamis
passages.text: They present a testament to the citizens, a binding testament, in which he urges them not to bring images into churches or into the cemeteries. "Watch yourselves and hold fast to the traditions you received. Do not turn aside to the right or to the left. And in this matter, beloved children, keep this in memory: do not bring images into churches or into the cemeteries of the saints. Instead, always keep God in memory in your hearts. But not even in a common house is this permitted, for a Christian must not be distracted through the eyes and the wanderings of the mind. Let what pertains to God be written and impressed on all. If anyone deliberately endeavors to comprehend the divine character of God's Word according to the incarnation from material colors, let him be anathema."

venerated.quote: do not bring images into churches or into the cemeteries of the saints
venerated.audited: Kept. 'Do not bring images into churches or into the cemeteries of the saints' (Greek μὴ ἀναφέρειν εἰκόνας ἐπ' ἐκκλησίας) forbids images in churches. ATTRIBUTION: the Testament survives only as cited by iconoclasts and quoted by Nicephorus, who denied it was Epiphanius's; its authenticity is disputed.

questions.question: On what basis does God predestine people to salvation, and is anyone predestined to condemnation?
shared_ground: God foreknows all things
Salvation is by God's grace, not earned
God is not the author of sin
Romans 8:29-30 and Ephesians 1 quoted on predestination without stating its basis
Some are saved and some are lost

positions.name: Election to life only

defined.source: Formula of Concord, Epitome, XI.4 (1577)
defined.quote: The predestination or eternal election of God, however, extends only over the godly, beloved children of God, being a cause of their salvation

positions.statement: God's election by grace is the cause of the salvation of the elect; there is no corresponding decree of reprobation, and the lost perish by their own fault.
positions.mark: The passage says God's predestination is only to salvation and that those who perish are not passed over or ordained to it by God's decree.
positions.first_defined: Formula of Concord, Article XI (1577)

positions.name: Election and reprobation (double predestination)

defined.source: Westminster Confession of Faith, 3.3 (1646)
defined.quote: By the decree of God, for the manifestation of his glory, some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life; and others foreordained to everlasting death.

defined.source: Canons of Dort, First Head, Article 15 (1619)
defined.quote: not all people have been chosen but that some have not been chosen or have been passed by in God's eternal election

positions.statement: By an unconditional decree God chose some for life and passed by the rest, leaving them to just condemnation for their sins.
positions.mark: The passage says God chose some and passed by or rejected others by his own decree, not because of foreseen merit or faith.
positions.first_defined: Synod of Dort (1619); Westminster Confession (1646)

positions.name: Predestination according to foreseen free choice

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 3 (1672)
defined.quote: But since He foreknew the one would make a right use of their free-will, and the other a wrong, He predestinated the one, or condemned the other.

defined.source: Assemblies of God position paper, The Assurance of Salvation (General Presbytery, 2017)
defined.quote: believers are chosen in Christ on the basis of His foreknowledge (Romans 8:29; Ephesians 1:4).

positions.statement: God predestines to glory those he foreknows will freely cooperate with his grace, and condemns those he foreknows will refuse it.
positions.mark: The passage says God predestines or chooses people because he foresees their faith, works or free response.
positions.first_defined: Synod of Jerusalem, Decree 3 (1672)

first_states.author: Origen of Alexandria
first_states.text: If someone insists these events could not have taken place, we respond that they might not have occurred, but it does not follow that if something is incapable of happening, it must either happen or fail to happen; events unfold not solely by necessity, but also as contingent possibilities, including the possibility of non-occurrence. The examination of what is possible engages both logical analysis and reflective insight, enabling one who turns inward to perceive the subtlety of arguments and grasp how even fortuitous occurrences do not obstruct the potential for something to be actual in multiple ways—one of many possibilities becoming real, not by compulsion. God foreknew that events would unfold not through necessity but as free possibilities, and the declaration that they would occur is not speculative guesswork but genuine foreknowledge. Let no one suppose we have remained silent o

double.audited: Origen says the cause of the purpose and of the foreknowledge lies in what is in our power, so election is not independent of the person. The grader's quote (bare Rom 8:29) did not support the verdict; the deciding words are given here.

The grader's quote, the bare 'those whom he foreknew, he also predestined', is shared ground; the verdict holds only on these words. Greek checked.

passages.author: Irenaeus
passages.text: Indeed, the very words He speaks reveal the ancient law of human freedom: "How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing?" (Matt 23:37). God made humanity free from the beginning, possessing a power of its own, just as it possesses its own soul, so that it might use God's judgment voluntarily and not be forced by God. For coercion does not come from God; rather, a good judgment is always present to us. And for this reason He gives good counsel to all. He placed the power of choice in man, just as He did in angels — for angels are rational — so that those who obeyed would justly possess the good, given by God but preserved by themselves. Those who did not obey, however, would not justly find the good and would receive the penalty they deserved, since God gave the good generously, but they did not guard it carefully, nor c

double.quote: God made humanity free from the beginning, possessing a power of its own... so that it might use God's judgment voluntarily and not be forced by God. For coercion does not come from God
double.audited: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 4.37: 'God made humanity free from the beginning, possessing a power of its own... so that it might use God's judgment voluntarily and not be forced by God. For coercion does not come from God... those who obeyed would justly possess the good, given by God but preserved by themselves. Those who did not obey... would receive the penalty they deserved, since God gave the good generously, but they did not guard it.' Both destinies turn on the human response to a good given to all - no decree choosing some and passing by others.

passages.author: Irenaeus
passages.text: In this world some run toward the light and, through faith, join themselves to God, while others turn away from the light and separate themselves from him. The Word of God comes bringing a dwelling suited to everyone: for those who are in the light, that they may enjoy it and the good things within it; for those who are in darkness, that they may share in the calamities that belong to them. Therefore he says that those on the right are called into the kingdom of the Father, but those on the left are sent into eternal fire, because they have deprived themselves of every good (Matt 25:34, 41). For this reason the Apostle declares: because they did not receive the love of God so as to be saved, God will send them a working of error, so that they believe a lie, so that all who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity may be judged (2 Thess 2:10-12). When that one comes, he will re

He placed in man the power of choice, just as in angels (for angels are rational), so that those who obeyed are justly good, possessing what was given by God but kept by themselves, while those who did not obey will not justly find the good and will receive the penalty they deserve, because God gave the good kindly but they did not keep it carefully nor count it precious but despised the surpassing goodness; therefore, rejecting the good and as if spurning it, all wil

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: But if you also want him understood as light around persons, when he sometimes rejects those approved, or as improvident, when he sometimes approves those to be rejected—as if he either condemns his past judgments or is ignorant of future ones—yet nothing so suits both a good person and a judge as both to reject and to elect according to present merits. Saul is elected, but not yet a despiser of the prophet Samuel. Solomon is rejected, but already possessed by foreign women and made over to the idols of Moabites and Sidonians. What should the Creator have done, lest he be blamed by Marcionites? Would he pre-condemn those still acting well already because of future delicts? But it was not of a good God to pre-condemn those not yet deserving. Likewise would he not refuse those now sinning because of former good deeds? But it was not of a just judge to forgive crimes when former goods had a

double.quote: nothing so suits both a good person and a judge as both to reject and to elect according to present merits
double.audited: Tertullian, Against Marcion 2.23: 'nothing so suits both a good person and a judge as both to reject and to elect according to present merits... Would he pre-condemn those still acting well already because of future delicts? But it was not of a good God to pre-condemn those not yet deserving.' God's electing and rejecting track present merits, and pre-condemnation ahead of demerit is expressly denied to a good God - an unconditional decree of election and passing-by is contradicted.

foreknowledge.audited: The same passage grounds God's sentences in PRESENT merits and refuses the future-looking mechanism outright: God will not 'pre-condemn those still acting well already because of future delicts,' nor refuse present sinners 'because of former good deeds.' Predestination because of foreseen response is the mechanism this argument rejects on the condemnation side.

passages.author: Origen of Alexandria
passages.text: od, for those called according to purpose; whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He might be the firstborn among many brothers; and whom He predestined, He also called; and whom He called, He also justified; and whom He justified, He also glorified. Therefore, let us follow the sequence of what has been said: God justifies because He called beforehand; He would not justify those He did not call; and He calls because He predestined beforehand; He would not call those He did not predestine; and it is to Him that the beginning of the call and justification belongs, not predestination. single.quote: having observed the inclination of certain people's free will toward piety... He foreknew them, knowing the present and foreknowing the future; and whom He so foreknew, He predestined
single.audited: Origen (third excerpt) states the ground expressly: God, 'having observed the inclination of certain people's free will toward piety, and their impulse toward it after that inclination, and as they will surrender themselves wholly to living according to virtue, He foreknew them... and whom He so foreknew, He predestined to be conformed as sons in the image of His Son.' Predestination rests on foreseen free-will inclination - election by grace alone is not its cause.

double.quote: having observed the inclination of certain people's free will toward piety... He foreknew them... and whom He so foreknew, He predestined
double.audited: God predestines those he foreknew would give themselves to virtue, so election depends on something foreseen in the person, which rules out an unconditional decree.

foreknowledge.quote: having observed the inclination of certain people's free will toward piety, and their impulse toward it after that inclination, and as they will surrender themselves wholly to living according to virtue, He foreknew them
foreknowledge.audited: 'Having considered the inclination of what is in our power in certain people toward piety... and that they will give themselves wholly to living by virtue, He foreknew them... and whom He so foreknew, He predestined' (κατανοήσας ῥοπὴν τοῦ ἐφ' ἡμῖν τῶνδέ τινων ἐπὶ εὐσέβειαν... καὶ οὓς οὕτω προέγνω, προώρισεν). Greek checked (Philocalia 25 text, Romans catena). TRANSLATION: the English 'toward security' mistranslates εὐσέβειαν ('piety').

passages.author: Origen of Alexandria
passages.text: We must not confuse the order of divine action: it is not that God first predestines and then calls, but that His foreknowledge precedes and undergirds both. The psalm’s words about sinners alienated from the womb are not to be read as a denial of human responsibility, but as a description of a condition that, from birth, inclines toward falsehood—yet even then, the capacity for choice remains, however dim. To imagine that infants could speak lies in unison at birth is to misunderstand both language and moral agency. But when we read Paul’s own words in Galatians, we see that his separation from the womb was not a mere natural endowment, but a divine act aimed at revealing Christ in him—thus grounding the apostolic calling in God’s purpose, not human merit. This is why we affirm that all things work together for good for those who love God, not because they earned it, but because they we

double.quote: foreknowledge leads to predestination...predestination is not the starting point...God's foreknowledge is not the cause of what comes to be, but the reflection of His knowledge of what will be
double.audited: Predestination is placed under foreknowledge of 'hearts inclined toward virtue', which grounds it in something foreseen in the person. Greek check: the English is a loose paraphrase; 'as if He arbitrarily chose some and rejected others' is not in the Greek, which targets those who bring in people 'saved by constitution and nature' (ἐκ κατασκευῆς καὶ φύσεως σωζομένους). The exclusion holds on the Greek of the following lines, not on that sentence.

foreknowledge.quote: He foreknew some as those who would yield to virtue
foreknowledge.audited: 'Foreknowledge precedes and undergirds' predestination, grounded in God's knowledge of 'hearts inclined toward virtue'. The Greek supports this (ἀνωτέρω δέ ἐστι τοῦ προορισμοῦ ἡ πρόγνωσις), but this English is an inflated paraphrase; cite b261abd049f379f3 for the exact words.

passages.author: Arnobius
passages.text: Does Christ not free all with equal munificence? Does he not free equally when he calls all equally? He opens the fountain of life to all; no one is forbidden to drink. If you scorn the gift, why does the one who invites wait? His only part is to set the fruit of his kindness under the decision of your own right (sub tui iuris arbitrio). Plato said the lot of choosing a life is not God’s doing as a cause forced on another; free decision (voluntatis libertas) sits in the power of the one who willed. God lays necessity on no one; he terrifies no one with bullying fear. Our salvation is not so necessary to him that he gains or loses something if he makes us gods or lets us dissolve into nothing.

double.quote: He opens the fountain of life to all; no one is forbidden to drink. If you scorn the gift, why does the one who invites wait?
double.audited: Arnobius: 'He opens the fountain of life to all; no one is forbidden to drink. If you scorn the gift, why does the one who invites wait? His only part is to set the fruit of his kindness under the decision of your own right... God lays necessity on no one.' Salvation is offered to all without exception and refusal is the scorner's own - no one is passed by decree.

passages.author: Diodorus of Tarsus
passages.text: Whom then did God glorify here? Those whom he justified. And whom did he predestine? Those whom he foreknew, those being called according to purpose, that is, those being worthy to be called and to be conformed to Christ through their own purpose. He brings forward the great proof of the love of God, having shown through his deeds that all things work together for our good through the love of God toward us, namely, those whom he found to be called according to purpose, which he demonstrated in not sparing the only-begotten (Rom 8:31–32); for what, if even death did not overpower the Savior, since even upon the Lord he cast down his soul and received it again? But nevertheless it must be observed that Christ subjected himself to sufferings for the sake of humans, fulfilling both his own and the will of the Father. Therefore, since God is managing all things for our sake, who will hinder?

double.quote: those being worthy to be called and to be conformed to Christ through their own purpose
double.audited: The predestined are 'those worthy to be called... through their own purpose', grounding the choice in the person's own purpose.

foreknowledge.quote: those being called according to purpose, that is, those being worthy to be called and to be conformed to Christ through their own purpose
foreknowledge.audited: 'Whom did he predestine? Those whom he foreknew... that is, those who are worthy to be called and conformed to Christ through their own purpose' (τοὺς διὰ τὴν ἰδίαν πρόθεσιν ἀξίους ὄντας κληθῆναι). Greek checked: faithful.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: Again, concerning Esau and Jacob, the apostle, as if speaking in a dilemma, says: 'What then shall we say to this? Is there injustice with God? May it never be!' (Romans 9:14). Because he had refuted injustice, he forced us to seek how there is not injustice with God. If it were so, as those who speak of foreknowledge say, we would rather find injustice in Him. 'I loved Jacob,' He says, 'but I hated Esau' (Romans 9:13). But one is hated or loved according to things done and according to things thought. How then does foreknowledge have room? Is injustice found with God? But he, refuting this, said: 'What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? May it never be!' Since there is no injustice, let the matter be sought in another way, how it has come to pass.

foreknowledge.quote: If it were so, as those who speak of foreknowledge say, we would rather find injustice in Him
foreknowledge.audited: 'If it were as those who speak of foreknowledge say, we would rather find injustice with Him... How then does foreknowledge have room?' (πῶς οὖν χώραν ἔχει ἡ πρόγνωσις;). Greek checked: faithful. Didymus rejects foreknowledge as the basis and grounds love and hate in things actually done and thought. That is not an unconditional decree, so it gives no support to 'double'.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: 9 From Origen's interpretation of 'according to the foreknowledge of God.' For God, having foreseen the faith and the works of men having been perfected in them through the evangelical teaching, foreknowingly chose them in Christ before the foundation of the world, having then predestined them to be sons through the participation of the spirit of sonship; for foreknowledge is to be regarded as nothing other than a vision of things to come, which is no longer foreknowledge, but is knowledge toward the existence of those having been foreseen; even so, according to foreknowledge, they were chosen, as Peter writes (1 Pet 1:2), but not now is the favor being made to them; thus he casts aside the myth concerning natures and the thought contained within.

double.quote: having foreseen the faith and the works of men... foreknowingly chose them
double.audited: Election rests on foreseen faith and conduct: 'having foreseen the faith and conduct (Προεωρακὼς... τὴν πίστιν καὶ πρᾶξιν)... he chose them'. That rules out a choice made without regard to anything foreseen.

foreknowledge.quote: having foreseen the faith and the works of men having been perfected in them through the evangelical teaching, foreknowingly chose them in Christ before the foundation of the world
foreknowledge.audited: 'Having foreseen the faith and conduct of men... he chose them in Christ before the foundation of the world, then predestining them' (Προεωρακὼς γὰρ ὁ θεὸς τὴν πίστιν καὶ πρᾶξιν... ἐξελέξατο αὐτούς... προορίσας). Greek checked: faithful. ATTRIBUTION: the catena heads this 'Ὠριγένους ἐκ τῆς ἑρμηνείας' (Origen's, from his commentary); the English mistranslates 'Ὠριγένους' as 'Originating', so it is Origen, not Didymus, and the year should not be 398.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: He might pass from one state to another. If he had not become one in the truth, not standing in it would not have brought him reproach. And behold the doctrine: how 'God wants all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth' (1 Tim 2:4)? If no one opposes His will, how is it that some are lagging behind, despite His wanting all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth—so that I may not say, the majority? If He wants it, and if we also want it, and a convergence of the two wills occurs, salvation happens; for no one is good against his will, no one who does not want is saved, and no one hurrying toward approaching God and having kept His law is able to know the truth.

double.quote: no one is good against his will, no one who does not want is saved
double.audited: 'God wants all men to be saved', and salvation needs 'a convergence of the two wills'. This fits the double position's own exclusion clause: he wills all to be saved.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: But did Paul speak according to foreknowledge? Foreknowledge is a theoretical viewing of what is coming to be. But according to kind, foreknowledge and knowledge are the same. They differ in time. For example, suppose I foreknow that tomorrow there will be thunder. When the thunder comes to be in the middle of the day, it is knowledge, no longer foreknowledge. And the knowledge of the thunder does not make it such, but what it is, that becomes the knowledge. Thus the known thing makes the knowledge, which does not receive the knowing from us. I use an image for the sake of the manner of foreknowledge: the one child is born so that he may demand, and the other, so that he may live in the house. What kind of justice is this of foreknowledge, if we take these things to happen according to foreknowledge? Foreknowledge both justifies and condemns. To foreknow and to know is also to condemn an

single.audited: Didymus: 'Foreknowledge both justifies and condemns. To foreknow and to know is also to condemn and to justify FROM THE THINGS BEING DONE AND BEING THOUGHT.' God's justifying verdict follows what is foreknown in the person - the things done and thought - so the salvation of the saved is not caused by election by grace alone, independent of what is foreseen in them.

foreknowledge.quote: Foreknowledge both justifies and condemns. To foreknow and to know is also to condemn and to justify from the things being done and being thought.
foreknowledge.audited: 'Foreknowledge both justifies and condemns. To foreknow and to know is also to condemn and to justify from the things being done and being thought.' God's verdicts of justification and condemnation are expressly grounded in the foreknown human acts and thoughts - predestination according to foreseen response, stated without the word.

passages.author: Asterius of Amasea

For, seeing the future by his secret foreknowledge, God allotted to the founder of the faith all who would later believe, to rank as his children.

double.quote: God allotted to the founder of the faith all who would later believe, to rank as his children
double.audited: Asterius, Homily 9: 'seeing the future by his secret foreknowledge, God allotted to the founder of the faith all who would later believe, to rank as his children.' The allotment runs on foreseen belief - the opposite of a decree made without regard to anything foreseen in the person.

foreknowledge.quote: God allotted to the founder of the faith all who would later believe, to rank as his children
foreknowledge.audited: 'For, seeing the future by his secret foreknowledge, God allotted to the founder of the faith all who would later believe, to rank as his children.' God assigns people because he foresees they will believe - this position's exact mark.

passages.author: Julian of Eclanum
passages.text: But this did not suffice for the issue. Such a teacher could not commend God's authority while leaving his justice undefended. Most consistently, then, Paul adds that vessels made for dishonor and those made for honor receive this as the wages of their own will: “If God, wishing to show his wrath and make his power known with great patience in vessels of wrath completed for destruction, and to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy which he prepared for glory, whom he also called, namely us, not only from Jews but also from the nations” (Romans 9:22–24). Here he certainly clears up what the previous debate had concealed: God brings wrath only upon vessels completed for destruction, while glory is given to those prepared for it. By whom such vessels are prepared to receive the things we have named, the apostle's own words disclose: “In a great house there are not only gold

single.quote: God brings wrath only upon vessels completed for destruction, while glory is given to those prepared for it.
single.audited: Julian of Eclanum: 'vessels made for dishonor and those made for honor receive this as the WAGES OF THEIR OWN WILL... God brings wrath only upon vessels completed for destruction... If, then, anyone cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel sanctified for honor, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work (2 Timothy 2:21).' Both lots - glory as well as wrath - are wages of the human will and self-cleansing; the elect's salvation is therefore not caused by God's gracious election as this position requires. (The graders' excludes reason - that the passage affirms a decree - inverts the text; the verdict stands on the election side.)

double.quote: vessels made for dishonor and those made for honor receive this as the wages of their own will
double.audited: 'Vessels made for dishonor and those made for honor receive this as the wages of their own will,' and a man becomes a vessel of honor by cleansing HIMSELF - destinies are earned by the will, not assigned by an unconditional decree that passes by the rest.

passages.author: Julian of Eclanum
passages.text: Consequently, it strongly opposed you too by saying that not everyone is formed for the condemnation into which you declare everyone goes. You habitually make the utterly absurd argument: “But those who are afterward freed are not formed for condemnation.” Yet not even the surface of the apostle's words can agree with you in that way. When you say, “Everyone is created for condemnation by the law of birth, but some, though very few, are freed from it through the mysteries”, you do not assert what he does. He proclaims not only that people are freed from among the condemned, but that not everyone is formed for condemnation: some are formed for dishonor, others for honor.

single.quote: some are formed for dishonor, others for honor
single.audited: Julian against Augustine's birth-condemnation: Paul 'proclaims not only that people are freed from among the condemned, but that not everyone is formed for condemnation: SOME ARE FORMED FOR DISHONOR, OTHERS FOR HONOR.' As written, the passage endorses a twofold forming that includes a forming for dishonor - against this position's insistence that God's forming/predestination runs only to salvation. (Julian's target is Augustine's claim that everyone is born condemned; judged on this excerpt's own words.)

questions.question: Do gifts such as tongues, prophecy and healing continue in the Church today, and is speaking in tongues the sign of a baptism in the Spirit?
shared_ground: The Holy Spirit gives gifts to the Church (1 Corinthians 12)
Love is greater than any gift (1 Corinthians 13)
Gifts are for building up the Church
Miracles were done by the apostles (as history)
The Spirit was poured out at Pentecost with tongues (Acts 2 retold)

(Isa 1:30; 1 Thess 5:19-20)

gifts-continue.quote: Others do not receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit and push prophetic grace far from them
gifts-continue.audited: Present tense: some contemporaries 'do not receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit and push prophetic grace far from them' and are fruitless for it - prophetic grace is the church's present possession, received or refused in Irenaeus's own day; no tongues-sign is taught.

revelatory-gifts-ceased.quote: Others do not receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit and push prophetic grace far from them

first_states.text: And blessed is the one who has a part in the first resurrection, who has kept the baptism of the Holy Spirit. Who is the one saved in another resurrection? passages.text: Among people who love wealth, certain little stones that gleam with bright colors have by nature come to be called precious. questions.question: After the incarnation, is Christ one nature, or two natures in one person, and how is the union to be stated?
shared_ground: Christ is truly God and truly man (all three positions)
The union is without confusion or change (all three)
Christ is one Lord and Son, worshipped with a single worship
Christ is consubstantial with the Father and with us
'Fully God and fully man' without saying 'one nature' or 'two natures'

passages.text: The source of this heretical error, I believe, is their refusal to recognize any distinction between the Son of God and the son of man. They think that by erasing the difference, they can easily prove Jesus Christ to be both man and God. They want the son of man to be identical with the Son of God, so that the man, the flesh, and that fragile human substance may be declared the very Son of God. Since they will not separate the son of man from the Son of God, but instead vindicate the son of man as the Son of God, they end up asserting that Christ is only a man, yet the same as the Son of God. By this maneuver they try to set aside the testimony that "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14), and that "you will call his name Emmanuel, which means God with us" (Matt 1:23). questions.question: Will Christ reign on earth for a thousand years after he returns (Revelation 20), or is the thousand years the present age?
shared_ground: Christ will return visibly in glory
The dead will be raised and all will be judged
Christ reigns now at the Father's right hand
Revelation 20 quoted without saying when the thousand years fall

positions.name: Christ returns before a thousand-year reign on earth

defined.source: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths
defined.quote: The second coming of Christ includes the rapture of the saints, which is our blessed hope, followed by the visible return of Christ with His saints to reign on earth for one thousand years.

defined.source: Church of God (Cleveland, TN), Declaration of Faith
defined.quote: In the premillennial second coming of Jesus. First, to resurrect the righteous dead and to catch away the living saints to Him in the air. Second, to reign on the earth a thousand years.

defined.source: International Pentecostal Holiness Church, Articles of Faith
defined.quote: We believe in the imminent, personal, premillennial second coming of our Lord Jesus Christ

positions.statement: Christ will return before a thousand-year reign on earth, raising the righteous first; the last judgment follows the thousand years.
positions.mark: The passage says Christ, or the saints with him, will reign on earth for a thousand years after his coming and a first resurrection, before the end.
positions.first_defined: No early creed defines it; taught by Papias, Justin (Dialogue 80-81) and Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.32-36). Modern confessional form: AG Statement of Fundamental Truths (1916)

first_states.author: Commodian
first_states.text: From heaven the city descends in the first resurrection. And what should we report of so great a heavenly fabric? We rise to it who were devoted to it, and they will already then be incorrupt, living without death, but neither any pain nor groan will be in it. Those also will come who conquer under Antichrist with strong martyrdoms, and they themselves live the whole time and receive goods, because they suffered evils.

premillennial.audited: Commodian, Instructions 43: 'From heaven the city descends in the first resurrection... Those also will come who conquer under Antichrist with strong martyrdoms, and they themselves live the whole time and receive goods, because they suffered evils.' A first resurrection at the descent, after which the risen saints live on and receive goods - the premillennial sequence (the excerpt does not itself number the thousand years).

amillennial.audited: The same passage distinguishes a first resurrection, in which the martyrs rise and then 'live the whole time,' from the end - not one return closing the present age with one general resurrection and one judgment.

postmillennial.audited: What precedes the descent is suffering under Antichrist and martyrdom, not a long age of gospel peace and righteousness; the saints' goods come only after the resurrection.

positions.name: The thousand years is the present age

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church 676
defined.quote: the Church has rejected even modified forms of this falsification of the kingdom to come under the name of millenarianism

defined.source: Augsburg Confession, Article XVII (1530), condemning the view
defined.quote: They condemn also others who are now spreading … that before the resurrection of the dead the godly shall take possession of the kingdom of the world, the ungodly being everywhere suppressed.

defined.source: Second Helvetic Confession, Chapter XI (1566), condemning the view
defined.quote: We further condemn … that there will be a golden age on earth before the Day of Judgment

positions.statement: There is no earthly thousand-year reign after Christ's return; the thousand years of Revelation 20 is Christ's present reign with his saints, ended by one return, one general resurrection and one judgment.
positions.mark: The passage says the thousand years is the present age or the Church's present reign, or rejects any earthly golden age of the saints either before or after Christ's return.
positions.first_defined: Augustine, City of God 20.7-9 (c. 426), for the reading; condemnations of an earthly kingdom in Augsburg XVII (1530), Second Helvetic XI (1566), Catechism 676 (1992)

positions.name: Christ returns after a golden age of the gospel

defined.source: Savoy Declaration of Faith and Order (1658)
defined.quote: we expect that in the latter days, antichrist being destroyed, the Jews called, and the adversaries of the kingdom of his dear Son broken, the churches of Christ being enlarged, and edified through a free and plentiful communication of light and grace, shall enjoy in this world a more quiet, peaceable and glorious condition than they have enjoyed.

positions.statement: Before Christ returns, the gospel will spread so widely that the Church enjoys a long age of peace and righteousness on earth; Christ returns after it.
positions.mark: The passage says that before Christ's return the Church will triumph through the gospel and enjoy a long earthly age of peace and righteousness.

And an innumerable people of the nations will be gathered from the whole circle of the earth and will besiege and surround the city. Then the last wrath of God will come upon the nations, and he will war them down to the last one. And first he will shake the earth as strongly as possible and from its motion the mountains of Syria will be split and the valleys will sink into the steep and the walls of all cities will fall. And God will set the sun for three days so that it not set and will inflame it, and i

premillennial.quote: the thousand years of the kingdom... have begun to end, will be loosed again... After these things there will be the last judgment
premillennial.audited: Lactantius, Institutes 7.26: 'when the thousand years of the kingdom - that is, the seven thousand - have begun to end,' Satan 'will be loosed again' and stir the nations 'that will then be under the justs' rule' against the holy city; 'After these things there will be the last judgment.' A future thousand-year kingdom of the just on earth, then revolt, then judgment - the premillennial order in full.

amillennial.quote: the thousand years of the kingdom — that is, the seven thousand — have begun to end, will be loosed again
amillennial.audited: The thousand years are a future kingdom that ends with Satan's loosing and a final war before the last judgment - not the present age of the Church.

postmillennial.quote: when the thousand years of the kingdom... have begun to end, will be loosed again... stir all the nations that will then be under the justs' rule to bring war on the holy city
postmillennial.audited: The thousand-year kingdom ends in war and apostasy and is closed by God's wrath and the last judgment; Christ's coming frames the kingdom rather than following a pre-return gospel triumph.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: I say this: that proclamation being made public here changes from being 'in part' 'prophecy or knowledge' (1 Cor 13:9) but becomes 'face to face'. This is the 'rising' according to the former dispensation. But what kind of 'time' shall we receive? The time of 'judgment'. But in what 'time' is it 'closed'? When the present age reaches its end. In this... the beginning and the end are one. The end of this day brings the beginning of the next... there is no separating time from time. Therefore, what is called 'now', which they say is noteworthy and the boundary of time, is the end of the past, the future of the present, and again the end of the present and the beginning of the future. If I say this, I say judgment and resurrection together; and it seems that the beginning is the end of the resurrection.

premillennial.quote: judgment and resurrection together; and it seems that the beginning is the end of the resurrection
premillennial.audited: Didymus on Ecclesiastes joins the two events the premillennial scheme separates: 'I say judgment and resurrection together; and it seems that the beginning is the end of the resurrection,' with 'no separating time from time' at the end of the present age - no interval of a thousand years between a first resurrection and the judgment.

questions.question: May the civil authority put a criminal to death?
shared_ground: Private murder is forbidden
Clergy do not pronounce or carry out a death sentence
The church may ask the judge for mercy
Necessary self-defense is not murder
Jesus' words against personal revenge, with no rule stated for the magistrate
You shall not kill, quoted with no statement about the magistrate
The sword named as a sign of state authority, without saying that it includes death

positions.name: The magistrate may put the guilty to death

defined.source: Genesis 9:6 (King James Version)
defined.author: Genesis 9:6
defined.quote: Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.

defined.source: Numbers 35:31 (King James Version)
defined.author: Numbers 35:31
defined.quote: Moreover ye shall take no satisfaction for the life of a murderer, which is guilty of death: but he shall be surely put to death.

defined.source: Romans 13:4 (King James Version)
defined.author: Romans 13:4
defined.quote: for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.

defined.source: Acts 25:11 (King James Version)
defined.author: Acts 25:11
defined.quote: if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die

defined.source: Augustine, City of God, book 1, chapter 21 (413-426)
defined.author: Augustine
defined.quote: These exceptions are of two kinds, being justified either by a general law, or by a special commission granted for a time to some individual. And in this latter case, he to whom authority is delegated, and who is but the sword in the hand of him who uses it, is not himself responsible for the death he deals. And, accordingly, they who have waged war in obedience to the divine command, or in conformity with His laws, have represented in their persons the public justice or the wisdom of government, and in this capacity have put to death wicked men; such persons have by no means violated the commandment, You shall not kill.

defined.source: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, question 64, article 3 (c. 1271)
defined.author: Aquinas
defined.quote: Now the care of the common good is entrusted to persons of rank having public authority: wherefore they alone, and not private individuals, can lawfully put evildoers to death.

defined.source: Martin Luther, Large Catechism, Fifth Commandment, paragraph 181 (1529)
defined.author: Luther
defined.quote: Therefore God and government are not included in this commandment, nor is the power to kill, which they have, taken away. For God has delegated His authority to punish evil-doers to the government instead of parents, who aforetime (as we read in Moses) were required to bring their own children to judgment and sentence them to death. Therefore, what is here forbidden is forbidden to the individual in his relation to any one else, and not to the government.

defined.source: Catechism of the Council of Trent, Part III, Fifth Commandment (1566; English of Jeremiah Donovan, 1829)
defined.author: Trent
defined.quote: this prohibition does not apply to the civil magistrate, to whom is intrusted power of life and death, by the legal and judicious exercise of which he punishes the guilty and protects the innocent. The use of the civil sword, when wielded by the hand of justice, far from involving the crime of murder, is an act of paramount obedience to this commandment which prohibits murder.

defined.source: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article XXXVII (1571)
defined.author: Article 37
defined.quote: The Laws of the Realm may punish Christian men with death, for heinous and grievous offences.

defined.source: Westminster Larger Catechism, question 136 (1648)
defined.author: Westminster
defined.quote: The sins forbidden in the sixth commandment are, all taking away the life of ourselves, or of others, except in case of public justice, lawful war, or necessary defense

defined.source: John Paul II, Evangelium Vitae 56 (25 March 1995)
defined.author: John Paul II
defined.quote: the nature and extent of the punishment must be carefully evaluated and decided upon, and ought not go to the extreme of executing the offender except in cases of absolute necessity: in other words, when it would not be possible otherwise to defend society. Today however, as a result of steady improvements in the organization of the penal system, such cases are very rare, if not practically non-existent.

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2267, as archived 25 July 2017, before the August 2018 revision
defined.author: Catechism
defined.quote: The traditional teaching of the Church does not exclude, presupposing full ascertainment of the identity and responsibility of the offender, recourse to the death penalty, when this is the only practicable way to defend the lives of human beings effectively against the aggressor.

defined.source: Russian Orthodox Church, Basis of the Social Concept, section IX.3 (2000)
defined.author: Russian Orthodox
defined.quote: The death penalty as a special punishment was recognised in the Old Testament. There are no indications to the need to abolish it in the New Testament or in the Tradition or in the historical legacy of the Orthodox Church either.

defined.source: Russian Orthodox Church, Basis of the Social Concept, section IX.3 (2000)
defined.author: Russian Orthodox
defined.quote: Keeping in mind that mercy toward a fallen man is always more preferable than revenge, the Church welcomes these steps by state authorities. At the same time, she believes that the decision to abolish or not to apply death penalty should be made by society freely, considering the rate of crime and the state of law-enforcement and judiciary, and even more so, the need to protect the life of its well-intentioned members.

positions.statement: The civil authority may justly put a guilty person to death for a grave crime. A Christian may hold that office. The church does not carry the sentence out, and it may ask the judge for mercy.
positions.mark: The passage says the civil authority may justly put a criminal to death, or that this is not murder, or that the ruler's sword includes putting the guilty to death.
positions.first_defined: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, on homicide (1271); Luther, Large Catechism, Fifth Commandment (1529); Catechism of the Council of Trent, on the Fifth Commandment (1566); Thirty-Nine Articles (1571); Westminster Larger Catechism (1648); John Paul II, Evangelium Vitae (1995); Catechism of the Catholic Church, before the revision (1997); Russian Orthodox Church, Basis of the Social Concept (2000)

first_states.author: Cyril of Alexandria
first_states.text: Cyril: And indeed he fines the one murdering with death, and by bringings-on of equals he reins back the unbridled boldness, and punishes the no-longer-bearable anger with an unbearable judgment and with evils going unto an end, proving very well beforehand the aim of the doer; and if the wronged should be willing, he takes away the pity. And he does not allow mutual-love to be unseemly, being crumbled not in season, and upon what least must, somehow being dragged down unto the softer. For he said thus: ‘And if someone should set upon the neighbor to kill him by deceit, and he should flee, from my altar you will take him, to put him to death.’ (Exodus 21:14) And if the suffering of the one forced advances for the striker only as far as being weak; he measures out the judgment, and commands the damage to become as far as money. For he said thus again: ‘And if two men should revile, and so

lawful-sword.quote: And if someone should set upon the neighbor to kill him by deceit, and he should flee, from my altar you will take him, to put him to death.
lawful-sword.audited: Cyril, On Adoration 1.24, in his own voice: the lawgiver 'fines the one murdering with death, and by bringings-on of equals he reins back the unbridled boldness, and punishes the no-longer-bearable anger with an unbearable judgment,' quoting Exodus 21:14 - 'from my altar you will take him, to put him to death.' The death penalty for murder is expounded as just retribution that restrains wickedness.

inadmissible.quote: he fines the one murdering with death
inadmissible.audited: Death for murder is presented as a divinely appointed, just penalty - a 'judgment' that restrains boldness - which contradicts the claim that the death penalty itself is inadmissible or unjust.

positions.name: Christians do not bear the sword

defined.source: Athenagoras, A Plea for the Christians, chapter 35 (c. 177)
defined.author: Athenagoras
defined.quote: For when they know that we cannot endure even to see a man put to death, though justly; who of them can accuse us of murder or cannibalism?

defined.source: Athenagoras, A Plea for the Christians, chapter 35 (c. 177)
defined.author: Athenagoras
defined.quote: But we, deeming that to see a man put to death is much the same as killing him, have abjured such spectacles. How, then, when we do not even look on, lest we should contract guilt and pollution, can we put people to death?

defined.source: Tertullian, On the Crown, chapter 11 (c. 211)
defined.author: Tertullian
defined.quote: Shall it be held lawful to make an occupation of the sword, when the Lord proclaims that he who uses the sword shall perish by the sword? And shall the son of peace take part in the battle when it does not become him even to sue at law? And shall he apply the chain, and the prison, and the torture, and the punishment, who is not the avenger even of his own wrongs?

defined.source: Schleitheim Confession, Article VI (24 February 1527)
defined.author: Schleitheim
defined.quote: The sword is ordained of God outside the perfection of Christ. It punishes and puts to death the wicked, and guards and protects the good. In the Law the sword was ordained for the punishment of the wicked and for their death, and the same (sword) is (now) ordained to be used by the worldly magistrates. In the perfection of Christ, however, only the ban is used for a warning and for the excommunication of the one who has sinned, without putting the flesh to death.

defined.source: Schleitheim Confession, Article VI (24 February 1527)
defined.author: Schleitheim
defined.quote: Finally it will be observed that it is not appropriate for a Christian to serve as a magistrate because of these points: The government magistracy is according to the flesh, but the Christian's is according to the Spirit.

positions.statement: The worldly magistrate may use the sword, including death. A Christian may not pronounce, demand, or carry out a death sentence, and may not serve as a magistrate or soldier who sheds blood. This does not say the penalty is unjust for the civil authority.
positions.mark: The passage says a believer may not pronounce, demand, or carry out a death sentence, or may not serve as a magistrate or soldier who sheds blood, without saying the penalty is unjust for the worldly authority.
positions.first_defined: Schleitheim Confession (1527)

positions.name: The death penalty is inadmissible

defined.source: Lactantius, Divine Institutes, book 6, chapter 20 (c. 313)
defined.author: Lactantius
defined.quote: For when God forbids us to kill, He not only prohibits us from open violence, which is not even allowed by the public laws, but He warns us against the commission of those things which are esteemed lawful among men. Thus it will be neither lawful for a just man to engage in warfare, since his warfare is justice itself, nor to accuse any one of a capital charge, because it makes no difference whether you put a man to death by word, or rather by the sword, since it is the act of putting to death itself which is prohibited. Therefore, with regard to this precept of God, there ought to be no exception at all; but that it is always unlawful to put to death a man, whom God willed to be a sacred animal.

defined.source: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective, Article 22 (1995)
defined.author: Mennonite
defined.quote: Led by the Spirit, and beginning in the church, we witness to all people that violence is not the will of God. We witness against all forms of violence, including war among nations, hostility among races and classes, abuse of children and women, violence between men and women, abortion, and capital punishment.

defined.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church 2267, revised text. Pope Francis approved it on 11 May 2018; the rescript is dated 1 August 2018
defined.author: Catechism
defined.quote: Recourse to the death penalty on the part of legitimate authority, following a fair trial, was long considered an appropriate response to the gravity of certain crimes and an acceptable, albeit extreme, means of safeguarding the common good. Today, however, there is an increasing awareness that the dignity of the person is not lost even after the commission of very serious crimes. In addition, a new understanding has emerged of the significance of penal sanctions imposed by the state. Lastly, more effective systems of detention have been developed, which ensure the due protection of citizens but, at the same time, do not definitively deprive the guilty of the possibility of redemption. Consequently, the Church teaches, in the light of the Gospel, that “the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person”, and she works with determination for its abolition worldwide.

defined.source: Pope Leo XIV, post of 10 October 2026, as quoted by Vatican News
defined.author: Leo XIV
defined.quote: The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person. The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.

positions.statement: The death penalty itself is inadmissible. The church works for its abolition. This is a judgment on the penalty, not only a rule that Christians decline the office.
positions.mark: The passage says the death penalty itself is inadmissible, unjust, or to be abolished, not only that Christians decline the office.
positions.first_defined: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995); Catechism of the Catholic Church, revised text (2018); Pope Leo XIV, 10 October 2026

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: The most excellent emperors had just staged a largesse; crowned soldiers were being discharged from camp. A certain soldier of God stood there, more steadfast than the rest of the brothers, men who had presumed they could serve two masters — he alone, bareheaded, with a laurel wreath idle in his hand. By now the Christians' discipline was notorious. Soon individuals began singling him out, mocking him from a distance, sneering up close. A murmur reached the tribune, and the man had already stepped forward in ranks. The tribune demanded at once, "Why do you look so different?" He denied that what the others did was permitted to him; pressed for a reason, he answered, "I am a Christian." O glorious soldier in God! From then on votes were cast, the case escalated, and the defendant was hauled before the prefects. There he accepted the harshest penalties, seeking discharge; he cast off the s

christians-do-not-wield.quote: he denied that what the others did was permitted to him

passages.author: Tertullian
passages.text: Before I take up the question of the military crown itself, I first have to investigate whether military service is compatible with Christianity at all. What is the point of debating the incidental details when the fault lies in the very foundation? Do we really think a human oath can override a divine one, or that we can serve another lord after Christ? Are we allowed to forsake father, mother, and every neighbor—people the Law commands us to honor and love after God, people the Gospel also honored without ranking them above Christ alone? Is it permitted to live by the sword when the Lord declared that whoever lives by the sword dies by the sword (Matthew 26:52)? Will the son of peace engage in battle when quarreling is unfitting for him? Will he administer chains, prison, torture, and execution when he is not an avenger of his own wrongs? passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Cyril: God honors the matter with death, and writes it among the last evils. And he said thus in Leviticus: ‘And a soul which should follow after ventriloquists or enchanters, so as to whore after them, I will set my face upon that soul, and I will destroy it from its people; and you will be holy, because I am holy—Lord your God.’ (Leviticus 20:6) And after other things again: ‘And a man or woman who should become among them a ventriloquist or enchanter, with death let them be put to death, and with stones stone them; they are liable.’ (Leviticus 20:27) For first he refuses that any must love to follow the buffoon star-prophecies, or then necromancies, saying the matter is as far as possible from holy-fitting citizenship, and altogether unfitting for those clinging to God; and he defines death of the second, and says even they themselves are liable; not allowing pity to be allotted from

lawful-sword.quote: ‘And a man or woman who should become among them a ventriloquist or enchanter, with death let them be put to death…’ (Leviticus 20:27)
lawful-sword.audited: Cyril, On Adoration 1.12, does not merely quote Leviticus 20:27 - he expounds it in his own voice: God 'honors the matter with death... he defines death... not allowing pity to be allotted from our side to those who have already been driven unto this baseness,' and 'God would not have fixed so bitter a justice' without reason. The death sentence in the law is affirmed as justice, and pity for the offenders is refused.

inadmissible.quote: ‘And a man or woman who should become among them a ventriloquist or enchanter, with death let them be put to death, and with stones stone them; they are liable.’ (Leviticus 20:27)
inadmissible.audited: The same exposition affirms the Levitical death sentence as God's 'bitter justice' and bars pity for the offenders - the penalty is presented as just, not as inadmissible or to be abolished.
